4.10 Summary
This chapter emphasized that social issues are only starting points for research,
not research problems in themselves. Statements such as “the education
system is bad” reflect public concern, but they lack the precision required for
academic inquiry. To become researchable, such concerns must be carefully
refined and framed within a clear academic structure.
An effective research problem must be specific, identifying who is affected,

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
where the issue occurs, and what aspect is being examined. For example,
instead of broadly criticizing education quality, a well-defined problem
focuses on Grade 3 reading fluency in rural government schools of Sindh. It
must also be evidence-based, drawing on assessment data, policy reports, or
prior studies rather than personal opinion. Equally important is
contextualization—recognizing local realities such as language medium,
school type, and resource constraints in Pakistan.
Clearly articulated research problems form the foundation of quality research.
When the problem is precise, research objectives become focused,
methodological choices become logical, and conclusions become defensible.
In the Pakistani academic context, where students often struggle with overly
broad or opinion-driven topics, learning to clearly identify and define the
research problem is a critical step toward producing credible and meaningful
academic work.
Chapter 5: Purpose, Objectives & Research Questions
Chapter overview
This chapter plays a critical role in thesis and research writing because it
establishes the direction, focus, and boundaries of the entire study. A wellwritten section on purpose, objectives, and research questions helps readers,
supervisors, and examiners immediately understand what the study intends to
do, why it is being conducted, and how it will be carried out. If this section is
unclear or weak, the rest of the thesis—no matter how well written—often
appears unfocused and poorly designed.
Many Pakistani students struggle with this part of the thesis due to conceptual
confusion rather than language difficulty. A common problem is mixing the
research aim, objectives, and research questions, treating them as
interchangeable statements. Another frequent issue is writing objectives that
are too broad, vague, or unrealistic, such as attempting to study an entire
province or country without adequate time, data access, or resources. These
weaknesses make the study difficult to implement and weaken its academic
credibility.
Examiners and supervisors pay close attention to this section because it
reflects the researcher’s clarity of thinking and methodological readiness.
They assess whether the purpose is clearly stated, whether the objectives are
specific and measurable, and whether the research questions logically flow
from the objectives. Poor alignment or unrealistic objectives often lead to
requests for revision or, in severe cases, rejection of the proposal.
Learning outcome
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to clearly
• Understand the difference between purpose, objectives, and research
questions
• Write clear, measurable, and context-appropriate objectives
• Align objectives with research questions
5.1 Understanding the Research Purpose
5.1.1 What Is the Research Purpose?
The research purpose, often referred to as the aim of the study, describes the
overall intention or main goal of the research. It answers the fundamental
question: What does this study seek to achieve? The purpose provides a clear
direction for the research and serves as a foundation upon which objectives,
research questions, methodology, and analysis are built.
A well-written research purpose is broad yet focused. It should be broad
enough to capture the overall scope of the study but focused enough to avoid
ambiguity. Importantly, the research purpose states what the study intends to
achieve, not how it will be conducted or what tools will be used. In academic
writing, the research purpose is usually expressed in one or two concise
sentences, allowing readers and examiners to quickly grasp the central focus
of the study.
For example, instead of describing multiple activities, a clear purpose
highlights the main direction of inquiry and sets realistic boundaries for the
research.
5.1.2 Language Used to Write Research Purpose
The language of the research purpose is formal, precise, and objective. Certain
academic verbs are commonly used because they clearly indicate the nature of
inquiry. These include verbs such as to examine, to explore, to investigate, and
to assess. Each of these verbs signals a thoughtful and analytical approach
rather than a descriptive or casual one.
Tense usage is also important. When writing a thesis or research proposal, the
research purpose is typically written in the present tense, as the study is
ongoing. For example, “The purpose of this study is to examine...”. In
contrast, when reporting on completed research, such as in a journal article or
final report, the past tense is used, for example, “The purpose of this study
was to examine...”. Correct tense usage reflects academic accuracy and
professionalism.
5.1.3 Common Mistakes by Pakistani Students
A frequent mistake made by Pakistani students is writing multiple research
aims instead of a single, unified purpose. This often results in a lack of focus
and creates confusion about the true direction of the study. Another common
issue is the use of vague and weak verbs, such as “to study,” “to see,” or “to
understand,” without clearly explaining what will be studied, seen, or
understood.
For instance, a purpose statement such as “This study aims to understand

education in Pakistan” is too broad and unclear. It does not specify the level
of education, the issue being examined, or the context. Such statements
weaken the academic strength of the research and often lead to negative
feedback from supervisors and examiners.
5.1.4 Local Examples of Research Purpose
In the education sector, a research purpose might focus on early grade
reading, such as examining the factors affecting reading fluency among Grade
3 students in government schools. Another common education-related purpose
could involve investigating the effectiveness of teacher professional
development programs in improving classroom teaching practices.
In management studies, research purposes often relate to organizational
issues. For example, a study may aim to assess the impact of employee
motivation on productivity in private sector organizations, or to examine
leadership styles adopted by managers in Pakistani organizations and their
influence on employee performance.
In the social sciences, research purposes are frequently linked to social
behavior and cultural norms. A study might aim to explore patterns of political
participation among urban youth in Pakistan, or to investigate gender norms
and their influence on girls’ education in rural communities. These examples
reflect realistic, context-specific purposes that are academically sound and
feasible within the Pakistani research environment.
5.2 Understanding Research Objectives
5.2.1 What Are Research Objectives?
Research objectives are the specific steps through which the overall research
purpose is achieved. While the research purpose provides a general direction,
objectives break this direction into clear, manageable, and measurable
components. In other words, objectives explain how the researcher intends to
accomplish the research purpose.
There is a direct relationship between purpose and objectives: one research
purpose usually leads to several research objectives. Each objective addresses
a particular aspect of the research problem and collectively, they help fulfill
the overall aim of the study.
5.2.2 Types of Research Objectives
Research objectives are commonly divided into general objectives and
specific objectives. The general objective restates the research purpose in a
slightly more focused manner, while specific objectives describe precise
actions that the researcher will take. Specific objectives are particularly
important because they guide data collection, analysis, and interpretation.
5.2.3 Writing Strong Research Objectives
Strong research objectives are written using clear action verbs that indicate
observable and measurable outcomes. Commonly used verbs include to
identify, to compare, to analyze, to measure, and to determine. These verbs
help clarify what the researcher will actually do during the study.
Weak verbs such as to know, to learn, or to understand should be avoided
because they are difficult to measure and do not clearly indicate research
activity. Objectives written with weak verbs often result in vague findings and
weak conclusions.
5.2.4 SMART Objectives
To ensure quality and feasibility, research objectives should follow the
SMART framework, adapted to the Pakistani context. Objectives should be
specific, clearly defining what is being studied. They must be measurable,
meaning that data can realistically be collected through surveys, interviews,
observations, or document analysis. Objectives should also be achievable,
considering limitations such as time, access, and resources. They must be
relevant to local issues and academic discipline, and finally, they should be
time-bound, ensuring completion within the duration of the thesis or research
project.
This approach helps students avoid overly ambitious objectives that are
difficult to implement in real research settings in Pakistan.
5.2.5 Local Examples of Research Objectives
In education research, objectives may include identifying classroom teaching
practices used by primary school teachers, or measuring improvements in
students’ reading comprehension after a specific intervention.
In management research, objectives often focus on analyzing organizational
performance indicators or determining levels of employee satisfaction in
public or private sector organizations.
In social sciences, research objectives may involve examining patterns of
social behavior among youth or exploring community perceptions regarding
social issues such as education, health, or gender roles. These examples
demonstrate how well-defined objectives translate the research purpose into
practical and achievable research actions.
5.3 Understanding Research Questions
Research questions are the core drivers of any academic study. While the
research purpose explains what the study intends to achieve and the objectives
outline the steps to achieve it, research questions clearly state what the
researcher wants to find out. In simple terms, research questions translate
objectives into answerable inquiries that guide data collection, analysis, and
interpretation.
5.3.1 What Are Research Questions?
Research questions are specific, focused questions that the study seeks to
answer through systematic investigation. Their primary purpose is to provide
direction and clarity to the research process. They help the researcher decide
what data to collect, from whom, and using which methods.
A common mistake among Pakistani students is confusing objectives with
research questions. Objectives are written as action statements (for example,
to identify, to examine, to analyze), whereas research questions are written as
direct questions. While an objective might state the intention to examine a

text:
phenomenon, the research question asks how, what, or why that phenomenon
occurs.
Research questions play a crucial role in guiding data collection. For instance,
a clearly worded question determines whether a researcher needs surveys,
interviews, classroom observations, or document analysis. Poorly framed
research questions often lead to irrelevant data and weak findings.
5.3.2 Characteristics of Good Research Questions
Effective research questions share three key characteristics. First, they are
clear and focused, avoiding vague or overly broad wording. A question should
address one issue at a time and clearly indicate the scope of the study.
Second, research questions must be answerable through research. This means
that data can realistically be collected within the available time, resources, and
institutional access. Questions that require national-level data or long-term
tracking are often unrealistic for student research in Pakistan.
Third, research questions must be aligned with the research objectives. Each
question should directly correspond to at least one objective. Misalignment
between objectives and questions is one of the most common reasons
supervisors ask students to revise their proposals.
5.3.3 Types of Research Questions
Research questions can take different forms depending on the purpose of the
study.
Descriptive research questions aim to describe a situation, condition, or
phenomenon as it exists. These are common in baseline studies and surveys.
Comparative research questions focus on identifying differences or
similarities between groups, settings, or time periods.
Exploratory research questions are used when little is known about a topic,
especially in new or under-researched contexts within Pakistan.
Explanatory research questions attempt to explain relationships, causes, or
effects between variables.
Understanding the type of question helps the researcher select appropriate
research methods and analytical approaches.
5.3.4 Language Patterns for Research Questions
Academic research questions commonly follow recognizable language
patterns. For example:
•
“What is...?” is often used for descriptive studies.
•
“To what extent...?” is used to measure degree or level.
•
“How does...?” explores processes or relationships.
•
“What factors influence...?” identifies causes or contributing
elements.
Using these patterns helps ensure that research questions are clear, formal, and
academically appropriate.
5.3.5 Local Examples of Research Questions
In education, research questions may focus on classroom practices or learning
outcomes. For example:
•
What teaching strategies are commonly used by primary school
teachers in government schools?
•
To what extent do socioeconomic factors contribute to student
achievement gaps in urban and rural schools?
In management studies, research questions often examine organizational
behavior or leadership:
•
What factors influence employee motivation in small and medium
enterprises in Pakistan?
•
How does leadership style affect job satisfaction in private sector
organizations?
In the social sciences, research questions frequently explore social behavior
and cultural dynamics:
•
How does social media influence political awareness among university
students?
•
What cultural attitudes shape gender roles in rural communities?
These examples demonstrate how research questions can be grounded in local
realities while maintaining academic rigor.
5.4 Aligning Purpose, Objectives, and Research Questions
Alignment between the research purpose, objectives, and research questions
is essential for producing a coherent and credible study. Examiners and
supervisors closely examine this alignment because it reflects the researcher’s
ability to design a logically structured investigation.
5.4.1 Why Alignment Is Critical
From an examiner’s perspective, alignment ensures that the study is internally
consistent. The purpose should clearly state the overall intent of the research,
the objectives should break that intent into achievable components, and the
research questions should directly emerge from those objectives.
A lack of alignment often results in confusion, weak analysis, and irrelevant
findings. When objectives and questions do not match, the research appears
poorly planned, even if the topic itself is important.
5.4.2 Alignment Mapping
A useful way to ensure alignment is to follow a simple structure: one research
purpose leads to several objectives, and each objective leads to one or more
research questions. This mapping helps avoid redundancy and prevents the
inclusion of questions that are not directly linked to the study’s goals.
Students should carefully review their work to ensure that:
•
No objective exists without a corresponding research question
•
No research question falls outside the stated objectives
5.4.3 Sample Alignment Tables
In an education study, the research purpose may be to examine teaching
practices in primary schools. The objectives might include identifying
commonly used strategies and assessing their effectiveness, while the research
questions would ask what strategies are used and how they influence student
learning.
In a management study, a purpose such as assessing employee motivation
would lead to objectives related to identifying motivational factors and
analyzing leadership roles, with research questions directly addressing those
areas.
In social sciences research, a purpose focused on understanding cultural
attitudes would be supported by objectives examining beliefs and practices,
with research questions exploring how and why those attitudes are formed.

Through clear alignment, the research becomes easier to implement, easier to
evaluate, and more persuasive to examiners and supervisors.
5.5 Common Errors and How to Fix Them (Pakistani Context)
This section addresses the most frequent weaknesses observed in research
proposals and theses submitted by Pakistani students. These errors are not
limited to language proficiency; rather, they stem from unclear research
thinking, limited exposure to research design, and unrealistic planning.
Understanding these issues—and learning how to correct them—significantly
improves the quality and feasibility of a study.
5.5.1 Frequent Errors
One of the most common mistakes is writing objectives that simply repeat the
research purpose. Instead of breaking the purpose into clear, actionable steps,
students often restate the aim using similar wording. For example, if the
purpose is “to examine teachers’ professional development practices,” an
objective such as “to examine teachers’ professional development” adds no
new direction and fails to guide data collection.
Another frequent problem is misalignment between research objectives and
research questions. In many theses, objectives focus on one aspect of the study,
while the research questions explore something else entirely. For instance, a
student may write an objective related to teaching methods but frame research
questions about student motivation. Such mismatches confuse examiners and
indicate weak research design.
A particularly serious issue in the Pakistani context is the formulation of
unrealistic objectives. Students often propose nationwide surveys, multiprovince comparisons, or large-scale institutional studies without having the
time, funding, or access required to carry them out. For example, an MPhil
student planning to survey “all public universities in Pakistan” within six
months is unlikely to complete the study successfully. Examiners view such
objectives as impractical and poorly planned.
5.5.2 Improved Versions (Before–After Examples)
Many weak objectives can be significantly improved by making them specific,
measurable, and contextually grounded.
A weak objective such as “To study the education system in Pakistan” does
not indicate what will be studied, how it will be studied, or where the study
will take place. A stronger version would narrow the focus and clarify the
action, for example: “To analyze the implementation of early grade reading
strategies in selected government primary schools in District Hyderabad.”
The revised objective is clearly defined, measurable, and realistic.
Similarly, unclear research questions often use vague language. A question
such as “What is the role of teachers in education?” is too broad to be
answered through research. A more precise research question would be: “How
do Grade 3 teachers in public schools implement reading instruction
strategies during classroom lessons?” This version clearly identifies the
population, context, and focus of inquiry.
By revising objectives and questions in this way, students move from general
statements to researchable inquiries, which strengthens the entire study.
5.6 Practical Writing Checklist
Before finalizing the purpose, objectives, and research questions, students
should use a practical checklist to evaluate the quality and feasibility of their
work. This step is especially important in the Pakistani academic environment,
where access and time limitations are common.
5.6.1 Objective Quality Checklist
Each research objective should be carefully reviewed to ensure academic
strength and clarity. Students should ask whether the objective is measurable,
meaning that data can realistically be collected to address it. An objective that
cannot be supported by evidence weakens the study.
It is equally important to consider whether relevant data is available in
Pakistan. Some objectives require datasets, institutional records, or access to
participants that may not exist or may be difficult to obtain. Students must also
ensure that the scope of the objective is manageable, given their degree level,
timeline, and available resources.
Finally, every objective should be clearly aligned with the research purpose.
If an objective does not directly contribute to achieving the stated purpose, it
should be revised or removed.
5.6.2 Context Realism Checklist
Beyond academic quality, objectives and research questions must be realistic
within the Pakistani context. Students should consider whether data can be
collected through Pakistani institutions such as schools, universities, NGOs,
or government departments, and whether formal permission is likely to be
granted.
Practical constraints such as time limitations, academic schedules, and
fieldwork duration must be taken into account. Ethical considerations,
including informed consent and institutional approval, are also essential and
should be planned in advance.
Finally, students should assess whether the sample size is realistic and
accessible. A smaller, well-defined sample often produces more reliable
results than an overly ambitious but poorly executed study.
By identifying common errors, learning how to correct them, and applying
practical checklists, students can ensure that their research objectives and
questions are clear, feasible, and academically sound. This careful planning
not only improves thesis quality but also increases the likelihood of timely and
successful completion.
5.7 Practice Exercises
This section provides guided practice to help students apply the concepts

discussed in this chapter. The exercises are designed around realistic Pakistani
research contexts so that students can immediately relate theory to practice
and avoid common mistakes observed in thesis proposals.
Exercise 1: Identify the Problem
In this exercise, students are given sample research purposes and asked to
critically analyze them to identify weaknesses. The focus is on recognizing
problems such as vagueness, lack of focus, unrealistic scope, or unclear
outcomes.
For example, a sample purpose such as “The purpose of this study is to study
the education system of Pakistan” appears broad and ambitious but lacks
clarity. Students are guided to ask key questions: What level of education?
Which region? What specific aspect of the system? Through this analysis,
students learn that a strong research purpose must be focused, context-specific,
and achievable.
Another example from management studies might include a purpose like
“This study aims to understand employee motivation in organizations”.
Students identify that the purpose does not specify the type of organization,
sector, or method of understanding motivation, making it difficult to design
the study.
Exercise 2: Rewrite Objectives
This exercise helps students transform vague or weak objectives into SMART
(Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound) objectives
suitable for research in Pakistan.
Students begin with poorly written objectives such as “To understand the
problems faced by teachers”. They are then guided to refine the objective by
specifying the context, participants, and method. For instance, the revised
objective might focus on identifying specific instructional challenges faced by
primary school teachers in public schools within a selected district.
Management students work with examples like “To improve employee
performance”, learning to rewrite this into a measurable objective that
examines particular performance indicators within a defined organizational
setting.
Through this exercise, students understand that objectives must clearly
indicate what will be studied, how it will be measured, and within what
context, ensuring feasibility and academic rigor.
Exercise 3: Match Objectives with Research Questions
In this alignment exercise, students are provided with sets of research
objectives and a list of possible research questions. Their task is to match each
objective with the most appropriate research question.
For example, an education-related objective focusing on identifying reading
challenges among Grade 3 students must align with a question that explores
the nature or extent of those challenges, rather than one that examines teacher
attitudes. Similarly, a social sciences objective related to community
perceptions must be paired with a question that captures opinions or
experiences, not statistical outcomes.
By working through local research scenarios, students learn that every
research question should directly serve an objective, and that misalignment
weakens the coherence of the study. This exercise reinforces logical thinking
and strengthens research design skills.
5.8 Chapter Summary
This chapter emphasized the central role of research purpose, objectives, and
research questions in shaping a successful thesis or research study. It
highlighted the importance of clearly distinguishing between these
components and ensuring that each one serves a distinct but connected
function within the research framework.
Students were reminded that clear, measurable, and context-appropriate
objectives form the foundation of a strong thesis. When objectives are well
written and properly aligned with research questions, the entire research
process—from data collection to analysis—becomes more focused and
manageable.
The next chapter builds on this foundation by addressing one of the most
challenging areas for Pakistani students: writing the literature review without
copy-paste. It will guide students on how to engage with existing research
critically, paraphrase effectively, and integrate sources ethically and
confidently into their academic writing.
PART III — Literature Review Without Copy-Paste
This part of the book focuses on helping Pakistani students move away from
copy-paste practices and develop a confident academic voice in their literature
reviews. It explains how to read, understand, paraphrase, and synthesize
sources rather than reproducing them. Emphasis is placed on using literature
to support arguments, not to decorate writing with quotations. Through
contextual Pakistani examples, this section guides students to balance
international research with credible local studies, avoid plagiarism driven by
fear of English, and write literature reviews that demonstrate understanding,
critical thinking, and relevance to local realities.
Chapter 6: Using Sources Correctly: From Copy-Paste to
Confident Academic Voice
Chapter Overview
One of the most persistent challenges faced by university students in Pakistan
is the effective and ethical use of academic sources. Despite being aware of
plagiarism policies and academic integrity rules, many students continue to
struggle with integrating sources into their writing in a meaningful and
original way. This difficulty does not stem from dishonesty alone; rather, it
reflects a lack of academic writing skills, limited exposure to research-based
writing, and fear of using English independently.
In Pakistani higher education, students often transition from an examinationoriented system—where memorization is rewarded—to a university
environment that expects analysis, synthesis, and original academic voice.

Without explicit instruction in how to paraphrase, summarize, and synthesize
research, students frequently resort to copying text from published sources,
particularly from foreign journals, believing that “good English” must be
borrowed rather than constructed.
This chapter addresses source misuse not as a moral failure, but as a skills gap
that can be systematically addressed. By focusing on practical strategies,
locally relevant examples, and step-by-step guidance, the chapter aims to build
students’ confidence in using sources responsibly while maintaining their own
academic voice.

Key Challenges Faced by Pakistani Students
The chapter is grounded in common realities of Pakistani classrooms and

•
Fear of writing in English

•
Examination culture and memorization

•
Limited training in paraphrasing and synthesis

•
Pressure to “sound academic”

By acknowledging these challenges, the chapter creates a supportive

Learning Outcomes
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to:
•
Understand what “using sources correctly” means in academic writing
•
Distinguish between quoting, paraphrasing, and summarizing
•
Recognize common forms of plagiarism in the Pakistani academic

•

•

•
Maintain their own academic voice while engaging with published

6.1 What “Using Sources Correctly” Really Means
For many Pakistani university students, the phrase “use sources correctly” is
confusing and intimidating. Students often assume that good academic writing
means copying sentences from books and journal articles written by experts—
especially foreign authors—and placing them into their own assignments.
Others believe that the more citations they add, the more “academic” their
work will appear. Both assumptions are incorrect.
Using sources correctly does not mean copying sentences, even if the source
is well-written or authoritative. Copying language, even with minor word
changes, does not demonstrate understanding; it only shows dependence.
Similarly, using sources does not mean filling pages with citations. A literature
review or research chapter is not judged by how many authors are mentioned,
but by how clearly the writer uses those sources to build an argument.
In academic writing, using sources means supporting your own argument.
Your ideas, questions, and interpretations should lead the discussion. Sources
exist to strengthen what you are saying, not to replace your voice.
A useful way to understand this is through a simple visual concept:
Your voice is the main road.
Sources are signboards, not drivers.
The main road represents your research focus—your topic, your research
questions, and your argument. Sources act like signboards along the road.
They point, guide, confirm direction, or warn of alternative paths, but they do
not control where the road goes. When sources begin to “drive” the text—
when paragraphs are built entirely from other people’s words—the writer loses
control of the argument.
There are three correct academic purposes for using sources.
1. To support your claim
The most common and legitimate use of sources is to support an idea you have
already
introduced.
For example, if a student writes:
“Teacher feedback plays a critical role in improving students’ reading skills
in early grades.”
A source may then be used to support this claim:
“This view is supported by studies conducted in both international and
Pakistani contexts, which highlight feedback as a key instructional practice.”
Here, the idea belongs to the student; the source strengthens it.
2. To compare ideas
Sources are also used to show how different researchers view the same issue.
For example:
“While international studies emphasize phonics-based instruction, local
research in Pakistan suggests that teacher capacity and classroom resources
remain equally important factors.”
This shows analytical thinking, not copying.

3. To challenge or extend previous research
At higher academic levels, students are expected not only to accept previous
research but also to question or extend it.
For example:
“Although previous studies highlight the effectiveness of scripted lesson plans,
findings from rural Sindh indicate that rigid scripts may limit teacher
responsiveness in multigrade classrooms.”
In this case, the student is engaging with research critically rather than
reproducing it.
6.2 Understanding Plagiarism in the Pakistani Context
Plagiarism is often presented as an ethical problem, but in the Pakistani
academic context, it is more accurately understood as a skill and confidence
problem. Many students plagiarize not because they intend to cheat, but
because they are unsure how to express academic ideas in English.
Common Local Forms of Plagiarism
Several patterns of plagiarism are repeatedly observed in Pakistani
universities:
•
Copy-paste with minor word
changes, such as replacing a
few words with synonyms while
keeping the original sentence
structure.
•
Heavy
quotation
without

paragraphs are quoted from
books or articles but not
discussed or interpreted.
•
Translating from Urdu and copying English sources, where
students first understand an idea in Urdu but then copy English text
because they feel unable to express it themselves.
•
Reusing seniors’ theses or assignments, often shared informally
within departments.

Myth: Good English means
copying good English.
✔ Reality: Good academic
English means clear thinking,
simple structure, and honest
engagement with sources.
These practices are widespread, but they weaken academic development and
place students at serious risk of academic penalties.
Why Plagiarism Happens
Understanding why plagiarism occurs is essential for overcoming it.
One major reason is the fear of grammar mistakes. Many students believe that
their English is “not good enough” for academic writing, so they rely on
published text that appears perfect. Another reason is the belief that foreign
English is automatically better. Students often feel that citing Western authors
in their original wording will make their work appear more scholarly.
In some cases, supervisory practices unintentionally reinforce plagiarism.
When feedback focuses heavily on the number of citations rather than the
quality of thinking, students learn to prioritize referencing over understanding.
Strong academic writing does not require complex vocabulary or long
sentences. It requires clarity, confidence, and practice. Learning to use sources
correctly is not about sounding foreign or sophisticated—it is about
developing your own academic voice and using evidence responsibly to
support it.
6.3 Types of Source Use (With Clear Distinction)
One of the most common problems in academic writing among Pakistani
students is the confusion between quoting, paraphrasing, and summarizing.
Many students believe that all three mean “using someone else’s work,” so
they use them interchangeably. In reality, each serves a different academic
purpose, and using the wrong type at the wrong place often weakens the
quality of writing and increases the risk of plagiarism.
Understanding these distinctions is essential for developing an independent
academic voice.
6.3.1 Quoting (When and When NOT to Use)
Quoting means using the exact words of another author, enclosed in quotation
marks and properly cited. While quoting is allowed in academic writing, it
should be used sparingly and strategically.
In Pakistani universities, students often overuse quotations because they fear
making grammatical mistakes or believe that foreign authors’ English is
always superior. However, excessive quoting usually signals lack of
understanding, not academic strength.
When Quoting Is Acceptable
Quoting is appropriate when:
•
The exact wording is important and cannot be changed without losing
meaning.
•
You are citing definitions, laws, policies, or official statements.
•
The source carries legal or authoritative weight, such as national
education policies or official government documents.
Example (acceptable use):
When defining a key concept:
According to the National Education Policy (2017), “literacy refers to the
ability to read, write, and comprehend age-appropriate texts.”
Here, changing the wording could distort the official meaning, so quoting is
justified.
When Quoting Is Weak or Inappropriate
Quoting becomes weak when:
•
Large blocks of text are copied from journals.
•
Quotes are used to replace explanation.
•
The literature review becomes a collection of quotations rather than an
analysis.
•
Quotes dominate the discussion section, where interpretation is
required.
This problem is especially visible in Pakistani theses where pages are filled
with quotations from foreign journals without any explanation of how they
relate to the local context.
Weak example (over-quoting):
“Reading fluency is defined as the ability to read text with speed, accuracy,
and
proper
expression”
(Smith,
2018,
p.
45).
“Fluency plays a crucial role in comprehension” (Johnson, 2019, p. 112).
“Without fluency, comprehension is compromised” (Brown, 2020, p. 78).
This paragraph contains quotations but no student voice.
Strong example (quote + explanation):
Reading fluency is commonly described as the ability to read with speed,

accuracy, and expression (Smith, 2018). This suggests that fluency is not
merely about speed but also about meaningful engagement with text. In the
Pakistani context, where early grade learners often struggle with decoding,
limited fluency may directly affect comprehension outcomes.
The strong example uses a short reference and then explains the idea in the
writer’s own words.
6.3.2 Paraphrasing (The Core Academic Skill)
Paraphrasing is the most important academic skill for university students. It
means expressing another author’s idea in your own words and sentence
structure, while keeping the original meaning intact.
True paraphrasing involves:
•
Changing the sentence structure
•
Using different vocabulary
•
Adjusting the emphasis, where appropriate
•
Maintaining the original meaning
Many Pakistani students believe paraphrasing means changing a few words
with synonyms. This is incorrect and still counts as plagiarism.
Common Paraphrasing Mistakes
The most frequent errors include:
•
Replacing words with synonyms while keeping the same sentence
structure
•
Keeping the original sentence order
•
Changing words but not understanding the idea
Incorrect paraphrase (common mistake):
Original:
“Teacher feedback plays a significant role in improving students’ reading
comprehension.”
Wrong paraphrase:
“Teacher response plays an important role in enhancing students’ reading
understanding.”
The structure and meaning remain almost identical.
The Golden Rule of Paraphrasing
If you can’t explain it in your own words, you don’t understand it yet.
Students should first understand the idea, not the sentence. Once the idea is
clear, writing becomes easier and safer.
Correct paraphrase:
Research indicates that students’ reading comprehension improves when
teachers provide timely and meaningful feedback during instruction.
Here, the structure and wording are different, but the idea remains the same.
6.3.3 Summarizing Multiple Sources
While paraphrasing focuses on one source, summarizing involves combining
multiple sources to show understanding of a broader research area. This skill
helps students move from description to synthesis, which is a key requirement
at the postgraduate level.
Purpose of Summarizing Multiple Sources
Summarizing multiple sources allows students to:
•
Demonstrate awareness of the research field
•
Identify patterns and trends
•
Avoid writing one paragraph per author
•
Show critical engagement with literature
This is particularly important in Pakistani theses, where students often write
literature reviews as a series of unrelated studies.
Example: Combining Studies on Reading Outcomes in Pakistan
Weak approach (source-by-source):
Khan (2018) studied reading outcomes in Punjab.
Ali (2019) examined reading levels in Sindh.
Ahmed (2020) focused on teacher training and literacy.
Strong summary (synthesized):
Several studies conducted across Punjab and Sindh highlight persistent
challenges in early grade reading outcomes, particularly in fluency and
comprehension (Khan, 2018; Ali, 2019). These findings are further supported
by Ahmed (2020), who emphasizes the role of teacher preparation in
addressing literacy gaps.
This approach shows understanding, not memorization.
6.4 Using Literature Review Language Correctly
Academic writing does not require complex or decorative English. Instead, it
relies on functional language that clearly shows how your work connects to
previous research. Many Pakistani students lose marks not because their ideas
are weak, but because they do not use appropriate literature review language.
This section introduces commonly accepted expressions inspired by English
for Thesis and Academic Writing, adapted for local use.
6.4.1 Referring to Previous Research
When discussing a body of research rather than a single study, writers use
general reference language.
Common functional expressions include:
•
“Previous studies indicate that...”
•
“Several researchers have reported...”
•
“Earlier research suggests...”
Local contextual example:
Previous studies conducted in Punjab and Sindh indicate persistent gaps in
early grade reading outcomes, particularly in rural and underserved areas.
This sentence signals that the claim is evidence-based, not personal opinion.
6.4.2 Referring to a Single Study
When highlighting one specific study, the goal is to focus on its key finding,
not its procedural details.
Purpose
•
To support a specific claim
•
To introduce evidence relevant to your argument
Example:
A study by the Sindh RSU (2021) reported that a significant proportion of
Grade 3 students were unable to read grade-level text with fluency.
The sentence clearly communicates what matters, without unnecessary
detail.
6.4.3 Referring to Researchers’ Ideas (Not Words)
Strong academic writing focuses on ideas, not sentences. This means students
should avoid copying language and instead engage with the arguments made
by researchers.
Focus
•
What the researcher claims, argues, or suggests
•
Not how beautifully it is written
Example:
Smith (2019) argues that teacher feedback plays a central role in improving
students’ learning outcomes.
Here, the emphasis is on the idea, not the original wording.
Closing Note for Students
Using sources correctly is not about impressing examiners with difficult
English. It is about thinking clearly, writing honestly, and engaging
confidently with existing knowledge—especially within the Pakistani context.
6.5 Valuing Local Research (Breaking the Foreign-Only Mindset)
One of the most persistent misconceptions among Pakistani university

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
students is the belief that only foreign research is valuable. As a result,
literature reviews often rely heavily on studies from the United States, the
United Kingdom, or Australia, while ignoring high-quality research
conducted within Pakistan. This “foreign-only mindset” weakens academic
writing because it removes the research from its real-world context.
Academic writing is strongest when theory is supported by evidence that
reflects the social, cultural, and institutional realities of the setting being
studied.
For Pakistani students, learning to value local research is not a lowering of
academic standards; rather, it is a move toward contextually meaningful
scholarship.
6.5.1 Why Local Studies Matter
Context Relevance
Local studies reflect the realities of Pakistani classrooms, communities,
institutions, and policies. Many international studies are conducted in
environments with stable infrastructure, low student–teacher ratios, strong
monitoring systems, and high levels of institutional support. These
conditions are often very different from those found in public-sector
institutions in Pakistan.
For example, a study conducted in Finland may recommend extensive use of
digital learning platforms to improve reading outcomes. However, in many
rural districts of Sindh or Balochistan, unreliable electricity, limited internet
access, and overcrowded classrooms make such recommendations
impractical. In contrast, a local study conducted in government schools of
Punjab or Sindh can highlight constraints such as multigrade teaching,
limited instructional time, and language diversity—factors that directly affect
learning outcomes.
Using local research allows students to demonstrate that they understand
their own context, which is a key expectation of academic research.
Policy Alignment
Local research is closely linked to national and provincial education policies,
development frameworks, and reform initiatives. In Pakistan, academic
research often informs or evaluates government programs related to
education, health, governance, and social protection. Referencing such
studies strengthens a thesis by showing alignment with national priorities.
For instance, research published in Higher Education Commission (HEC)–
recognized journals or evaluation reports produced by provincial education
departments directly relate to curriculum reforms, teacher professional
development, and assessment strategies. A literature review that includes
such sources demonstrates that the researcher is engaging with ongoing
policy debates rather than writing in isolation from the system.
Moreover, supervisors, examiners, and policymakers are more likely to value
research that connects academic inquiry with local policy implications.
Cultural and Systemic Realities
Culture, language, social norms, and institutional practices significantly
shape how policies and interventions function. Foreign studies often assume
cultural conditions that do not exist in Pakistan, such as high parental
literacy, strong school–home collaboration, or uniform language of
instruction.
For example, an international study may conclude that parental involvement
significantly improves student achievement. While this may be true, local
studies in Pakistan often show that parental engagement is influenced by
factors such as parents’ own education levels, socioeconomic constraints,
and language barriers. Without acknowledging these realities,
recommendations become unrealistic and ineffective.
Local research captures these nuances and helps students develop arguments
that are grounded in lived realities rather than idealized assumptions.
Why Foreign Solutions Often Fail Locally
Foreign solutions frequently fail in Pakistan not because they are incorrect,
but because they are transplanted without adaptation. When students rely
solely on international literature, they risk proposing recommendations that
ignore local capacity, resources, and institutional structures.
For example, performance-based teacher appraisal systems may work
effectively in countries with strong accountability frameworks and low
political interference. However, local research has shown that in Pakistan,
such systems often face resistance due to administrative constraints and lack
of implementation capacity. Without local evidence, students may
unknowingly propose solutions that are academically sound but practically
unworkable.
A strong literature review therefore balances international theory with local
evidence, ensuring that conclusions are both scholarly and realistic.
6.5.2 Examples of Acceptable Local Sources
Local research in Pakistan exists in many credible and academically
recognized forms. The following sources are widely accepted in university
research when used critically and appropriately:
•
HEC-recognized research journals, which publish peer-reviewed
studies across disciplines.
•
Punjab Education Foundation (PEF) reports, which provide
empirical evidence on school quality, teacher performance, and
student learning outcomes.
•
Sindh Reform Support Unit (RSU) assessments and evaluation
reports, particularly in areas related to early grade reading, teacher
training, and school monitoring.
•
Government white papers and policy documents, such as national
education policies, sector plans, and official reform frameworks.
•
University-led action research, including theses, dissertations, and
faculty-supervised studies conducted in local institutions.
When integrated thoughtfully, these sources strengthen academic arguments
by anchoring them in the Pakistani context.
Warning Box: Credible Local Research vs Opinion Sources
Not all local material qualifies as academic research. Students must learn to
distinguish between credible sources and opinion-based content.
Credible local research:
•
Clearly states methodology
•
Uses data (quantitative or qualitative)
•
Is published or issued by recognized institutions
•
Includes references and limitations
Non-academic or weak sources:
•
Personal blogs without evidence
•
Social media posts or opinion columns

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
•
News articles without research backing
•
Motivational or advocacy content lacking data
Using opinion blogs in place of research weakens academic credibility and
may lead to rejection or low evaluation scores. Students should use such
material only for background understanding, not as academic evidence.
Valuing local research is not about rejecting international scholarship; it is
about integrating global knowledge with local evidence. Pakistani students
who learn to use credible local studies alongside international literature
produce research that is not only academically sound but also socially
meaningful and practically relevant.
6.6 Combining International and Local Literature Effectively
One of the most common weaknesses in Pakistani students’ literature reviews
is over-reliance on international studies without meaningful connection to the
local context. Many students assume that citing foreign authors automatically
strengthens their work. In reality, academic writing becomes powerful only
when international theory is grounded in local evidence.
International studies are important because they provide theoretical
frameworks, tested models, and global perspectives. However, research
conducted in different countries operates under social, economic, linguistic,
and institutional conditions that often differ significantly from those in
Pakistan. Therefore, international literature should inform your thinking, not
replace local realities.
Local studies—such as reports by the Higher Education Commission (HEC),
Punjab Education Foundation, Sindh Reform Support Unit (RSU), and
Pakistani universities—offer contextual evidence. These sources reflect
ground realities such as classroom conditions, teacher preparation, resource
constraints, and policy implementation challenges. When international theory
and local evidence are combined, the literature review demonstrates both
academic depth and contextual relevance.
The Ideal Balance
A strong literature review maintains a balance between:
•
International theory – to explain what should work and why
•
Local evidence – to show what actually happens in Pakistan
This balance reassures the reader that the study is informed by global research
while remaining sensitive to local conditions.
Model Paragraph Structure
An effective paragraph that combines international and local literature
typically follows three steps:
1. Introduce an international concept or theory
2. Present local evidence related to the concept
3. Interpret the relationship in the Pakistani context
Illustrative Example
While international studies emphasize phonics-based instruction as a critical
component of early reading development, findings from Sindh RSU
assessments indicate that limited teacher capacity and inadequate classroom
support continue to hinder effective implementation. This suggests that
although phonics-based approaches are theoretically sound, their success in
the Pakistani context depends largely on sustained teacher training and
instructional support.
In this example:
•
The international concept (phonics-based instruction) provides
theoretical grounding.
•
The local evidence (Sindh RSU assessments) introduces contextual
reality.
•
The interpretation explains why results differ and what this means for
Pakistan.
This approach moves the student from simply reporting studies to thinking
academically.
6.7 From Source Description to Source Synthesis
Another frequent issue in student writing is the tendency to describe sources
one by one, often dedicating an entire paragraph to a single author. This results
in a descriptive literature review, where studies are listed but not connected.
Although such writing may contain many citations, it shows limited critical
engagement.
Weak Literature Review: One Author per Paragraph
In a weak literature review:
•
Each paragraph summarizes one study
•
Sources are isolated from each other
•
The writer’s voice is minimal
•
There is no clear argument
Descriptive Example
Smith (2018) studied reading strategies in primary schools and found that
phonics instruction improved reading accuracy. Johnson (2019) examined
teacher training programs and reported that professional development
improved classroom practices. Khan (2020) investigated literacy outcomes in
rural Pakistan and noted low student achievement levels.
This paragraph is not incorrect, but it is academically weak because the
studies are presented as separate pieces of information, with no relationship or
interpretation.
Strong Literature Review: Theme-Based Discussion
In a strong literature review:
•
Studies are grouped by themes
•
Multiple sources are discussed together
•
The writer evaluates similarities and differences
•
The paragraph supports a clear argument
Analytical Example
Research on early grade reading consistently highlights the importance of
instructional methods and teacher capacity. International studies emphasize
phonics-based instruction as an effective approach for improving reading
accuracy (Smith, 2018). Similarly, research on teacher professional
development suggests that well-structured training enhances instructional
quality (Johnson, 2019). However, evidence from rural Pakistan indicates that
despite awareness of effective strategies, limited teacher preparation and
resource constraints continue to affect student outcomes (Khan, 2020). These
findings suggest that instructional methods alone are insufficient unless
accompanied by sustained teacher support within the local context.
In this improved version:
•
Sources are integrated, not isolated
•
The paragraph follows a theme (instruction and teacher capacity)
•
Local and international studies are compared
•
The writer’s analytical voice is clear
Key Takeaway for Students
A literature review is not a list of who said what. It is a conversation between

text:
studies, guided by your research focus. When you shift from describing
sources to synthesizing them, you demonstrate true academic maturity and
reduce the temptation to copy text directly from sources.
Practical Tip Box
Before finalizing a paragraph, ask yourself:
•
Am I connecting studies or just listing them?
•
Have I explained why these studies matter together?
•
Is my voice visible in the paragraph?
6.8 Safe Paraphrasing: A Step-by-Step Method
For many Pakistani students, paraphrasing is the most frightening part of
academic writing. Students often say, “Sir, if I change the words, the meaning
may become wrong,” or “If I write in my own words, my English will sound
weak.” Because of this fear, students either copy sentences directly or change
only a few words, which still counts as plagiarism.
Paraphrasing, however, is not about showing advanced English. It is about
showing understanding. A well-paraphrased sentence may use simple English,
but it clearly reflects the idea of the original source in the student’s own
academic voice.
To make paraphrasing safe and manageable, this book introduces the 5-Step
Paraphrase Method, especially designed for Pakistani university students.
Step 1: Read and Understand the Source
The first step is reading for meaning, not for vocabulary. Students should ask:
•
What is the main idea?
•
What is the key finding or claim?
•
Why is this point important for my research?
Many students try to paraphrase while they are still confused about the content.
This almost always leads to copying.
Key rule:
If you cannot explain the idea in Urdu or simple English, you are not ready to
paraphrase it yet.
Step 2: Close the Source
After understanding the paragraph, close the book, article, or screen.
This step is critical. When the source remains open, students unconsciously
follow the same sentence structure and vocabulary. Closing the source forces
the brain to rely on understanding rather than memory of words.
Step 3: Write from Memory
Now, write the idea as if you are explaining it to a classmate.
Do not worry about grammar at this stage. Focus on:
•
Explaining the idea clearly
•
Using your natural sentence structure
•
Keeping the meaning accurate
This step helps students develop confidence in their own academic voice.
Step 4: Compare Meaning (Not Words)
After writing, open the source again and compare:
•
Is the meaning the same?
•
Have I added or removed anything important?
•
Are the sentence structures different?
Students should not compare word by word. Some similar academic words
(e.g., education, students, learning) are unavoidable and acceptable.
Step 5: Add the Citation
Even after paraphrasing, the idea still belongs to the original author.
Therefore:
•
Always add an in-text citation
•
Use the required referencing style (APA, etc.)
Important reminder:
Paraphrasing without citation is still plagiarism.
Example Walkthrough: From Source to Safe Paraphrase
Original Paragraph
“Teacher quality has been identified as one of the most significant factors
influencing student learning outcomes, particularly in low-resource
educational settings.”
Wrong Paraphrase
“Teacher quality is one of the most important factors that influence student
learning outcomes, especially in low-resource education systems.”
Why this is wrong:
•
Sentence structure is almost the same
•
Only a few words are replaced
•
Still too close to the original
Correct Paraphrase
“In schools with limited resources, students’ learning is strongly affected by
the skills and effectiveness of their teachers (Author, Year).”
Why this is correct:
•
Sentence structure is different
•
Focus is shifted to context
•
Meaning is preserved
•
Citation is included
6.9 Practice Section: Paraphrase Without Fear
This practice section is designed to build confidence gradually, starting from
simple sentences and moving toward combining sources.
Practice 1: Sentence-Level Paraphrasing
Original sentence:
“Several studies have shown that early reading skills are closely linked to later
academic success.”
Student task:
•
Close the sentence
•
Write the idea in your own words
Sample acceptable answer:
“Research indicates that children who develop reading skills at an early stage
are more likely to perform well in later grades.”
✔ Meaning preserved
✔ Structure changed
✔ Language simplified
Practice 2: Paragraph-Level Paraphrasing
Original paragraph:
“Limited access to teaching and learning materials remains a major challenge
in public schools, particularly in rural areas. This lack of resources affects both
teaching quality and student engagement.”
Guided hints for students:
•
Identify the main problem
•
Identify the impact
•
Rewrite using two shorter sentences
Sample paraphrase:
“Many public schools in rural areas face shortages of teaching and learning
materials. As a result, teachers struggle to deliver effective lessons, and
students show lower levels of engagement.”
Practice 3: Combining Two Sources (International + Pakistani)
Source A (International):
“Effective teacher training programs improve classroom practices and student
outcomes.”
Source B (Pakistani context):
“Reports from Sindh indicate that many teachers receive limited follow-up
support after training.”

text:
Student task:
•
Combine both ideas into one analytical paragraph
Sample combined paraphrase:
“Although international research highlights the positive impact of teacher
training on classroom practices, evidence from Sindh suggests that limited
post-training support reduces the long-term effectiveness of these programs.”
Shows synthesis
Links global theory with local evidence
Demonstrates academic thinking
Closing Reflection for Students
Paraphrasing is not about hiding the source.
It is about showing that you understand it.
When students gain confidence in paraphrasing:
•
Plagiarism decreases naturally
•
Academic voice becomes stronger
•
Writing becomes clearer and more original
6.10 Common Pakistani Student Errors in Using Sources
Despite having access to journals, reports, and online databases, many
Pakistani students struggle to use sources effectively in their literature
reviews. These difficulties are not caused by lack of intelligence or effort, but
by a combination of fear of English, exam-oriented learning habits, and
limited exposure to academic writing conventions. The most common errors
are discussed below with contextual explanations and corrected examples.
Over-Quoting Foreign Authors
One of the most frequent mistakes is excessive reliance on long quotations
taken from foreign journal articles. Students often believe that copying the
exact words of international authors makes their work sound more “academic”
or “authentic.” As a result, literature review sections sometimes appear as a
collection of quotations with very little original writing.
For example, a student writing about teacher professional development may
include a half-page quotation from a European study, followed by another
quotation from an American journal, without any explanation in between.
While the sources themselves may be credible, the student’s own voice
disappears completely.
Corrected approach:
Instead of quoting extensively, students should paraphrase key ideas and
briefly explain why the cited study is relevant to their own research context.
Short quotations should be used only when the original wording is essential,
such as in definitions or policy statements.
No Explanation After Citation
Another common issue is placing a citation at the end of a sentence without
explaining its significance. Many students assume that simply adding an
author’s name and year is enough to demonstrate understanding.
For instance, a sentence such as “Teacher motivation plays an important role
in learning outcomes (Smith, 2018)” is often left unexplained. The reader is
not told how motivation affects learning, why it matters, or how it relates to
the Pakistani context.
Corrected approach:
Every citation should be followed by one or two explanatory sentences that
interpret the source and connect it to the research topic. The citation should
support the student’s argument, not replace it.
Citation Without Argument
In many literature reviews, citations are listed one after another without a clear
argument guiding them. This results in descriptive writing rather than
analytical discussion. Students may summarize several studies, but fail to
show what these studies collectively suggest or how they inform the current
research.
For example, a paragraph may describe three different studies on classroom
assessment practices, yet never explain what problem remains unresolved or
what gap the current study intends to address.
Corrected approach:
Students should begin each paragraph with a clear idea or claim, and then use
sources to support, compare, or contrast that idea. In academic writing, your
argument comes first; sources come second.
Fear-Driven Copying
Perhaps the most serious, yet least acknowledged, issue is fear-driven copying.
Many Pakistani students copy text not because they intend to cheat, but
because they lack confidence in their English writing ability. They worry that
their own sentences will sound “too simple” or grammatically incorrect, so
they rely heavily on published text.
This fear is often reinforced by past experiences where language accuracy was
valued more than clarity of thought.
Corrected approach:
Students must understand that clear, simple English is preferred in academic
writing. Examiners and supervisors are more interested in understanding the
student’s thinking than in reading complex vocabulary. Building confidence
through guided paraphrasing practice significantly reduces the urge to copy.
6.11 Self-Assessment Checklist for Students
Before submitting a literature review, students are encouraged to pause and
reflect using the following self-assessment questions. This checklist helps
ensure that sources are being used thoughtfully and ethically.
•
Is my voice dominant in this section?
Can the reader clearly see my ideas, or does the text sound like a
collection of other people’s words?
•
Have I explained every citation?
After each reference, have I clarified why it is important and how it
relates to my study?
•
Do I rely only on foreign authors?
Have I included relevant Pakistani studies, government reports, or
local research where appropriate?
•
Can I explain each source without looking at it?
If I cannot explain a source in my own words, I may not fully
understand it yet.
Students who can confidently answer “yes” to these questions are far less
