likely to face plagiarism concerns and far more likely to produce meaningful
academic work.
6.13 Chapter Summary
This chapter emphasized that using sources correctly is not about decorating
writing with difficult language, but about thinking critically and
communicating ideas clearly. Academic sources are tools to strengthen an
argument, not substitutes for original thought.
The chapter also highlighted that local research is valid, valuable, and often
more relevant than international studies when addressing Pakistani
educational and social contexts. Students should feel confident drawing upon
national and provincial research alongside global literature.
Finally, the chapter demonstrated that paraphrasing is a learnable skill, not a
talent reserved for native speakers. With practice and confidence, students can
move away from fear-driven copying and toward a strong, independent
academic voice. Confidence, more than vocabulary, is the most effective
safeguard against plagiarism.
Chapter 7: Agreeing, Comparing, and Critiquing
Literature
Chapter Overview
In Pakistani universities, many students are able to collect relevant research
articles and summarize them accurately. However, a recurring weakness in
theses and research assignments is that students often describe what other
researchers have said without engaging critically with those ideas. As a result,
literature review chapters frequently read like a list of studies rather than a
coherent academic argument.
One of the key expectations of examiners is that students move beyond simply
reporting previous research and instead demonstrate the ability to agree with,
compare, and critically evaluate existing literature. Academic writing is not
about proving that earlier researchers were right or wrong; rather, it is about
showing how different studies relate to one another and how they inform the
current research within a specific context.
A major challenge for Pakistani students is the tendency to show excessive
deference to foreign authors, particularly studies conducted in Western or
high-income countries. Many students hesitate to question or even
contextualize these studies, assuming that disagreement is disrespectful or
academically unsafe. This mindset often leads to uncritical acceptance of
findings that may not fully apply to Pakistani social, educational, or
institutional realities.
At the same time, fear of plagiarism causes some students to rely heavily on
direct quotations, believing that copying exact words is safer than
paraphrasing. Unfortunately, this approach weakens analytical depth and
increases the risk of academic misconduct.
This chapter addresses these challenges by guiding students on how to engage
with literature confidently and ethically. It explains how to agree with previous
studies without copying, how to compare research conducted in different
contexts, and how to express disagreement in a respectful and academically
acceptable manner. By developing these skills, students can produce literature
reviews that demonstrate originality, critical thinking, and contextual
awareness—qualities highly valued by supervisors and examiners.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to:
1. Distinguish clearly between listing studies and synthesizing literature
in academic writing.
2. Use appropriate academic language to agree with previous research
without copying or over-quoting.
3. Compare findings from different studies and explain contextual
differences, particularly between international and Pakistani research.
4. Express respectful academic disagreement using hedging and
evidence-based reasoning.
5. Reduce the risk of plagiarism by applying effective paraphrasing and
synthesis strategies.
6. Develop confidence in positioning themselves as emerging
researchers, rather than passive reporters of others’ work.
7.1 What It Means to “Engage with Literature”
Many Pakistani students believe that writing a literature review means
collecting studies and summarizing them one by one. As a result, their chapters
often read like a long list of authors and years, with little connection between
ideas. However, academic writing—especially at university level—expects
students to engage with literature, not merely report it.
Engaging with literature means showing that you understand what previous
researchers have said, how their ideas relate to each other, and how they
connect to your own study. This engagement demonstrates that you are not
just a reader of research, but a participant in an academic conversation.
7.1.1 Moving Beyond Summary
A summary tells the reader what a study found. An evaluation explains why
that study matters, how it relates to other studies, and what its limitations might
be.
For example, writing:
“Ahmed (2019) studied teacher training in public schools and found positive
effects on teaching practices.”
is a summary. It is accurate, but incomplete from an academic perspective.
An evaluated version would be:
“Ahmed (2019) found that teacher training positively influenced classroom
practices in public schools; however, the study focused primarily on urban
settings, which limits its applicability to rural contexts.”
Here, the student goes beyond reporting and begins to analyze.
What Supervisors Look for in Literature Review Chapters
University supervisors and examiners typically look for the following:
•
Evidence that the student understands key themes in the field
•
Connections between different studies
•
Awareness of context, especially local vs international research
•
Identification of gaps that justify the current study

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
A literature review that only summarizes studies suggests that the student has
read the literature. A literature review that evaluates and compares studies
shows that the student has understood it.
7.1.2 Academic Respect vs Blind Agreement
Respecting previous researchers is an essential part of academic writing.
However, respect does not mean accepting every published study as
unquestionable truth.
Many Pakistani students hesitate to critique or even question well-known
international authors. This hesitation often comes from:
•
Language insecurity
•
Cultural norms of deference
•
Fear of being “wrong”
In academic research, however, respectful questioning is not disrespect. It is
expected.
For example, instead of writing:
“Smith (2018) is correct and proves that technology improves learning
outcomes.”
A more academically appropriate version would be:
“Smith (2018) provides evidence that technology integration can enhance
learning outcomes, particularly in well-resourced educational settings.”
This sentence respects the author while recognizing that findings may depend
on context.
Your Role as a Researcher (Even as a Student)
Once you begin writing a thesis or research paper, you are no longer just a
student repeating knowledge—you are a researcher contributing to
knowledge. Your role includes:
•
Assessing relevance
•
Identifying limitations
•
Comparing contexts
•
Offering reasoned interpretations
Your voice matters, as long as it is supported by evidence.
7.2 How to Agree with Previous Studies (Without Copying)
Agreeing with previous research is one of the most common tasks in academic
writing. However, agreement must be expressed in your own analytical voice,
not by copying or lightly modifying original sentences.
7.2.1 What Academic Agreement Looks Like
Academic agreement involves interpretation and restatement, not repetition.
Agreement IS:
•
Interpreting the author’s findings
•
Restating ideas using your own sentence structure
•
Connecting findings to your study or context
Agreement IS NOT:
•
Copying sentences with quotation marks removed
•
Replacing a few words with synonyms
•
Keeping the same sentence structure as the original text
For instance, changing “teacher professional development improves
instructional quality” to “teacher training enhances teaching quality”
without deeper reformulation is still considered poor paraphrasing.
True academic agreement reshapes the idea, not just the words.
7.2.2 Language Structures for Agreement
To express agreement clearly and professionally, students can use established
academic structures such as:
•
“The findings of X align with...”
•
“This study supports the argument that...”
•
“Similar results were reported by...”
•
“Consistent with earlier research...”
These phrases signal agreement while allowing the student to maintain an
independent academic voice.
7.2.3 Practical Pakistani Examples
Example 1: Education
“The findings of this study align with Ahmed (2019), who reported that
teacher training improves classroom practices in public schools.”
This sentence:
•
Shows agreement
•
Uses the student’s own structure
•
Clearly links previous research to current findings
Example 2: Technology and Education
“Similar outcomes were observed in Punjab government schools, where
digital tools improved student engagement.”
Here, the student:
•
Connects international ideas with local evidence
•
Grounds agreement in Pakistani context
•
Avoids unnecessary quotation
Such contextualization strengthens the credibility of the literature review.
7.2.4 Practice Activity
Activity 1: Rewrite for Academic Agreement
Original quoted sentence:
“Technology integration significantly enhances student learning outcomes”
(Smith, 2018).
Student rewrite:
“Smith (2018) demonstrates that the integration of technology can positively
influence student learning outcomes, particularly in structured learning
environments.”
Activity 2: Identify Copying vs Paraphrasing
Sentence A:
“Teacher motivation plays an important role in improving student
achievement.”
Sentence B:
“Teacher motivation is a key factor in enhancing student performance.”
This is not strong paraphrasing.
Improved version:
“Previous studies suggest that motivated teachers contribute more effectively
to improved learning outcomes among students.”
Engaging with literature means thinking, evaluating, and responding—not
copying. When Pakistani students learn to agree thoughtfully and
contextually, their academic writing becomes clearer, more confident, and
more credible.
7.3 Comparing Studies Across Contexts
One of the most important skills in academic writing is the ability to compare
research findings across different contexts. Many Pakistani students believe
that if two studies reach different conclusions, one of them must be “wrong.”
In reality, differences in findings are often expected and valid, because
research does not take place in a vacuum. Studies are shaped by the context in
which they are conducted.
7.3.1 Why Comparison Is Essential
Research findings often differ because studies are conducted in different
countries, different socioeconomic environments, and different institutional
settings. For example, a study conducted in a well-resourced school system in
a developed country may report strong positive effects of technology
integration. However, the same intervention may produce limited or mixed
results in a developing-country context such as Pakistan.
In Pakistan, factors such as limited infrastructure, large class sizes, lack of
teacher training, and inconsistent electricity supply significantly influence
how educational interventions function in practice. Therefore, when students
compare studies, they must ask not only what the findings are, but also where

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
and under what conditions those findings were produced. Comparison allows
researchers to demonstrate critical thinking, contextual awareness, and
research maturity—all of which are highly valued by supervisors and
examiners.
7.3.2 Common Comparison Structures
To compare studies effectively, students need clear and neutral language
structures. Academic comparison does not involve emotional or judgmental
wording; instead, it uses balanced and objective phrasing.
Common structures used in comparative academic writing include:
•
“While X focuses on..., Y highlights...”
•
“In contrast to urban settings...”
•
“Compared to international studies...”
These structures help the writer place studies side by side and show similarities
or differences without attacking the original researchers.
7.3.3 Pakistani Context Comparison
Comparison becomes especially powerful when international research is
interpreted through a Pakistani lens. For instance, many international studies
emphasize the transformative role of educational technology. However,
Pakistani researchers often highlight structural constraints that limit the
effectiveness of such interventions.
For example:
“While Smith (2018) emphasizes technology integration as a key driver of
student engagement, studies conducted in Pakistani rural schools suggest that
inadequate infrastructure and unreliable electricity remain major barriers to
effective implementation.”
This sentence does not reject Smith’s findings. Instead, it repositions them
within a different context, showing that what works in one environment may
not automatically succeed in another. This type of comparison signals
academic confidence and contextual understanding.
7.3.4 Comparative Paragraph Model
An effective comparative paragraph usually follows a clear logical structure.
First, the writer introduces Study A, briefly summarizing its main finding.
Next, Study B is introduced, often from a different country or context.
The third sentence explicitly compares the findings, highlighting similarities
or
differences.
Finally, the writer explains the contextual reason for this difference, such as
resources, policy environment, or institutional capacity.
When Pakistani students use this structure, they move from simple reporting
to analytical academic writing, which is a key expectation at postgraduate
level.
7.4 How to Disagree Respectfully in Academic Writing
Many students hesitate to disagree with published research, especially when
the authors are senior scholars or from well-known international institutions.
However, academic disagreement is not only allowed—it is expected.
Knowledge advances when researchers question, test, and refine existing
claims.
7.4.1 Why Disagreement Is Allowed (and Expected)
In academic writing, disagreement does not mean disrespect. Scholars do not
criticize authors personally; they evaluate evidence, methods, and context.
When a student respectfully disagrees with previous findings, it demonstrates
independence of thought and engagement with the research problem.
Examiners often look for evidence that students can move beyond agreement
and show critical judgment, especially in literature review and discussion
chapters.
7.4.2 Softening Language for Disagreement
Academic disagreement is usually expressed through hedging language,
which softens claims and avoids absolute statements. Hedging allows writers
to question findings without sounding aggressive or dismissive.
Common hedging expressions include:
•
“The findings did not fully support...”
•
“This study was unable to confirm...”
•
“The evidence remains inconclusive...”
•
“This may be due to contextual differences...”
Such language signals caution, fairness, and professionalism.
7.4.3 Pakistani Examples of Polite Disagreement
The following examples illustrate how disagreement can be expressed
respectfully within a Pakistani research context.
“Although Khan (2017) reported positive outcomes of digital learning
initiatives, the current study did not observe similar improvements in rural
classrooms.”
Here, the writer acknowledges the earlier study before explaining why the
results were different.
Another example is:
“This study was unable to confirm the effectiveness of digital learning tools
in schools lacking stable electricity.”
This statement does not claim that digital tools are ineffective everywhere.
Instead, it limits the disagreement to a specific contextual condition, which
strengthens the academic credibility of the argument.
By learning how to compare studies across contexts and disagree respectfully,
Pakistani students develop a stronger academic voice. These skills allow them
to contribute meaningfully to research discussions while remaining grounded
in local realities. When used correctly, comparison and critique transform a
literature review from a summary of studies into a coherent, analytical
argument.
7.5 Explaining Differences in Findings
In academic writing, it is common for a student’s findings to differ from those
reported in previous studies. For Pakistani students, this situation often creates
anxiety, as many assume that differing results indicate a weakness in their
research. In reality, differences in findings are normal and academically
acceptable, provided they are explained logically and supported by context.
Research does not take place in a vacuum. Studies conducted in different
countries, provinces, institutions, or time periods naturally produce varying
outcomes. Therefore, instead of viewing differences as a problem, students
should treat them as an opportunity to demonstrate critical thinking and
contextual understanding.
7.5.1 Acceptable Reasons for Differences
There are several legitimate and widely accepted reasons why research
findings may differ from earlier studies. Pakistani students are encouraged to
reflect carefully on these factors when interpreting their results.

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
One common reason is sample size. Many international studies are conducted
with large samples, often involving hundreds or thousands of participants. In
contrast, student research in Pakistan frequently relies on smaller samples due
to limited time, access, or institutional constraints. A study conducted in five
schools in one district may not produce the same results as a nationwide or
multi-country study.
Another important factor is location, particularly the difference between urban
and rural settings in Pakistan. Urban schools often have better infrastructure,
trained staff, and access to technology, whereas rural schools may face
shortages of teachers, electricity, internet access, and learning materials. As a
result, findings related to teaching methods, technology use, or student
performance may vary significantly depending on location.
Availability of resources also plays a critical role. For example, a study
conducted in well-resourced private schools is likely to report different
outcomes compared to research carried out in government schools where
classrooms are overcrowded and instructional materials are limited. Such
differences do not invalidate the research; rather, they highlight the
importance of context.
Finally, policy implementation gaps are a particularly relevant issue in
Pakistan. Although policies, training programs, or reforms may exist on paper,
their implementation often varies across provinces, districts, and even schools.
As a result, a policy that appears effective in one study may show limited
impact in another due to inconsistent or partial implementation.
7.5.2 Language for Explaining Differences
When explaining differences in findings, students should use careful, nonconfrontational language. Academic writing avoids strong or emotional
statements and instead relies on neutral expressions that invite interpretation.
Common and acceptable expressions include:
•
“This variation may be explained by differences in sample size and
research setting.”
•
“A possible reason for this difference is the limited availability of
resources in rural schools.”
•
“Contextual constraints may have influenced the outcomes of the
present study.”
Such language allows the writer to acknowledge differences without directly
rejecting or undermining previous research.
7.5.3 Model Explanation Paragraph
The following paragraph demonstrates how to explain differences in findings
in a clear and structured manner:
The findings of this study differ from those reported by Smith (2018), who
observed significant improvements in student learning following the
integration of digital tools. A possible reason for this difference is the research
context. While Smith’s study was conducted in well-resourced urban schools,
the present study focused on rural government schools in Sindh, where limited
access to electricity, internet connectivity, and digital devices remains a
challenge. These contextual constraints may have influenced the effectiveness
of technology-based interventions.
This paragraph:
1. Clearly states the difference
2. Provides a logical explanation
3. Links the explanation to the local Pakistani context
7.6 Synthesizing Multiple Studies (Advanced Skill)
As students progress in academic writing, they are expected to move beyond
discussing one study at a time. This more advanced skill is known as
synthesis, and it is a key indicator of research maturity.
7.6.1 What Synthesis Means
Synthesis involves combining ideas from multiple studies to present a
broader understanding of a research issue. Instead of writing one paragraph
per author, students group studies based on shared themes, patterns, or
conclusions.
In other words, synthesis is about ideas, not authors. The focus shifts from
who said what to what the collective research suggests. This approach makes
the literature review more analytical, coherent, and persuasive.
7.6.2 Synthesis Example
The following example illustrates synthesis in the context of Pakistani
education:
Several studies (Ali, 2016; Ahmed, 2019; Rahman, 2021) suggest that teacher
training improves instructional quality in public schools. However, these
gains remain limited in contexts where adequate teaching materials and
continuous professional support are lacking.
In this example:
•
Multiple studies are grouped together
•
A shared finding is identified
•
A limitation relevant to the Pakistani context is highlighted
•
The paragraph demonstrates analysis rather than summary
Being able to explain differences in findings and synthesize multiple studies
shows that a student is thinking like a researcher, not merely completing an
assignment. These skills strengthen the literature review and significantly
improve the overall quality of a thesis or research paper.
7.7 Common Mistakes Pakistani Students Make
Despite having access to relevant literature, many Pakistani students struggle
to engage with sources in an academic manner. These difficulties are not due
to lack of intelligence, but rather to limited exposure to analytical academic
writing. The following are the most frequently observed mistakes in theses
and research assignments across Pakistani universities.
Overusing Quotations
One of the most common mistakes is the excessive use of direct quotations.
Students often believe that quoting well-known authors strengthens their
work. As a result, paragraphs become collections of quoted sentences rather
than original academic arguments.
For example, a student may write:
“Technology enhances learning outcomes” (Smith, 2018).
“Digital tools increase student engagement” (Brown, 2019).

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
Such writing demonstrates reading, but not thinking. Academic writing
expects the student to interpret these ideas, not simply reproduce them.
Examiners want to see the student’s understanding of the literature in their
own words.
A stronger academic version would be:
Several studies have demonstrated the positive role of technology in
education, particularly in improving student engagement and learning
outcomes (Smith, 2018; Brown, 2019).
Here, the student’s voice leads the sentence, while sources support the claim.
Fear of Disagreeing with Foreign Authors
Many Pakistani students hesitate to question or challenge international
authors. There is a common belief that disagreeing with a foreign researcher
is disrespectful or academically unsafe. This fear results in literature reviews
that appear uncritical and descriptive.
However, academic disagreement does not mean rejection. It means
contextual evaluation. Research conducted in developed countries may not
fully apply to Pakistan due to differences in infrastructure, resources, and
policy implementation.
For instance:
While Smith (2018) emphasizes technology integration as a key driver of
student achievement, studies conducted in rural Pakistani schools suggest that
limited infrastructure and inconsistent electricity supply significantly restrict
the effectiveness of such interventions.
This type of disagreement is polite, evidence-based, and contextually
grounded. It demonstrates maturity as a researcher.
Mixing Opinion with Evidence
Another frequent issue is the blending of personal opinion with research
findings. Students sometimes write statements that sound confident but lack
scholarly support.
For example:
Teachers are not motivated and do not take interest in training programs.
This sentence expresses an opinion, not an academic claim. Without evidence,
such statements weaken the credibility of the research.
An academically acceptable version would be:
Previous studies indicate that teacher motivation remains a challenge in
professional development programs, particularly when training is not linked
to classroom support mechanisms (Ahmed, 2020; Khan, 2021).
Academic writing requires evidence first, opinion last—and even opinions
must be grounded in data.
Writing One Study per Paragraph
Many students organize their literature review by assigning one paragraph to
each study. While this approach seems logical, it results in fragmented writing
and weak synthesis.
For example:
•
Paragraph 1: Study by Ali (2017)
•
Paragraph 2: Study by Ahmed (2019)
•
Paragraph 3: Study by Khan (2021)
This structure leads to repetition and prevents meaningful comparison.
Instead, literature should be organized around themes, not authors.
A synthesized approach would be:
Several studies have explored the impact of teacher training on instructional
quality in public schools. Ali (2017) and Ahmed (2019) both report
improvements in classroom practices following structured training programs;
however, Khan (2021) notes that these improvements are not sustained
without ongoing mentoring and resource support.
This paragraph demonstrates comparison, agreement, and critique within a
single coherent discussion.
7.8 Practice Tasks
To develop confidence in engaging with literature, students are encouraged to
complete the following practice tasks.
Task 1: Identify Agreement, Comparison, or Disagreement
Read the following sentence and identify whether it shows agreement,
comparison, or disagreement:
“While international studies highlight the effectiveness of digital learning
tools, evidence from Pakistani public schools indicates that teacher readiness
remains a significant challenge.”
Students should explain their answer briefly.
Task 2: Rewrite a Weak Literature Paragraph
Weak version:
Smith (2018) studied technology in education. Brown (2019) also studied
technology. Khan (2020) studied technology in Pakistan.
Task: Rewrite the paragraph to show comparison and synthesis instead of
listing studies.
Task 3: Convert a Summary into a Synthesized Paragraph
Summary version:
Ali (2017) found teacher training effective. Ahmed (2019) found similar
results. Rahman (2021) found limited impact.
Task: Combine these findings into one analytical paragraph that explains
similarities and differences.
7.9 Chapter Checklist (For Students)
Before finalizing your literature review, ask yourself the following questions:
•
Have I paraphrased ideas instead of copying sentences from sources?
•
Have I compared at least two studies within a single paragraph?
•
Have I linked international research findings to the Pakistani context?
•
Is my disagreement respectful, cautious, and supported by evidence?
If the answer to any of these questions is “no,” the section requires further
revision.
7.10 Chapter Summary
This chapter highlights that agreeing with previous studies is not about
copying their words, but about demonstrating understanding. When a student
appropriately aligns their findings with earlier research—by paraphrasing and
interpreting ideas in their own academic voice—it builds credibility. For
example, a Pakistani education student may support international research on
teacher training while restating it in relation to public schools in Sindh or
Punjab, showing both respect for scholarship and originality.
Comparison of studies reflects deeper understanding of research literature. By
comparing findings across different contexts—such as urban versus rural
schools, or international versus Pakistani settings—students demonstrate that
they can analyze similarities and differences rather than merely describe them.
For instance, comparing technology integration studies from developed
countries with evidence from Pakistani rural schools helps explain why

outcomes may differ due to infrastructure or resource constraints.
Critiquing literature is a sign of research maturity, not disrespect. This chapter
shows that students are expected to question findings when evidence does not
fully align with their context or data. Using cautious and respectful language—
such as “this study was unable to confirm”—allows Pakistani students to
challenge conclusions while maintaining academic tone, especially when local
realities do not support generalized claims.
Finally, the chapter emphasizes that context matters, particularly in Pakistan.
Factors such as school infrastructure, language of instruction, socioeconomic
conditions, and policy implementation significantly influence research
outcomes. Strong academic writing acknowledges these contextual realities,
enabling students to position their work as both globally informed and locally
grounded.
PART IV — Methodology in Clear, Simple English
This part of the book helps Pakistani students write the methodology chapter
clearly, accurately, and confidently without using unnecessary complex
English. Many students believe that methodology must sound “difficult” to be
academic; as a result, they write long, confusing sentences that hide the actual
research process. This section corrects that misconception by showing that
clarity, precision, and simplicity are the hallmarks of good academic
methodology writing.
Using step-by-step explanations, locally relevant examples (such as school
surveys, classroom observations, and interviews in Pakistani institutions), and
clear tense guidance, this part teaches students how to describe what they did,
how they did it, and why they did it. The focus remains on past tense, logical
sequencing, and transparent procedures, enabling readers to understand and
replicate the study.
By the end of this part, students will be able to write a methodology section
that is methodologically sound, linguistically simple, ethically clear, and
aligned with Pakistani research contexts, without fear of grammar or
“academic” vocabulary.
Chapter 8: Writing Methodology Without Complex
English
Chapter Overview
This section explains the purpose of the methodology chapter and clarifies
common misconceptions among Pakistani students. Many students believe
that examiners expect complex language and advanced terminology in
methodology writing. This section emphasizes that examiners value clarity,
accuracy, and transparency over vocabulary. By addressing frequent examiner
comments and expectations, this section prepares students to write
methodology chapters that clearly describe what was done, how it was done,
and why it was done.
Learning Outcomes
After completing this section, students will be able to:
•
Understand the true purpose of the methodology chapter
•
Recognize why clarity is more important than complex vocabulary
•
Identify common examiner criticisms of weak methodology chapters
•
Write methodology sections using simple and correct English
•
Use past tense accurately when describing completed research
•
Describe research procedures step by step
•
Avoid unnecessary technical or copied language
8.1 Purpose of the Methodology Chapter
The methodology chapter explains how the research was actually conducted.
It tells the reader what the researcher did, who was involved, what tools were
used, and how the data were collected and analyzed. For many Pakistani
students, this chapter becomes difficult not because the research is weak, but
because the language used to describe it is unclear or unnecessarily complex.
In Pakistani universities, examiners read the methodology chapter to judge
whether the study is credible, systematic, and doable. They are not impressed
by difficult vocabulary or long sentences copied from international journals.
Instead, they look for clarity, honesty, and logical flow. A good methodology
chapter should allow the examiner to clearly imagine how the research was
carried out in real classrooms, schools, offices, or communities.
In simple terms, the methodology chapter should answer one question clearly:
“If another student wanted to repeat this study in Pakistan, could they do so
by reading this chapter?”
If the answer is yes, the methodology is well written.
8.1.1 What Examiners Expect from Pakistani Students
Examiners in Pakistani universities generally expect the methodology chapter
to be clear, straightforward, and contextually grounded. They are more
concerned with what was done than how sophisticated the language sounds.
Many students believe that using complex vocabulary will make their thesis
look more “academic.” However, in practice, complex language often creates
confusion. For example, instead of clearly stating how many teachers were
surveyed, students sometimes use long sentences filled with abstract terms
such as paradigm, framework, or instrumentation process without explaining
the actual steps.
In examiner reports and viva feedback, the following comments are very
common in Pakistan:
•
“Method is unclear”
This usually means that the student did not explain the procedure step
by step. For example, the examiner cannot understand who collected
the data, where it was collected, or how long the process took.
•
“Too much theory, little procedure”
This comment appears when students spend several pages explaining
research designs from textbooks but write only a few unclear lines
about what they actually did in their own study.
•
“Copied methodology”
This comment suggests that the methodology sounds generic and does

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
not reflect the Pakistani context. For example, mentioning “online
surveys” in rural public schools without internet access immediately
raises doubts.
Therefore, students must understand that methodology is about clarity, not
vocabulary. Simple English that accurately describes real research activities
in Pakistan is always preferred over copied or overly complex language.
8.2 Understanding Tense in Methodology Writing
One of the most common language problems in Pakistani theses is incorrect
use of tense in the methodology chapter. Many students mix present, past, and
future tenses without realizing it, which makes the chapter confusing and
unprofessional.
Understanding tense is important because tense shows time—whether an
action has already happened, is happening now, or will happen in the future.
8.2.1 Why Past Tense Is Mostly Used
The methodology chapter describes actions that have already been completed.
The data have already been collected, the questionnaires have already been
distributed, and the interviews have already been conducted. Therefore, past
tense is used in most parts of the methodology chapter.
For example:
•
This study uses questionnaires to collect data.
•
This study used questionnaires to collect data.
The incorrect sentence gives the impression that the research is still ongoing.
The correct sentence clearly tells the examiner that the work has already been
completed.
Similarly, consider a common Pakistani research context:
•
The researcher visits government schools and conducts interviews.
•
The researcher visited government schools and conducted
interviews.
Using past tense reassures the examiner that the research was actually carried
out, not merely planned.
8.2.2 When Present Tense Is Acceptable
Although past tense is mostly used, present tense is acceptable in specific
situations.
First, present tense can be used when describing tables, figures, or instruments
included in the thesis. For example:
•
Table 3.1 shows the demographic information of the respondents.
•
The questionnaire consists of three sections.
Second, present tense may be used when referring to the structure of the
chapter or thesis. For example:
•
This chapter describes the research design and data collection
procedures.
In these cases, the focus is not on what happened in the past, but on what the
reader is currently seeing in the document.
8.2.3 Common Tense Errors by Pakistani Students
Pakistani students often make predictable tense-related errors due to prior
learning habits and translation from Urdu.
Mixing Past and Present Tense
Students sometimes change tense within the same paragraph, which confuses
the reader. For example:
•
The researcher distributed questionnaires and collects responses
from teachers.
This sentence should remain in past tense throughout.
Using Future Tense Unnecessarily
Some students describe completed research as if it is still planned:
•
The researcher will analyze the data using percentages.
In a completed thesis, this should be written in past tense.
Translating Tense from Urdu Thinking
In Urdu, tense is often implied rather than strictly marked. When students
translate ideas directly from Urdu into English, tense errors occur. This results
in vague or incorrect time references in methodology writing.
Practice Box 8.1: Tense Correction Exercise
Read the paragraph below and identify tense errors. Rewrite it using correct
tense.
This study uses a questionnaire to collect data from government school
teachers. The researcher distributes the questionnaires personally and will
analyze the data using percentages.
Hint for Students:
Ask yourself: Has this action already happened? If yes, use past tense.
8.3 Core Components of a Clear Methodology Chapter
A methodology chapter becomes difficult not because research is difficult, but
because students try to make it sound difficult. In reality, examiners are not
looking for complex language. They want to clearly understand what was
done, how it was done, and why it was done in that way. This section explains
the core components of a methodology chapter using simple language and
familiar Pakistani research contexts.
8.3.1 Research Design
What research design means (in simple words)
Research design explains the overall plan of the study. It tells the reader what
type of study you conducted and how you approached the research problem.
In simple terms, research design answers the question:
“What kind of study is this?”
Many Pakistani students confuse research design with data collection tools or
statistical techniques. However, research design is only about the nature of the
study, not its technical details.
Common research designs used in Pakistan
In Pakistani universities, most student research falls into a few common
categories:
•
Survey research, where data are collected through questionnaires
•
Descriptive studies, where a situation or perception is described as it
exists
•
Mixed-method studies, where both quantitative (numbers) and
qualitative (interviews or observations) data are used
Students should choose a design that matches their research question, not one
that sounds impressive.
Example written in simple English
“This study adopted a descriptive research design to explore teachers’
perceptions regarding classroom teaching practices.”
This sentence works because it clearly states:
•

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
the type of study (descriptive),
•
the purpose (to explore perceptions),
•
and avoids unnecessary technical terms.
8.3.2 Research Population and Sample
Understanding population and sample
The population refers to the entire group that the researcher wants to study.
The sample is a smaller group selected from the population to represent it.
Pakistani students often struggle here because they try to use formal or
exaggerated language. The best approach is to explain population and sample
clearly and realistically.
Pakistani contextual example
“The population of the study consisted of government primary school teachers
in District Thatta. A sample of 120 teachers was selected using random
sampling.”
This example clearly answers two important questions:
•
Who was included in the study?
•
How many participants were selected?
Common mistakes made by students
One frequent mistake is the overuse of the word “universe”, which is
unnecessary and outdated in most academic writing. Another common issue
is failing to explain how participants were selected, which raises questions
about the credibility of the study.
Students should always explain their sampling method briefly and clearly.
8.3.3 Research Instruments
What research instruments are
Research instruments are the tools used to collect data. In Pakistani academic
research, the most commonly used instruments include:
•
Questionnaires
•
Observation checklists
•
Interview guides
Students often make the mistake of explaining the theory behind these tools
instead of explaining how they were actually used.
Key rule for writing about instruments
When describing research instruments, students should focus on what was
used, why it was used, and how it was used—not theoretical definitions.
For example, instead of explaining what a questionnaire is, explain:
•
what type of questionnaire was used,
•
what kind of information it collected,
•
and how respondents answered it.
8.4 Writing About Data Collection Procedures Clearly
After explaining research design and instruments, the next step is to describe
how the data were collected. This part should read like a clear story of the
research process.
8.4.1 Step-by-Step Writing Strategy
To write data collection procedures clearly, students should answer five
simple questions:
1. Who collected the data?
2. From whom were the data collected?
3. How were the data collected?
4. When were the data collected?
5. Where were the data collected?
If these five questions are answered, the methodology automatically becomes
clear.
8.4.2 Pakistani Example 1: Survey of Government Teachers
Model paragraph (simple English)
“Data were collected through a structured questionnaire. The questionnaire
was administered to 120 government primary school teachers from selected
schools in Hyderabad district. The researcher personally visited the schools
and distributed the questionnaires. Out of 120 questionnaires, 110 were
returned and used for analysis.”
Why this paragraph works
This paragraph is effective because:
•
it uses past tense consistently,
•
it explains the procedure step by step,
•
and it avoids unnecessary academic vocabulary.
An examiner can immediately understand what was done.
8.4.3 Pakistani Example 2: Classroom Observation in Public Schools
Model paragraph
“Classroom observations were conducted in 20 public primary schools. An
observation checklist was used to record teaching practices and student
engagement. Each classroom was observed for one full lesson. The
observations were conducted during regular school hours.”
This paragraph clearly explains:
•
where the observations took place,
•
what tool was used,
•
and how long each observation lasted.
Common errors in observation writing
Many students write long explanations about observation theory but fail to
mention practical details, such as duration or setting. Another common error
is not explaining what was actually observed.
8.4.4 Pakistani Example 3: Interviews with Head Teachers
Model paragraph
“Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 head teachers. Each
interview lasted approximately 30–40 minutes. The interviews were conducted
in Urdu and later translated into English for analysis.”
This example is effective because it:
•
clearly states the number of participants,
•
mentions the duration,
•
and explains the language used during interviews.
Such clarity builds examiner confidence in the research process.
A strong methodology chapter does not depend on difficult English. It depends
on clear thinking and honest description. When students write what they
actually did—using simple past tense and step-by-step explanation—the
methodology becomes both strong and credible.
8.5 Ethical Considerations (Simple & Honest Writing)
Ethical considerations are an essential part of research writing, especially in
studies conducted in schools, colleges, and public institutions in Pakistan.
Many students assume that ethics require complex language or lengthy
explanations. In reality, examiners expect ethical considerations to be written
clearly, briefly, and truthfully, focusing on what was actually done during the
research process.
In Pakistani academic research, ethics mainly involve three simple
responsibilities: obtaining permission from relevant authorities, taking
informed consent from participants, and ensuring confidentiality of the
information collected. These steps show respect for institutions and
individuals and help establish the credibility of the research.

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
8.5.1 What Ethics Means in Pakistani Research
In Pakistan, most educational research is conducted in government schools,
colleges, or universities, where formal permission is required before data
collection. Students must clearly state that approval was obtained from the
concerned authorities, such as the District Education Office, school principals,
or institutional heads. Examiners do not expect legal language; they expect a
clear statement that permission was taken.
For example, if a study involves government primary schools, the researcher
should mention that approval was obtained from the relevant education
department and school administration before visiting the schools.
Another important ethical requirement is informed consent. This means that
participants were clearly informed about the purpose of the study and agreed
to take part voluntarily. In the Pakistani context, consent is often verbal,
especially when research is conducted in public schools or rural areas.
Students should not hesitate to mention this honestly. There is no requirement
to exaggerate or claim written consent if it was not obtained.
Confidentiality is the third key ethical principle. Participants must be assured
that their identities will not be disclosed and that the information they provide
will be used only for academic purposes. This is particularly important in
studies involving teachers, head teachers, or students, where responses may
include opinions about teaching practices or institutional challenges.
Example
In a study involving classroom observations and teacher surveys in
government schools, ethical considerations were addressed by first seeking
permission from the concerned school authorities. Teachers were informed
about the purpose of the study and were assured that their participation was
voluntary. They were also informed that their names and schools would not be
mentioned in the research report. All collected data were used strictly for
academic analysis.
Model Paragraph (Simple & Examiner-Friendly)
Permission was obtained from the relevant education authorities before data
collection. Participants were informed about the purpose of the study, and
their consent was obtained prior to participation. All information collected
during the research was kept confidential and was used only for academic
purposes.
Important Reminder for Students
Ethical considerations should:
•
Be short and factual
•
Avoid unnecessary academic jargon
•
Reflect what actually happened during the research
•
Match the Pakistani institutional context
Writing honestly and clearly about ethics builds examiner trust and
strengthens the overall quality of the research.
8.6 Data Analysis: Writing Without Fear
For many Pakistani students, the data analysis section is the most intimidating
part of the thesis. This fear does not come from statistics or interviews
themselves, but from the belief that this section must be written in very
complex English. In reality, examiners do not look for difficult language. They
look for clarity, accuracy, and honesty in how data were analyzed.
Data analysis writing should answer one simple question:
What did you do with the data after collecting it?
If the reader can clearly understand this, your analysis writing is successful.
8.6.1 Quantitative Data Analysis
Quantitative data analysis refers to working with numbers, such as responses
from questionnaires, test scores, or survey results. In Pakistani university
research—especially in education, management, and social sciences—this
usually involves descriptive statistics, such as frequencies, percentages, and
averages.
Students often believe they must explain statistical theory. This is
unnecessary. What is required is a clear description of the steps taken.
A simple and effective way to write this section is shown below:
“The collected data were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Frequencies
and percentages were calculated to summarize the responses.”
This short paragraph is academically correct and fully acceptable because it
clearly explains:
•
what was analyzed (the collected data),
•
how it was analyzed (descriptive statistics),
•
and for what purpose (to summarize responses).
Contextual Pakistani Example
In a study on teaching practices in government schools, a student may write:
“The data collected through questionnaires were analyzed using descriptive
statistics. Frequencies and percentages were calculated to examine teachers’
responses regarding lesson planning and classroom management.”
This explanation is sufficient. There is no need to explain formulas or repeat
textbook definitions unless your supervisor specifically asks for them.
8.6.2 Qualitative Data Analysis
Qualitative data analysis is used when the data consist of words rather than
numbers, such as interview responses, open-ended questions, or observation
notes. In Pakistani research, this is common in studies involving teachers, head
teachers, students, or parents.
The most commonly used approach is thematic analysis, which means
identifying patterns or themes in responses.
A clear and simple way to describe this process is:
“Interview responses were analyzed thematically. Similar responses were
grouped into common themes.”
This sentence tells the reader exactly what happened to the data—nothing
more is required.
Contextual Pakistani Example
For interviews conducted with head teachers, the analysis can be described as
follows:
“The interview responses were analyzed thematically. Similar responses
related to teacher supervision, school leadership, and resource availability

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
were grouped into common themes.”
This explanation shows:
•
the method used (thematic analysis),
•
and the nature of the themes (relevant to Pakistani schools).
Common Pakistani Mistake: Mentioning Software Without Explanation
A frequent mistake among Pakistani students is writing the names of software
tools without explaining what was done using them. For example, students
often write:
“Data were analyzed using SPSS.”
This sentence is incomplete. Software is a tool, not a method. Examiners want
to know how the software was used.
A better version is:
“The data were analyzed using SPSS. Frequencies and percentages were
calculated to summarize the responses.”
Similarly, for qualitative analysis:
“Interview data were coded manually, and themes were developed based on
recurring responses.”
Always remember: software supports analysis; it does not replace
explanation.
8.7 Common Methodology Mistakes by Pakistani Students
Despite having good research ideas, many Pakistani students lose marks in the
methodology chapter due to avoidable mistakes. These errors generally fall
into two categories: language-related and content-related.
8.7.1 Language-Related Errors
One common issue is the overuse of passive voice. While passive voice is
acceptable in academic writing, excessive use makes sentences long and
unclear. For example:
“Data were collected and were analyzed and were interpreted in accordance
with...”
Such sentences confuse readers. Simple and direct sentences are preferred.
Another frequent mistake is copying long sentences from international
research journals. These sentences often do not match the student’s research
design or context and create inconsistency in language quality.
Students also tend to use complex words incorrectly, believing that difficult
vocabulary makes writing more academic. In reality, incorrect usage weakens
credibility. Simple words used correctly are always better than complex words
used wrongly.
8.7.2 Content-Related Errors
A serious methodological error is not mentioning the sample size. Examiners
cannot evaluate a study if they do not know how many participants were
involved.
Another common problem is failing to explain the procedure clearly. Many
students mention tools such as questionnaires or interviews but do not explain:
•
who administered them,
•
where they were administered,
•
or how long the process took.
Finally, copy-paste methodology is a widespread issue in Pakistani
universities. When students copy methodology from previous theses without
adapting it, the method often does not match the research questions, leading
to examiner criticism.
Data analysis writing is not about showing technical brilliance. It is about clear
communication. If you explain your analysis in simple, honest English and
connect it to the Pakistani context, your methodology chapter will be strong,
readable, and examiner-friendly.
8.8 Practice Section: From Complex to Clear
One of the most common problems in Pakistani theses is the belief that
complex English equals good research. Many students feel pressured to use
long sentences and unfamiliar words because they think examiners expect
“heavy language.” In reality, examiners look for clear thinking and transparent
procedures, not decoration through vocabulary.
This section helps students learn how to simplify their methodology without
losing academic quality.
8.8.1 Example of Overly Complex Methodology
Consider the following sentence, which is commonly found in student theses:
“The research methodology employed a multi-dimensional quantitative
paradigm utilizing stratified sampling mechanisms to elicit empirically valid
data from heterogeneous educational stakeholders.”
At first glance, this sentence appears academic. However, when examined
closely, it creates several problems:
•
The meaning is unclear
•
Too many technical words are used unnecessarily
•
The reader does not clearly understand what was actually done
•
The sentence sounds copied from a journal rather than written by the
researcher
Most importantly, this sentence does not help the examiner visualize the
research process.
8.8.2 Rewritten in Plain English
Now read the same idea written in clear and simple English:
“The study used a quantitative survey method. Teachers were selected through
random sampling.”
This version is effective because:
•
The meaning is immediately clear
•
The procedure is easy to understand
•
The language is correct and professional
•
The examiner can quickly grasp the research design
In Pakistani universities, clarity builds trust. When examiners clearly
understand what you did, they are more confident in your research—even if
the language is simple.
8.8.3 Student Practice Tasks
To develop confidence in clear academic writing, students should regularly
practice simplifying their methodology language.
Task 1: Rewrite Complex Language
Students are given a complex methodology paragraph taken from a thesis or
journal article and asked to rewrite it in simple English without changing the
meaning.
Task 2: Correct Tense Usage
Students identify sentences written in present tense and rewrite them in the
correct past tense. For example:
•
This study uses questionnaires to collect data.
•
This study used questionnaires to collect data.
Task 3: Reduce Length Without Losing Meaning
Students shorten long methodology paragraphs by removing unnecessary
words while keeping all essential information. This helps them learn that
shorter writing is often stronger writing.
