8.9 Methodology Writing Checklist (Before Submission)
Before submitting the thesis, students should carefully review their
methodology chapter using the following checklist:
✔ Past tense is used correctly to describe completed research activities
✔ The sample is clearly defined with size, location, and participant type
✔ Data collection procedures are written step by step
✔ The Pakistani context (schools, districts, institutions) is clearly
mentioned
✔ The language is simple, direct, and free from unnecessary complexity
Using this checklist helps students avoid the most common reasons for
examiner confusion and negative comments.
8.10 Chapter Summary
This chapter emphasizes a simple but powerful idea: methodology is about
clarity, not decoration. Complex language does not make research stronger;
clear language does.
Simple English allows examiners to understand:
•
What the researcher did
•
How the data were collected
•
Why the study can be trusted
When methodology is written clearly, the research tells a logical and
convincing story. This confidence in communication is what separates a weak
thesis from a strong one.
PART V — Presenting Data & Findings
This part of the book focuses on helping students present research data clearly,
objectively, and academically. Pakistani students often struggle at this stage
by either repeating tables and figures without explanation or adding personal
opinions instead of analysis. Part V addresses this gap by guiding students on
how to describe results using appropriate academic language, correct tense,
and logical structure.
Students learn how to introduce tables, charts, and figures, highlight key
patterns and significant findings, and explain results in relation to research
questions without overinterpretation. Practical examples are drawn from
Pakistani research contexts, such as education surveys, classroom
observations, and institutional assessments, to ensure relevance and clarity.
The section emphasizes that presenting findings is not about telling a story or
proving assumptions, but about accurately reporting what the data shows in a
clear and professional manner.
By the end of this part, students are able to move confidently from raw data to
well-written findings that form a strong foundation for discussion and
conclusions.
Chapter 9: Describing Tables, Charts & Results
Chapter Overview
This chapter helps students learn how to describe research results clearly,
accurately, and objectively using tables, charts, and figures. Many Pakistani
students struggle not because their data is weak, but because they do not know
how to explain what the data shows in academic English.
The chapter moves students from:
•
Simply inserting tables → to interpreting results
•
Repeating numbers → to highlighting meaning
•
Emotional language → to objective academic reporting
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to:
•
Correctly introduce tables, charts, and figures in academic writing
•
Use appropriate academic language to describe key findings
•
Distinguish between reporting results and interpreting results
•
Write result paragraphs using education-related Pakistani data
•
Avoid common errors such as emotional language and repetition of
figures
9.1 Purpose of the Results Section
For many Pakistani university students, the Results section is one of the most
confusing parts of a thesis or research report. Students often assume that this
section requires strong opinions, explanations, or even recommendations. In
reality, the Results section has a very specific and limited purpose: it presents
what the data shows, nothing more and nothing less.
Understanding this purpose is essential because examiners and supervisors
expect a clear separation between results and discussion. When these two
sections are mixed, the credibility and clarity of the research are weakened.
9.1.1 What the Results Section Does
The Results section objectively presents the findings of the study. It reports
the outcomes of data collection using tables, charts, figures, and short
explanatory text. The role of the researcher at this stage is not to judge or
interpret the findings, but to guide the reader through the data in a clear and
logical manner.
For example, in an education research study conducted in Sindh, the Results
section may state:
“Table 5.1 shows that 38% of Grade 2 students achieved the minimum reading
fluency benchmark, while 62% performed below the expected level.”
This sentence simply tells the reader what happened. It does not explain why
the majority of students performed poorly, nor does it suggest how the
situation should be improved. Those explanations belong to the Discussion
section.
In short, the Results section answers the question:
“What does the data show?”
It does not answer:
“Why did this happen?” or “What should be done?”
9.1.2 What the Results Section Does NOT Do
Equally important is understanding what the Results section must avoid.
Many Pakistani students unintentionally weaken their research by including
elements that do not belong in this section.
The Results section does not include:
•
Personal opinions
•
Recommendations for improvement
•
Policy or administrative suggestions
For instance, the following sentence is inappropriate for the Results section:

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
“These results are very disappointing and show that the education system has
failed.”
Such a statement contains emotion and judgment, which are not part of
objective reporting. A more appropriate Results statement would be:
“The data indicates that a majority of students did not meet the required
reading benchmark.”
Another common mistake is giving solutions too early:
“Therefore, teachers should be provided with more training.”
This is a recommendation and belongs in the Conclusion or Recommendations
section, not in Results.
A widespread misconception among Pakistani students is captured in the
commonly heard statement:
“Results aur discussion aik hi cheez hoti hain.”
This belief leads students to explain causes, criticize systems, and suggest
reforms within the Results section. Academic writing, however, requires a
clear boundary:
•
Results present the data
•
Discussion explains and interprets the data
9.2 Introducing Tables, Charts, and Figures
Tables, charts, and figures are essential tools in academic writing because they
allow readers to quickly understand complex data. However, these visual
elements must always be properly introduced and explained in text. Simply
inserting a table without explanation is considered poor academic practice.
9.2.1 How to Refer to Tables and Figures Properly
In academic writing, tables and figures are always referred to using
standardized structures. This ensures clarity and helps the reader locate and
understand the information.
Common academic expressions include:
•
“Table 4.1 shows...”
•
“Figure 3 illustrates...”
•
“As shown in Table 2...”
These structures signal to the reader that the writer is about to describe key
information presented visually.
A localized example from an education study in Pakistan may read:
“Table 4.2 shows the percentage of Grade 2 students achieving reading
fluency benchmarks in Sindh.”
This sentence:
•
Clearly identifies the table
•
Briefly explains what the table contains
•
Prepares the reader to understand the data
The reader now knows what to look for before examining the table.
9.2.2 Positioning Tables and Figures
The placement of tables and figures is just as important as the language used
to describe them. In academic writing, a table or figure should never appear
without prior or immediate reference in the text.
As a general rule:
•
A table should be introduced before or immediately after it appears
•
Every table and figure must be mentioned at least once in the text
For example, it is incorrect to place a table in the middle of a chapter without
explanation. Instead, the writer should guide the reader, as in the following
example:
“Table 3 presents the distribution of student responses regarding access to
reading materials at home.”
Only after this sentence should the table be inserted.
This approach ensures that tables and figures support the narrative, rather than
interrupt it. They are not decorative elements; they are evidence that
strengthens the written explanation.
9.3 Describing Key Findings (Not Every Number)
One of the most common mistakes made by Pakistani students in the Results
section is the attempt to describe every number in a table or chart. While this
may appear thorough, it often weakens the quality of academic writing.
Examiners do not expect students to repeat all figures; rather, they look for the
student’s ability to identify what is most important in the data.
Academic writing values selection and emphasis. A strong results paragraph
highlights the most meaningful findings and guides the reader toward
understanding the overall pattern emerging from the data.
A useful guiding question for students is:
“Agar examiner sirf aik cheez yaad rakhe, woh kya honi chahiye?”
If students can answer this question clearly, they are likely focusing on the
right aspects of their data.
9.3.1 Selecting What Is Important
When describing tables, charts, or figures, students should focus on key
features rather than complete numerical detail. In most cases, important
findings fall into one or more of the following categories:
Highest values
These show where performance, agreement, or frequency is strongest.
Example: If one district shows the highest reading score, it deserves attention
because it may indicate effective practices or better conditions.
Lowest values
These indicate areas of concern or limited performance.
Example: A very low percentage of students meeting a benchmark highlights
a gap that requires attention, even if the student does not explain it at this stage.
Major differences
Large gaps between groups, time periods, or categories are often more
important than small variations.
Example: A sharp difference between urban and rural schools is more
significant than small differences among urban schools themselves.
Clear trends
Trends over time—such as improvement, decline, or stability—help the reader
understand overall direction.
Example:
An increase from baseline to midline followed by a slight decline at endline
suggests a pattern worth noting.
Students should remember that the purpose of the Results section is to show
what the data reveals, not to tell the entire numerical story.

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
9.3.2 Language for Highlighting Key Findings
Once important results have been selected, students must use appropriate
academic language to highlight them clearly and objectively. Certain sentence
patterns are especially useful for this purpose.
Common and effective expressions include:
•
“The majority of...”
Used when more than half of respondents or cases show a similar
pattern.
•
“A significant proportion of...”
Useful when a large but not necessarily dominant group shares a
characteristic.
•
“Only a small percentage of...”
Effective for emphasizing limited occurrence or low performance.
Example:
“The majority of students demonstrated basic word recognition skills, while
only a small percentage achieved the fluency benchmark.”
Such language allows students to emphasize key findings without repeating
exact figures or overloading the paragraph with numbers.
9.4 Localized Examples from Pakistan
To better understand how key findings should be described, this section
presents localized examples commonly used in Pakistani research, particularly
in education studies.
9.4.1 EGRA-Style Results (Early Grade Reading)
Consider the following results description:
“Table 5.1 indicates that only 34% of Grade 2 students were able to read 45
correct words per minute, while 66% remained below the benchmark.”
This sentence effectively highlights the core finding of the table without listing
multiple figures. The emphasis is on the contrast between students meeting the
benchmark and those who did not.
Teaching Point
When reporting EGRA-style results:
•
Focus on achievement versus benchmark
•
Highlight overall performance patterns
•
Avoid emotional or judgmental language such as alarming, disturbing,
or disappointing
Instead of writing:
“The results are alarming and show very poor performance,”
students should write:
“The results indicate that a majority of students did not meet the fluency
benchmark.”
This maintains academic neutrality and strengthens credibility.
9.4.2 Student Survey Data (Questionnaire Results)
Survey data often involves percentages and comparisons between groups. The
following example demonstrates effective reporting:
“Out of 200 students surveyed, 58% reported limited access to English reading
materials at home, while 42% indicated regular access.”
This sentence:
•
Clearly states the sample size
•
Uses percentages appropriately
•
Makes a direct comparison without interpretation
Skills Emphasized
•
Accurate use of percentages
•
Neutral and factual tone
•
Clear contrast between groups
Students should resist the urge to explain why access is limited at this stage.
Such explanations belong in the Discussion chapter.
9.4.3 Teacher Feedback Percentages
Teacher feedback is often reported using levels of agreement. Consider the
following example:
“Figure 6 shows that 72% of teachers agreed that scripted lesson plans
improved classroom organization, whereas 18% remained neutral.”
This sentence demonstrates balanced reporting. Instead of focusing only on
positive responses, it acknowledges neutrality, which strengthens objectivity.
Key Learning Point
Effective results writing:
•
Reports agreement, neutrality, and disagreement where relevant
•
Avoids selective reporting
•
Presents a complete but concise picture of teacher responses
Balanced reporting increases the trustworthiness of the findings and reflects
sound academic practice.
9.5 Describing Trends and Patterns
When presenting results, it is not enough to state individual numbers.
Academic writing requires students to identify patterns and trends in the data.
Trends help the reader understand how values change over time or how
different groups compare, without overloading the text with statistics.
In Pakistani research writing, students often list percentages from tables but
fail to explain what direction the data is moving in. Examiners, however,
expect students to summarize trends using precise and neutral academic
language.
9.5.1 Upward, Downward, and Stable Trends
Trends are usually described using verbs that indicate movement or stability.
The most commonly used verbs in academic results writing are:
•
Increased – to show growth or improvement
•
Decreased – to show decline or reduction
•
Remained stable – to show little or no change
•
Fluctuated – to show irregular rise and fall
These verbs should be used carefully and accurately, based on what the data
actually shows.
Contextual Example (Education – Pakistan)
Consider a study measuring reading performance of Grade 2 students in
government schools using EGRA-style assessments at three points: baseline,
midline, and endline.
A weak results sentence would list numbers only:
“At baseline the score was 28, at midline it was 36, and at endline it was 33.”
A stronger academic sentence focuses on the trend:
“Reading scores showed a gradual increase from baseline to midline,
followed by a slight decline at endline.”
This sentence:
•
Avoids unnecessary numbers
•
Highlights direction of change
•
Maintains a neutral, objective tone
Additional Local Examples
•
“Teacher attendance increased steadily during the first two quarters
of the academic year.”
•
“Student participation remained stable across urban schools but
decreased slightly in rural settings.”
•
“Performance levels fluctuated across districts, with no consistent
upward trend observed.”
Key Reminder for Students
Always ask:
Am I showing how the data changes, or am I only repeating numbers?
9.6 Linking Text with Tables and Figures

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
Tables and figures are supporting tools, not replacements for written
explanation. In academic writing, every table or figure must be clearly
connected to the text. Pakistani students often insert tables without proper
explanation, assuming the reader will “understand on their own.” This
weakens the quality of the results section.
9.6.1 Avoiding Disconnection Between Text and Data
A common mistake is referring to a table without explaining its significance.
Bad Example
“Table 3 shows the results.”
This sentence is weak because it:
•
Adds no meaning
•
Fails to highlight key findings
•
Forces the reader to interpret the data alone
Improved Academic Example
“As shown in Table 3, students taught using leveled readers demonstrated
higher comprehension scores than those in control schools.”
This improved version:
•
Refers clearly to the table
•
Highlights the main finding
•
Compares groups effectively
•
Guides the reader’s attention
Contextual Example (Teacher Feedback – Pakistan)
Instead of writing:
“Figure 5 shows teacher responses.”
A better academic sentence would be:
“As illustrated in Figure 5, a majority of teachers (72%) reported improved
classroom organization after using scripted lesson plans.”
Key Principle
A table shows data.
The text explains meaning.
Mini Checklist for Students
✔ Have I described the direction of change (increase, decrease,
stability)?
✔ Have I linked each table or figure to a clear finding?
✔ Have I avoided vague phrases like “shows the results”?
9.7 Common Mistakes Made by Pakistani Students
Despite collecting valid data, many Pakistani students lose marks in the
Results chapter because of how they present their findings rather than what
they find. Examiners frequently report that tables are inserted correctly, but
the accompanying text either repeats numbers mechanically, expresses
personal emotions, or explains causes prematurely. This section highlights the
most common mistakes and demonstrates how they can be corrected.
9.7.1 Repeating Table Numbers Without Explanation
One of the most frequent errors in results writing is simply repeating numerical
values from a table without explaining what they mean. Students often assume
that listing percentages is sufficient, but examiners expect students to guide
the reader toward the key message of the data.
For example, a student describing a table on Grade 2 reading performance may
write:
“Table 4 shows 45%, 30%, and 25%.”
This sentence provides numbers but no interpretation of importance. The
reader is left to guess what these percentages represent and why they matter.
A more effective academic description focuses on the dominant pattern in the
data:
“Table 4 shows that nearly half of the students fell into the lowperformance category.”
In this improved version, the student:
•
Refers to the table
•
Highlights the most significant finding
•
Avoids listing unnecessary figures
In Pakistani contexts—such as EGRA-style assessments or district-wise
comparisons—this approach helps examiners quickly understand the
educational implications of the data without reading the table repeatedly.
9.7.2 Using Emotional or Judgmental Language
Another common mistake is the use of emotional or judgmental language in
the Results section. Many students feel personally invested in their research
and unintentionally express frustration, disappointment, or surprise in their
writing.
For example:
“The results are very disappointing and shocking.”
While this sentence reflects the writer’s feelings, it is not academically
appropriate. Results sections must remain neutral and objective, allowing the
data to speak for itself.
A more acceptable academic alternative would be:
“The results indicate lower-than-expected performance across all
districts.”
This revised sentence:
•
Maintains a neutral tone
•
Communicates the seriousness of the finding
•
Leaves interpretation and explanation for the Discussion chapter
In Pakistani research contexts—especially in education, social sciences, and
development studies—emotional language can weaken the credibility of the
research and should be strictly avoided.
9.7.3 Mixing Results with Discussion
Many Pakistani students struggle to separate the Results and Discussion
chapters. As a result, they often begin explaining why the findings occurred
while still presenting the data.
For example:
“This happened because teachers were not trained.”
This statement introduces causal explanation, which belongs in the Discussion
chapter, not the Results section.
A more appropriate way to handle this in the Results chapter is to acknowledge
the pattern without explaining it:
“This pattern is discussed further in Chapter 5.”
By doing so, the student:
•
Maintains the integrity of the Results section
•
Signals to the reader that interpretation will follow later
•
Demonstrates clear academic structure
This distinction is particularly important in thesis writing, where examiners
closely assess whether students understand the purpose of each chapter.
9.8 Step-by-Step Results Paragraph Structure (With Contextual
Examples)
To present research findings clearly and professionally, students should follow
a consistent and logical paragraph structure in the Results chapter. Examiners
often note that weak results writing is not caused by poor data, but by unclear
organization and lack of focus. The four-step structure outlined below helps

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
students avoid common mistakes such as repeating numbers, using emotional
language, or mixing results with discussion.
Step 1: Reference the Table or Figure
Every results paragraph must begin by referring to the relevant table or figure.
This tells the reader where the data is located and establishes a clear link
between the written text and the visual evidence.
Contextual example (EGRA-style data):
“Table 4.1 presents the reading fluency levels of Grade 2 students across the
sampled districts.”
This opening sentence does not explain the results; it simply directs the reader
to the data source, which is a key expectation in academic writing.
Step 2: State the Main Finding
After referencing the table or figure, the paragraph should immediately
highlight the most important finding. Students should avoid listing multiple
percentages and instead focus on the dominant outcome.
Contextual example:
“The results show that a majority of students did not meet the minimum
reading fluency benchmark.”
This sentence guides the examiner to the key message without overwhelming
them with numbers.
Step 3: Highlight a Key Comparison or Trend
Once the main finding is established, the paragraph should briefly point out a
notable comparison or trend, such as differences between groups, districts, or
time periods.
Contextual example (district comparison):
“Students from urban schools demonstrated higher fluency scores compared
to those from rural schools.”
or
Contextual example (survey trend):
“An upward trend was observed in student participation levels from baseline
to endline.”
This step adds depth to the results while still remaining descriptive rather than
explanatory.
Step 4: End Without Interpretation
The paragraph should end without explaining why the results occurred.
Interpretation, causes, and implications must be reserved for the Discussion
chapter. Ending the paragraph objectively maintains academic discipline and
clarity.
Contextual example:
“These findings provide an overview of student reading performance across
the selected schools.”
This closing sentence signals completion of the results description without
crossing into analysis or recommendations.
Complete Model Results Paragraph (Putting All Steps Together)
“Table 4.1 presents the reading fluency levels of Grade 2 students across the
sampled districts. The results show that a majority of students did not meet the
minimum reading fluency benchmark. Students from urban schools
demonstrated higher fluency scores compared to those from rural schools.
These findings provide an overview of student reading performance across the
selected schools.”
This paragraph:
•
Refers to the table
•
Highlights the main finding
•
Identifies a key comparison
•
Ends without interpretation
Why This Structure Matters
When Pakistani students consistently apply this structure, their results writing
becomes:
•
Clear and logical
•
Examiner-friendly
•
Aligned with international academic standards
•
Easy to separate from the Discussion chapter
Most importantly, it allows students to let the data speak, which is the central
purpose of the Results section.
9.9 Practice Activities
Practice is essential for developing confidence in describing tables, charts, and
results. Many Pakistani students understand their data well but struggle to
express it objectively in academic English. The following activities are
designed to help students apply the language patterns introduced in this
chapter using realistic, familiar data.
Activity 1: Writing an EGRA Results Paragraph
In this activity, students are provided with a sample table presenting EGRAstyle reading results for Grade 2 students. The table may include indicators
such as correct words per minute, comprehension scores, or percentage of
students meeting a benchmark.
Students are required to write a 5–6 sentence results paragraph based on the
table.
The purpose of this activity is to help students learn how to:
•
Introduce a table properly
•
Highlight key findings rather than repeating all numbers
•
Maintain a neutral, academic tone
Contextual example
Suppose the table shows that:
•
34% of Grade 2 students met the reading fluency benchmark
•
66% remained below the benchmark
A strong results paragraph would focus on the overall pattern, not every figure.
For example, instead of listing all percentages, the student should emphasize
that a majority of students did not achieve the expected level of reading
fluency.
Students are encouraged to:
•
Begin by referring to the table (e.g., “Table 5.1 shows...”)
•
Identify the most important finding
•
Avoid explaining why the results occurred
This activity helps students move away from memorizing numbers and toward
analytical reporting, a skill expected by examiners and thesis supervisors in
Pakistani universities.
Activity 2: Error Correction — Language and Objectivity
This activity focuses on one of the most common weaknesses observed in
student theses and research reports: the use of emotional language and
interpretation in the Results section.
Students are given short sample sentences taken from results paragraphs that
contain:
•
Emotional or judgmental words (e.g., shocking, disappointing,
alarming)
•
Interpretations or explanations (e.g., because teachers were not
trained)
Students must:
1. Identify emotional language
2. Remove interpretation and explanation
3. Rewrite the sentence using objective academic language

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
Contextual example
An original sentence might read:
“The results are very disappointing and show that teachers are not doing their
job properly.”
After correction, the sentence should focus only on what the data shows, for
example:
“The results indicate lower performance levels across all observed
classrooms.”
Through this activity, students learn that:
•
The Results section is not a place for opinions or blame
•
Academic writing values neutral description over emotion
•
Interpretation belongs to a later chapter
This practice is especially important in Pakistani contexts, where students
often write with strong feelings about education issues but are penalized for
lack of objectivity.
9.10 Chapter Summary
This chapter has focused on helping students understand how to describe
tables, charts, and results clearly and objectively. The key message is that the
Results section exists to present evidence, not to argue or explain it.
Students have learned that:
•
Results describe what the data shows, not what the researcher thinks
about it
•
Tables and figures support the written text, but never replace it
•
Objectivity and neutrality are essential features of academic writing
•
Interpretation, explanation, and implications must be reserved for the
Discussion chapter
By mastering these skills, Pakistani students can significantly improve the
clarity, credibility, and academic quality of their research writing.
Chapter 10: Making Sense of Results (Not Just Reporting)
Chapter Overview
This chapter focuses on helping students move beyond simply reporting
research results to meaningfully interpreting them. Many students are able to
present tables, figures, and percentages correctly, but struggle to explain what
these findings actually mean within the Pakistani context. This chapter
addresses that gap by guiding students on how to analyse results thoughtfully,
connect them to local realities, and express interpretations in clear, simple
academic English. By the end of this chapter, students will be better prepared
to write analytically and to transition smoothly into the Discussion chapter of
their thesis.
Learning Outcomes
After completing this chapter, students will be able to:
1. Differentiate between reporting and interpreting research
findings
Understand the distinction between describing data and explaining its
significance.
2. Explain what research findings mean within the Pakistani context
Link results to local educational, social, or institutional realities
rather than presenting data in isolation.
3. Write analytical interpretations using clear and appropriate
academic language
Develop confidence in explaining findings without relying on overly
complex or technical English.
4. Prepare effective groundwork for the Discussion chapter
Use interpreted findings as a logical bridge between the Results and
Discussion sections of a thesis or research report.
10.1 Reporting vs. Interpreting Results: Understanding the
Difference
Many Pakistani students believe that once they have presented tables, figures,
and percentages, their work is complete. While accurate reporting of data is
essential, academic writing requires more than listing numbers. Examiners and
supervisors expect students to go a step further by explaining what those
numbers mean in relation to the research problem, the local context, and
practical realities in Pakistan. Understanding the difference between reporting
and interpreting results is therefore a crucial academic skill.
10.1.1 What Is Reporting?
Reporting refers to the clear and factual presentation of research results. At
this stage, the researcher simply tells the reader what the data shows without
offering explanations or judgments. Reporting involves stating numbers,
percentages, and observable trends and directing the reader to relevant tables,
charts, or figures.
For example, a student studying teacher professional development may write:
“Table 4.2 shows that 62% of teachers received training during the academic
year.”
This sentence is an example of correct reporting. It accurately reflects the data
and refers the reader to a specific table. However, it stops there. The reader is
informed about what happened, but not why it matters or what it implies for
teaching and learning in Pakistan.
Reporting is necessary and forms the foundation of the Results chapter, but on
its own it does not demonstrate analysis or critical thinking.
10.1.2 What Is Interpretation?
Interpretation goes beyond reporting by explaining the significance of the
findings. When interpreting results, the researcher connects the data to
context, policy, practice, or existing challenges. Interpretation answers the
question: What do these results tell us about the research problem?
Using the same example, an interpretive statement would read:
“Although a majority of teachers received training, this did not translate into
improved student outcomes, suggesting gaps in classroom-level support.”
Here, the writer moves beyond numbers to highlight an important issue. The
interpretation links teacher training to student learning and raises a concern
that is highly relevant in the Pakistani context, where professional
development programs are often implemented without sufficient follow-up,
mentoring, or instructional materials.
Interpretation shows the reader that the student understands not only the data
but also the realities of implementation in Pakistani institutions.
Common Mistakes Made by Pakistani Students

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
One of the most common mistakes Pakistani students make is repeating the
same numbers in different words without adding meaning. For example:
“Table 4.2 shows that 62% of teachers received training. This means that
more than half of the teachers were trained.”
While this sentence restates the data, it does not interpret it. Another frequent
error is ending the Results section immediately after reporting figures, without
explaining their implications for policy, practice, or future research.
Such writing may be grammatically correct, but it fails to demonstrate
analytical thinking, which is a key requirement at the university level.
10.2 Asking the Right Question: “So What?”
To move from reporting to interpretation, students must develop the habit of
asking one simple but powerful question: “So what?” After presenting any
result, the researcher should pause and reflect on its significance.
Students should ask themselves:
•
So what does this result actually mean?
•
Why is this finding important for Pakistan?
•
Who is affected by this outcome—students, teachers, institutions, or
policymakers?
•
What problem does this result help explain or highlight?
For example, if a study finds that trained teachers are not producing better
student outcomes, this raises important questions about the quality of training,
classroom resources, monitoring mechanisms, and systemic constraints in
public-sector schools.
Practice Prompt
To strengthen analytical thinking, students should regularly reflect on the
following question:
“If this result were shared with a policymaker in Pakistan, what would they
learn from it?”
If the answer is unclear or limited to numbers, the result likely needs deeper
interpretation. This mindset helps students write research that is not only
academically sound but also meaningful and relevant to Pakistan’s real-world
challenges.
10.3 Linking Findings to the Pakistani Context
Interpreting research findings requires more than restating numbers or trends.
In Pakistan, research results must be understood within the social,
institutional, and classroom realities in which data is generated. Without
acknowledging context, interpretations remain incomplete and, at times,
misleading. This section explains why contextual understanding is essential
and demonstrates how students can meaningfully connect their findings to the
Pakistani setting.
10.3.1 Why Context Matters in Pakistan
Pakistan’s education system is highly diverse, and research findings cannot be
interpreted in the same way across all settings. One of the most significant
contextual factors is the difference between urban and rural environments.
Urban schools often have better access to infrastructure, teaching resources,
and trained staff, while rural schools frequently face shortages of materials,
limited supervision, and difficult learning conditions. A result that appears
modest in an urban context may actually reflect substantial effort in a rural
setting.
Another important factor is resource constraints in public-sector institutions.
Many government schools operate with limited budgets, insufficient teaching
and learning materials, and minimal ongoing professional support for teachers.
When interpreting findings related to teaching quality or student achievement,
these limitations must be considered. For example, weak learning outcomes
may not indicate poor teaching practices alone but may reflect systemic
challenges beyond the teacher’s control.
Language of instruction also plays a critical role in shaping learning outcomes.
In Pakistan, students may be taught in Urdu, Sindhi, English, or a combination
of languages, often differing from the language spoken at home. When
interpreting reading or comprehension results, it is essential to consider
whether students are being assessed in a familiar language or one that poses
additional cognitive demands.
Finally, classroom realities such as large class sizes and multigrade teaching
significantly influence teaching effectiveness. In many public schools, a single
teacher manages 40–60 students or teaches multiple grade levels
simultaneously. Under such conditions, even well-designed training programs
may have limited immediate impact. Recognizing these realities allows
students to produce fair, balanced, and academically sound interpretations of
their data.
10.3.2 Contextual Interpretation Example (Education)
Consider the following research finding:
“Students in trained teachers’ classrooms showed only marginal improvement
in reading scores.”
A weak interpretation of this finding would be:
“The training was not effective.”
This statement is overly simplistic and ignores the context in which the
training was implemented. It places full responsibility on the training program
without considering environmental or systemic factors.
A strong contextual interpretation would be:
“The limited improvement may be due to the absence of adequate reading
materials and large class sizes commonly found in government schools in
rural Pakistan.”
This interpretation demonstrates analytical thinking by acknowledging that
training alone may not be sufficient in settings where teachers lack
instructional resources and face heavy classroom demands. It reflects an
understanding of the Pakistani education context and avoids unfair or
unsupported conclusions.
10.4 Interpreting Results Beyond Numbers
Good academic writing moves beyond numbers to explain why results appear
as they do. Interpretation involves exploring possible reasons for findings
while remaining cautious and evidence-based. This is particularly important
in Pakistan, where research environments are complex and influenced by
multiple interacting factors.

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
10.4.1 Explaining Possible Reasons
When interpreting findings, students should use cautious academic language
rather than absolute or emotional statements. Phrases such as may be due to,
could be explained by, may suggest, and it is possible that allow researchers
to present reasonable explanations without overstating their claims.
For example:
“The findings may be explained by the fact that teachers received training
without ongoing classroom mentoring.”
This sentence acknowledges a likely explanation while recognizing that other
factors may also be involved. Such language reflects academic maturity and
protects the writer from making unsupported claims.
10.4.2 Avoiding Over-Claiming
A common weakness in student writing is over-claiming, where conclusions
are stated more strongly than the evidence allows. Statements such as:
•
“This proves that...”
•
“This clearly shows that...”
•
“This confirms that training is useless...”
are rarely appropriate in academic research, especially in small-scale or
context-specific studies.
Instead, students should use more measured alternatives, such as:
•
“The findings suggest...”
•
“The results indicate...”
•
“The data points toward...”
These expressions communicate confidence while respecting the limits of the
data. They also align with international academic standards and are
particularly important when addressing complex systems like education in
Pakistan.
10.5 Connecting Findings to Research Objectives
One of the most important aspects of academic interpretation is demonstrating
how research findings respond directly to the objectives and questions stated
at the beginning of the study. Many Pakistani students present their results
accurately but fail to explicitly link these results back to what the study
originally set out to investigate. As a result, examiners and supervisors often
feel that the findings are disconnected or incomplete.
Connecting findings to research objectives requires the researcher to revisit
each research question and clearly show how the data answers it. This does
not require complex language; rather, it requires clarity and focus. Each major
finding should be discussed in relation to a specific research question or
objective, making it evident to the reader that the study has achieved its
intended purpose.
At the same time, students must avoid introducing new ideas, explanations, or
themes that were not part of the original research design. For example, if the
study examined the impact of teacher training on student reading performance,
the interpretation should remain within that scope and should not suddenly
introduce issues such as parental involvement or school leadership unless
these were explicitly studied.
10.5.1 Revisiting Research Questions
A practical way to connect findings to objectives is to explicitly refer back to
the research questions when interpreting results. This helps guide the reader
and strengthens the logical flow of the thesis.
For example, if a research question asked whether teacher training improved
reading outcomes among Grade 3 students in government schools, the
interpretation should directly address this relationship:
“This finding directly addresses Research Question 2, which examined the
relationship between teacher training and student reading performance.”
The researcher may then briefly explain what the data reveals about that
relationship, whether it shows improvement, limited impact, or no significant
change. This approach reassures the reader that the findings are purposeful
and analytically grounded rather than descriptive.
10.6 Linking Findings to Existing Pakistani and International
Studies
Interpreting findings also involves positioning the study within the broader
body of existing research. Academic research does not exist in isolation;
rather, it builds on, confirms, or challenges previous studies. For Pakistani
students, this step is especially important, as it demonstrates awareness of both
local and international research while highlighting contextual differences.
10.6.1 Supporting Existing Research
When findings are consistent with previous studies, students should clearly
state this alignment. Doing so strengthens the credibility of the research and
shows that the results are not unusual or isolated.
For instance, if a study finds that teacher training alone does not significantly
improve reading outcomes, this can be linked to earlier Pakistani research that
emphasizes the need for classroom resources:
“These findings align with previous studies conducted in Pakistan, which
highlight the importance of instructional materials alongside teacher
training.”
Such statements demonstrate that the current study reinforces existing
evidence and contributes to a growing understanding of the issue within the
local context.
10.6.2 Explaining Differences Between Studies
In some cases, findings may differ from international research, particularly
studies conducted in high-income countries. Rather than viewing these
differences as weaknesses, students should interpret them as reflections of
contextual realities.
For example, research conducted in well-resourced education systems may
show strong gains from teacher training alone. However, in Pakistan, public
schools often face challenges such as overcrowded classrooms, limited
teaching materials, and insufficient ongoing support. These conditions must
be acknowledged when interpreting results.
This can be expressed academically as follows:
“Unlike studies conducted in high-income contexts, the present findings
reflect structural constraints faced by public schools in Pakistan.”
By explaining differences in this way, students demonstrate critical thinking

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
and contextual awareness. They show that their findings are meaningful within
their specific setting and that variation across studies is often shaped by
economic, institutional, and systemic factors rather than methodological
flaws.
By systematically linking findings to research objectives and situating them
within existing literature, students move from simple reporting to genuine
academic interpretation. This approach not only strengthens the Results and
Discussion sections but also enhances the overall coherence and credibility of
the research.
10.7 From Findings to Implications: What Do These Results
Suggest?
Interpreting research findings is incomplete unless the researcher explains
what those findings imply for decision-making and practice. In the Pakistani
context, research is often expected to inform policy reform, program design,
and institutional improvement. Therefore, students must learn to move from
analysis to implication—that is, from understanding what the data shows to
explaining what should be considered or changed as a result.
Implications do not mean giving personal opinions or making unrealistic
recommendations. Instead, they involve drawing reasonable, evidence-based
suggestions that logically follow from the findings and remain grounded in the
realities of Pakistani institutions.
10.7.1 Policy Implications
Policy implications address what ministries, departments, donor agencies, or
public institutions should consider when planning or revising programs. In
Pakistan, this often includes bodies such as provincial education departments,
curriculum authorities, teacher training institutions, and development partners.
For example, if a study finds that teacher training programs have been
implemented widely but student learning outcomes remain weak, the
implication is not that training is ineffective. Rather, the findings may suggest
that training alone is insufficient when other enabling conditions are missing.
In an education study conducted in public primary schools, findings may show
that while a large proportion of teachers have attended professional
development workshops, classrooms lack basic learning materials such as
leveled storybooks or teaching aids. In this case, a policy-level implication
could be framed as follows:
The findings suggest that teacher professional development programs should
be accompanied by the provision of classroom reading materials.
This implication directly connects evidence to policy planning. It encourages
decision-makers to design integrated interventions, where training, materials,
and monitoring are planned together rather than as separate activities.
Importantly, the implication does not overstate the findings but remains
cautious and realistic.
10.7.2 Practice-Level Implications
Practice-level implications focus on what the findings suggest for teachers,
head teachers, school leaders, and institutions. These implications are
especially important in Pakistan, where classroom realities—such as large
class sizes, limited supervision, and multigrade teaching—strongly influence
outcomes.
For instance, research may reveal that teachers attended training sessions but
struggled to apply new strategies in daily classroom practice. This could
indicate that one-time workshops are insufficient to change teaching behavior,
particularly in under-resourced schools.
A practice-level implication may therefore be expressed as:
Teachers may require ongoing coaching rather than one-time training
workshops.
This implication highlights the need for continuous support, such as classroom
observation, mentoring, and feedback. It also recognizes that professional
learning is a process rather than a single event. For head teachers and school
leaders, such findings may suggest the importance of instructional leadership
and regular follow-up at the school level.
10.8 Model Paragraph: From Data to Meaning (Annotated)
The following paragraph demonstrates how students can move from
presenting findings to interpreting their meaning in a clear and structured way:
The findings suggest that teacher training alone may not improve reading
outcomes unless supported by classroom materials. Although 78% of teachers
reported receiving professional development, student reading scores
remained low. This may be due to the lack of age-appropriate reading
resources in classrooms, a challenge frequently observed in public schools in
Pakistan. These results indicate that training initiatives should be integrated
with material support to achieve meaningful learning gains.
Annotation
•
First sentence – Main interpretation: States the key message derived
from the findings.
•
Second sentence – Evidence from findings: Refers directly to data to
support the interpretation.
•
Third sentence – Contextual explanation: Links the findings to
classroom realities in Pakistan.
•
Fourth sentence – Implication: Explains what the findings suggest
for future action or planning.
Why This Structure Matters
This structured approach helps students write interpretations that are:
•
Evidence-based
•
Contextually grounded
•
Academically cautious
•
Directly useful for policy and practice
Most importantly, it helps students avoid merely repeating results and instead
demonstrate critical academic thinking, which is a key expectation in thesis
evaluation and viva examinations.
10.9 Common Errors Made by Pakistani Students When
Interpreting Results
Many Pakistani students successfully present tables, percentages, and figures
in the Results chapter, yet their work loses academic strength at the point
where interpretation is required. This weakness often does not stem from a
lack of understanding of the data, but from uncertainty about how to explain
findings in an academic and contextual manner. The most common errors are
discussed below.

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
Treating Interpretation as Personal Opinion
A frequent mistake is confusing interpretation with personal opinion. Students
often write statements such as “I think the training was not useful” or “In my
view, students are not serious about learning.” While such expressions may
be acceptable in informal writing, they are inappropriate in academic research.
Interpretation must always be grounded in evidence and framed using cautious
academic language. Instead of expressing personal beliefs, students should
explain what the data suggests.
For example, rather than writing “I believe teacher training is ineffective,” a
more academic interpretation would be “The findings suggest that teacher
training alone did not lead to measurable improvements in student reading
performance.”
Using Emotional or Judgmental Language
Another common issue is the use of emotional or judgmental language.
Students sometimes describe results using words such as poor, failure, very
bad, or extremely disappointing. Such language reflects emotion rather than
analysis and weakens the credibility of the research.
For instance, writing “The results are very disappointing and show complete
failure of the system” should be avoided. A more appropriate academic
interpretation would be “The results indicate limited improvement,
highlighting gaps in the current implementation approach.”
Academic writing requires neutrality. The role of the researcher is not to blame
or praise, but to explain patterns and outcomes logically.
Ignoring Local Constraints
Many interpretations remain incomplete because students ignore the realities
of the Pakistani context. Findings are sometimes explained as if schools,
universities, or organizations operate under ideal conditions. This results in
conclusions that appear unrealistic or disconnected from ground realities.
For example, a student may write “Teachers did not apply new methods
despite receiving training” without considering factors such as large class
sizes, lack of teaching materials, or administrative workload. A stronger
interpretation
would
acknowledge
these
constraints:
“The limited application of new teaching methods may be linked to large class
sizes and the absence of classroom resources commonly observed in public
schools in Pakistan.”
By recognizing contextual constraints, interpretations become more realistic
and academically sound.
Writing Conclusions Instead of Interpretations
Another frequent error is writing conclusions too early. Students sometimes
treat the interpretation section as a place to give final recommendations or
strong judgments. However, interpretation should focus on explaining
findings, not on closing the study.
For example, writing “Therefore, the government must completely change its
training policy” moves beyond interpretation and enters the conclusion or
recommendation stage. At this point, the student should instead focus on what
the findings indicate, such as:
“These findings suggest the need for further examination of how teacher
training programs are supported at the classroom level.”
Keeping interpretation analytical rather than prescriptive is essential for
maintaining proper thesis structure.
10.10 Guided Practice Activities
To strengthen students’ ability to interpret findings accurately, the following
guided activities are designed to encourage practice and reflection.
Activity 1: Identify Interpretation
Students are given a set of sentences and asked to classify each one as either
reporting or interpretation.
Example Sentences
1. “Table 5 shows that 68% of teachers attended professional
development training.”
2. “This suggests that training coverage was relatively high among the
sampled schools.”
3. “Student reading scores increased by only 4% over one academic
year.”
4. “The small increase may indicate that training alone was insufficient
to improve learning outcomes.”
Task
Students mark each sentence as:
•
Reporting
•
Interpretation
This activity helps students clearly distinguish between describing data and
explaining its meaning.
Activity 2: Improve the Interpretation
In this activity, students are provided with weak or problematic interpretations
and asked to rewrite them using appropriate academic language and Pakistani
context.
Weak Interpretation Example
“The results are bad and show that teachers are not serious.”
Student Task
Rewrite the sentence by:
•
Using cautious academic language
•
Linking the explanation to Pakistani classroom realities
Improved Example
“The findings suggest limited improvement in teaching practices, which may
be influenced by contextual factors such as workload, limited resources, and
large class sizes in public schools.”
This exercise encourages students to move away from emotional judgments
and towards evidence-based, context-aware interpretation.
Strong interpretation does not require complex vocabulary. It requires clear
thinking, awareness of context, and respect for evidence. By avoiding
common errors and practicing analytical explanation, students can
significantly improve the quality of their research writing and prepare
effectively for the Discussion chapter.
10.11 Chapter Summary
This chapter highlighted the critical distinction between reporting and
interpreting research findings. While reporting focuses on describing what the
data shows, interpretation explains why those findings are important and what
they imply. Strong academic writing requires students to move beyond
numbers and percentages by linking results to the research objectives and the
broader context in which the study was conducted. In the Pakistani context,
interpretation must be informed by local realities such as limited resources,
institutional constraints, classroom conditions, and socio-cultural factors,

ensuring that findings are meaningful, realistic, and relevant rather than
abstract or disconnected from practice.

Recommendations
This part of the book guides students in interpreting findings, drawing
meaningful conclusions, and proposing realistic recommendations within the
Pakistani context. It helps students move beyond simply reporting results to
explaining what the findings mean, how they relate to existing literature, and
why they matter for policy and practice. Emphasis is placed on linking results

cultural

Chapter 11: Writing Discussion with Confidence
Chapter Overview
The discussion chapter is often the most challenging part of academic writing
for Pakistani students. While many students are able to collect data and present
results accurately, they frequently struggle to interpret their findings, relate
them to existing literature, and explain results within the local research
context. As a result, discussion sections often become a repetition of results or
a collection of memorized phrases rather than a critical academic argument.
This chapter guides students in developing a clear, confident, and analytical
discussion by explaining how to move beyond “what was found” to “what the
findings mean.” Drawing on commonly used discussion expressions from
academic writing conventions, the chapter demonstrates how these
expressions should be used purposefully, not mechanically. Special emphasis
is placed on contextualizing findings within Pakistan, including institutional,
cultural, socioeconomic, and policy-related factors that influence research
outcomes.
Through practical examples based on Pakistani studies, this chapter shows
students how to compare their findings with previous local and international
research, explain similarities and contradictions, and use cautious academic
language to avoid overgeneralization. By the end of the chapter, students will
understand how the discussion section functions as the intellectual core of the
thesis or research report, where interpretation, reasoning, and scholarly voice
are most clearly demonstrated.
Chapter Objectives
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to:
1. Differentiate clearly between results and discussion, and
understand the distinct purpose of each section in a thesis or research
report.
2. Interpret research findings logically, explaining what the results
mean in relation to the study’s research questions or objectives.
3. Use appropriate academic language (e.g., cautious claims, modal
verbs, and hedging expressions) to discuss findings without making
unsupported or absolute statements.
4. Compare their findings with previous studies, including both
international research and studies conducted in Pakistan.
5. Explain similarities and contradictions between their findings and
earlier research by considering contextual factors such as location,
sample characteristics, resources, and time.
6. Integrate Pakistan-specific contextual explanations, including
educational, social, cultural, and institutional realities, into the
discussion.
7. Address unexpected, weak, or mixed findings in an academically
honest and analytical manner.
8. Link discussion points back to research questions and objectives,
ensuring coherence and logical flow throughout the chapter.
9. Avoid common discussion-writing errors made by Pakistani
students, such as repetition, overgeneralization, and unsupported
personal opinions.
10. Develop confidence in academic voice, enabling students to present
their interpretations clearly, critically, and professionally.
11.1 Understanding the Purpose of the Discussion Chapter
For many Pakistani students, the discussion chapter is the most difficult
section of a thesis or research report. Despite collecting data carefully and
presenting results accurately, students often struggle to explain what the
findings actually mean. As a result, examiners frequently comment that the
discussion section is either “too descriptive” or “repetitive,” leading to loss of
marks.
The primary purpose of the discussion chapter is to interpret the research
findings, not to repeat them. In this chapter, the researcher moves beyond
numbers, tables, and percentages to explain why certain results occurred, how
they relate to existing research, and what they imply for the local context.
What the Discussion Is
The discussion section:
•
Explains the meaning of the findings
•
Interprets results in relation to research questions and objectives
•
Compares findings with previous studies
•
Explains similarities and contradictions
•
Situates results within the Pakistani context
•
Highlights practical and policy implications
What the Discussion Is Not
The discussion section is not:
•
A repetition of tables and figures
•
A summary of percentages already presented in the results chapter
•
A personal opinion or emotional judgment
•
A place to introduce new data
Difference Between Results and Discussion Sections
This distinction is critical:
•
Results Section answers:
What was found?
•
Example:
“Sixty-two percent of teachers reported using phonics-based
instruction.”
•
Discussion Section answers:
What does this mean, why did it happen, and how does it relate
to existing knowledge?
•
Example:
“The relatively high use of phonics-based instruction may be
attributed to recent teacher training initiatives; however, classroom
observations suggest inconsistent implementation, indicating a gap between
training and practice.”
Why Pakistani Students Commonly Lose Marks

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
Pakistani students often lose marks in the discussion chapter because:
•
They repeat results word-for-word
•
They avoid interpretation due to fear of “wrong English”
•
They rely heavily on foreign studies without contextual adaptation
•
They fail to explain results in relation to local realities, such as:
o Multigrade classrooms
o Language of instruction issues
o Limited teaching resources
o Socioeconomic constraints
Key Clarification
A simple but powerful way to remember the role of the discussion chapter is:
Results = What was found
Discussion = What it means, why it happened, and how it fits existing
knowledge
Understanding this distinction helps students write discussions that are
analytical, confident, and academically sound.
11.2 Structure of a Strong Discussion Chapter
A well-written discussion chapter follows a logical and coherent structure,
guiding the reader from findings to interpretation and finally to implications.
Rather than presenting ideas randomly, the discussion should flow
systematically.
Recommended Flow of the Discussion Chapter
1. Brief Restatement of Key Findings
The chapter should begin by summarizing the most important findings
without repeating tables or figures.
Example:
“This study found that while teacher attendance was high, student
engagement during reading lessons remained limited.”
2. Interpretation of Findings
The researcher explains why these findings may have occurred.
Example (Pakistan context):
“This may be due to large class sizes and limited availability of ageappropriate reading materials in public schools.”
3. Comparison with Previous Studies
Findings are compared with:
o Pakistani research studies
o Regional or international literature
Example:
“These findings are consistent with studies conducted in rural Sindh,
which also reported low student participation despite regular teacher
presence.”
4. Explanation of Similarities and Differences
Any agreement or contradiction with previous research must be explained.
Example:
“Unlike studies conducted in private schools, this research did not observe
interactive teaching practices, possibly due to differences in teacher
training and classroom resources.”
5. Contextual Factors (Pakistan-Specific)
Strong discussions acknowledge local realities such as:
o Language barriers (Urdu, Sindhi, English)
o Multigrade teaching
o Rural–urban disparities
o Policy implementation gaps
Example:
“The multilingual classroom environment may have affected students’
comprehension and participation.”
6. Implications for Practice and Policy
The chapter concludes by explaining what the findings mean for:
o Teachers
o Institutions
o Policymakers
Example:
“These findings suggest the need for classroom-focused coaching rather
than one-time training workshops.”
Visual Mapping of the Discussion Process
A helpful way to conceptualize the discussion chapter is:
Results → Interpretation → Comparison → Context → Implications
This sequence ensures that the discussion remains:
•
Logical
•
Analytical
•
Contextually grounded
•
Relevant to Pakistani academic and policy settings
A strong discussion chapter does not require complex vocabulary or
exaggerated claims. What examiners value most is clear thinking, logical
interpretation, and contextual awareness. When students focus on explaining
why results occurred and what they mean for Pakistan, confidence in academic
writing naturally follows.
11.3 Restating Key Findings Without Repeating Results
One of the most common challenges faced by Pakistani students in thesis
writing is understanding how to restate key findings in the discussion section
without simply repeating the results section. Many students assume that
discussion means rewriting tables, percentages, or entire result paragraphs.
However, the purpose of restating findings is not to reproduce data, but to
remind the reader of the main outcomes so they can be interpreted and
explained.
In the discussion chapter, findings are usually restated by referring back to the
research objectives or hypotheses introduced earlier in the study. This helps
the reader clearly see how the results answer the research questions. Instead
of presenting numbers again, the writer summarizes the overall pattern or key
trend observed in the data.
Writers commonly use neutral and academic sentence starters such as:
•
This study found that...
•
The findings indicate that...
•
The results suggest that...
These expressions allow the researcher to restate findings concisely and
confidently without repeating technical details already presented in the results
chapter.
Pakistani Contextual Examples
For instance, in a study examining classroom practices in government primary
schools in Sindh, the results chapter may have included detailed observation
checklists and frequency tables. In the discussion chapter, the finding can be
restated more broadly:
This study found that student-centered instructional practices were observed
infrequently in most classrooms, despite the availability of lesson plans.
Similarly, when discussing teacher survey data, rather than repeating
percentage figures, the discussion might state:
The findings indicate that a majority of teachers expressed confidence in using
the new curriculum; however, this confidence was not consistently reflected in
their classroom practices.
In the case of student assessment data, instead of reproducing test scores, the
researcher may write:
The results suggest that students demonstrated basic decoding skills, but
struggled with reading comprehension tasks that required higher-order
thinking.
These restatements provide a clear entry point into interpretation while
avoiding unnecessary repetition.
