PART VII — Language Accuracy Made Simple
This section addresses one of the most common challenges faced by Pakistani
students: language accuracy in academic writing. Many students have strong
ideas and sound research, but their work is weakened by unclear sentence
structure, incorrect tense usage, and poor logical flow. This part of the book
simplifies academic language rules and presents them in a practical, easy-toapply manner, avoiding complex grammar terminology.
Instead of teaching English as a subject, this section teaches English as a tool
for academic communication. It focuses on the most frequently used language
features in theses and research reports, such as correct tense selection, use of
logical connectors, and sentence clarity. Through short explanations, local
examples, and common error corrections, students learn how to express their
ideas accurately and confidently.
The aim of this part is to help students reduce language-related fear, improve
clarity, and ensure that language does not become a barrier to demonstrating
academic understanding.
Chapter 13: Tenses in Thesis Writing
Chapter Overview
Tenses in Thesis Writing (Without Confusion)
This chapter addresses one of the most persistent challenges faced by Pakistani
university students: the correct use of verb tenses in thesis and research
writing. Many students possess a basic understanding of English grammar, yet
they struggle to apply tenses accurately in academic contexts such as
introductions, literature reviews, methodology, findings, and discussion
sections. As a result, their writing often appears inconsistent, unclear, or
unpolished, despite strong research content.
Rather than presenting tense rules in isolation, this chapter adopts a functionbased approach, demonstrating that tense selection depends on what the writer
is doing—describing a general fact, reporting completed research, referring to
previous studies, or interpreting results. Drawing inspiration from the English
for Thesis and Academic Writing framework, the chapter simplifies tense
usage into practical rules supported by clear tables, chapter-wise guidance,
and Pakistan-relevant examples.
Special attention is given to common errors made by Pakistani students,
particularly those arising from Urdu-to-English translation, overgeneralization
of present tense, and confusion between past and present perfect forms.
Through explanations, before–after examples, and guided practice, the chapter
aims to build students’ confidence so they can use tenses accurately and
consistently throughout their thesis.
Learning Outcomes
After completing this chapter, students will be able to:
1. Understand the functional logic of tense usage in academic and
thesis writing rather than relying on memorized grammar rules.
2. Differentiate clearly between present tense, past tense, and present
perfect tense and explain when and why each is used in a thesis.
3. Apply correct tenses across different thesis chapters, including
Introduction, Literature Review, Methodology, Findings, Discussion,
and Conclusion.
4. Identify and correct common tense-related errors frequently made
by Pakistani students in academic writing.
5. Use tense-consistent sentences and paragraphs to improve clarity,
coherence, and academic tone.
6. Employ modal verbs appropriately (e.g., may, might, can) to express
caution and academic judgment in discussion and conclusion sections.
7. Self-edit thesis drafts using a practical tense checklist, reducing
dependence on supervisors for repeated corrections.
13.1 Why Tenses Confuse Pakistani Students
One of the most frequently corrected aspects of thesis writing in Pakistani
universities is the use of verb tenses. Students often receive repeated
comments such as “check your tense,” “be consistent,” or “this should be in
past tense,” yet many remain unsure why these corrections are necessary. This
confusion does not arise from a lack of intelligence or effort; rather, it is rooted
in how English is learned and used in the Pakistani academic context.

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
A major source of difficulty is the direct translation from Urdu into English.
In Urdu, tense usage is more flexible and often inferred from context rather
than strictly marked throughout a paragraph. When students mentally draft a
sentence in Urdu and then translate it into English, the result is frequently a
sentence where the tense sounds natural in Urdu but appears incorrect or
inconsistent in English academic writing. For example, an Urdu sentence
describing a completed action may still feel appropriate in present tense when
translated, even though English academic conventions require past tense.
Another common issue is the memorization of grammar rules without
understanding their application. Many students can correctly recite definitions
such as “present tense is used for current actions” or “past tense is used for
completed actions,” yet they struggle to apply these rules when writing a
methodology or presenting findings. This gap between knowing the rule and
using it in real academic writing creates uncertainty and hesitation.
As a result, students often mix tenses within a single paragraph, sometimes
even within the same sentence. For instance, a student may begin a paragraph
by describing what the study was conducted to do, then immediately shift to
what the study shows, without realizing that these two actions belong to
different time frames. This mixing makes the writing difficult to follow and
signals a lack of control over academic style, even when the research itself is
sound.
Perhaps the most widespread problem is the overuse of present tense
everywhere. Many Pakistani students believe that academic writing must
always be in present tense because it “sounds formal.” Consequently, they
write sentences such as “The researcher collects data from 100 teachers”
even though the data collection has already been completed. This habit often
leads to repeated corrections from supervisors, which can discourage students
and make tense usage feel like a constant struggle.
Because of these challenges, students frequently ask similar questions during
supervision meetings:
•
“Should I write is or was here?”
•
“Can I use present tense in the findings section?”
•
“Why does my supervisor keep correcting my tenses when my meaning
is clear?”
These questions reflect not carelessness, but overthinking and uncertainty. The
purpose of this chapter is to reduce this anxiety by showing that tense selection
in thesis writing is not confusing or arbitrary. Instead, it follows a small
number of clear, logical principles that can be learned and applied with
confidence.
13.2 The Golden Rule of Tenses in Academic Writing
The most important principal students must understand is this:
In academic writing, tense depends on the function of the sentence, not on
the chapter title.
Many students assume that each chapter of a thesis has a fixed tense—for
example, that the introduction must always be in present tense or that the
findings must always be in past tense. In reality, a single chapter may contain
more than one tense, depending on what the writer is doing at a particular
moment.
To simplify tense selection, students should ask themselves three guiding
questions before writing any sentence.
First, is the sentence describing a general fact or accepted knowledge?
If the information is always true, widely accepted, or still valid at the time of
writing, present tense is usually appropriate. For example, statements about
the importance of education or the role of assessment systems typically fall
into this category.
Second, is the sentence describing a completed action in my own study?
If the action has already been carried out—such as collecting data, conducting
interviews, or analyzing results—past tense should be used. This applies
especially to the methodology and findings sections, where the researcher
reports what was done and what was found.
Third, is the sentence referring to research conducted by others?
If the sentence refers to a general body of existing research that remains
relevant, present perfect tense is often appropriate. However, if the sentence
refers to a specific study conducted at a specific time, past tense is usually
required.
By consistently applying these three questions, students can make accurate
tense choices without guessing. Instead of memorizing long grammar lists,
they learn to match tense with meaning, which is the foundation of clear and
professional academic writing.
13.3 Present Tense – When the Fact Is Always True
In academic writing, the present tense is used to express ideas, facts, and
conditions that are generally true, widely accepted, or still valid at the time of
writing. Pakistani students often hesitate to use the present tense in theses
because they assume that “academic writing must be in past tense.” This
assumption leads to unnecessary errors and weak expression.
The key principle to remember is simple:
If a statement is true now, was true before, and will remain true in the
future, the present tense should be used.

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
In thesis writing, the present tense commonly appears when the writer is
describing established knowledge, definitions, or the structure and content of
the thesis itself. For example, concepts such as education, literacy, poverty,
governance, or learning outcomes are not limited to a specific time period;
therefore, they should be written in the present tense.
Consider the following sentence:
Education plays a critical role in national development.
This statement expresses a general and universally accepted truth. It is not
linked to a specific year or study, so the present tense plays is appropriate.
Writing this sentence in the past tense would incorrectly suggest that education
was important only in the past, which is not the intended meaning.
The present tense is also used when referring to tables, figures, and chapters
in a thesis because these elements exist within the document and remain
relevant for the reader. For example:
Table 4.2 shows the reading scores of Grade 3 students.
Although the data were collected earlier, the table itself currently shows the
information to the reader. Therefore, the verb shows is correctly written in the
present tense.
Pakistani students often make the mistake of using the past tense in such
situations, especially when translating directly from Urdu or when trying to
sound “more academic.” A common error is:
Education played an important role in society.
This sentence incorrectly implies that education is no longer important. The
correct academic version is:
Education plays an important role in society.
Using the present tense accurately helps make academic writing clearer,
stronger, and more confident.
13.4 Past Tense – When the Action Is Completed
The past tense is used in academic writing to describe actions, processes, or
events that were completed before the thesis was written. In simple terms, if
something has already happened and is finished, it should be written in the
past tense.
In thesis writing, the past tense is most commonly used when the student is
describing what they did, how the data were collected, what was found, or
what previous researchers did in a specific study. These actions belong to a
definite time in the past and are not ongoing.
For this reason, the past tense is dominant in the Methodology and Results
chapters. When students describe their research design, sample, tools, or
procedures, they are reporting completed actions. For example:
Data were collected from 120 teachers in Sindh.
This sentence clearly indicates that the data collection process has already
been completed. Using the present tense here would be grammatically
incorrect and academically misleading.
Similarly, when describing how a study was carried out, the past tense is
required:
The survey was conducted in government schools.
This sentence reports a finished activity. It does not describe a general truth or
an ongoing process, so the present tense should not be used.
A very common mistake among Pakistani students is writing the methodology
in the present tense, as shown below:
Data are collected from 120 teachers.
This sentence suggests that data collection is still happening, which is not true
in a completed thesis. The correct academic form is:
Data were collected from 120 teachers.
Using the past tense consistently in such sections helps establish clarity,
accuracy, and academic credibility. It also signals to examiners and
supervisors that the student understands the difference between reporting
actions and stating general facts.
13.5 Present Perfect – When Research Connects Past to Present
One of the most confusing tenses for Pakistani students in thesis writing is the
present perfect tense (has/have + past participle). This confusion often arises
because Urdu does not use tense in the same functional way as English
academic writing. As a result, students either avoid the present perfect entirely
or use the simple past tense everywhere.
The present perfect tense is used in academic writing when an action began in
the past but remains relevant in the present. In thesis writing, this tense helps
the writer show that earlier research is not outdated or finished, but rather
forms part of an ongoing academic conversation. It is especially important
when describing research trends, patterns, or gaps.
In Pakistani theses, the present perfect is most commonly used in the
Introduction and Literature Review sections. For example, when a student
wants to show that a topic has been widely studied in Pakistan, but still
requires further investigation, the present perfect tense is the most appropriate
choice.
Consider the following examples:
Several studies have examined teacher motivation in Pakistan.
This sentence does not refer to one specific study or a completed event in the
past. Instead, it indicates that research on teacher motivation started earlier and
continues to be relevant today.
Similarly, the present perfect is used effectively to highlight research gaps:
Limited research has focused on rural classrooms in Sindh.

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
Here, the writer emphasizes that although some work may exist, the issue
remains underexplored at present. This is a powerful academic strategy
because it naturally leads to the justification of the current study.
A common mistake made by Pakistani students is the incorrect use of the
simple past tense when the intention is to describe an ongoing research trend.
For example:
Many researchers studied teacher motivation.
This sentence suggests that research on teacher motivation is complete and no
longer relevant, which is usually not the writer’s intention.
The correct form is:
Many researchers have studied teacher motivation.
This version clearly communicates that research began in the past and
continues to influence current understanding. Using the present perfect tense
in this way allows students to position their work confidently within existing
literature and demonstrate academic awareness.
13.6 Simple Rule Table: Choosing the Right Tense
To reduce confusion and help students make quick, accurate decisions, tense
usage in thesis writing can be simplified by focusing on the purpose of the
sentence, rather than memorizing complex grammar rules. The table below
provides a practical guide that Pakistani students can use while drafting or
revising their thesis.

By applying this simple rule-based approach, students can avoid unnecessary

only improves grammatical accuracy but also enhances the overall clarity and
professionalism of thesis writing.
13.7 Tense Use by Thesis Chapter: A Clear Map for Students
One of the most effective ways to reduce confusion about tenses is to
understand that each chapter of a thesis serves a different purpose, and
therefore requires different tense choices. Pakistani students often make errors
because they try to use one tense consistently throughout the thesis, instead of
adjusting tense according to the function of each section. This section provides
a clear, chapter-wise guide to help students select the correct tense with
confidence.
Introduction
The Introduction usually performs two main functions:
(1) presenting general facts and background information, and
(2) identifying a research gap.
For general facts and established knowledge, the present tense is used because
these statements are still true at the time of writing.
Example:
Education plays a vital role in the socio-economic development of Pakistan.
When referring to existing research as a whole in order to highlight what has
or has not been done, the present perfect tense is more appropriate. This tense
helps connect past research with the present study.
Example:
Several studies have examined early grade reading outcomes in Pakistan;
however, limited attention has been given to rural classrooms in Sindh.
Using the correct tense in the Introduction helps establish both authority and
clarity from the very beginning of the thesis.
Literature Review
The Literature Review discusses previous research, but not all references
require the same tense. The choice depends on whether the writer is talking
about research trends or specific studies.
When discussing general trends, ongoing debates, or a body of research, the
present perfect tense is used.
Example:
Researchers have highlighted the importance of teacher professional
development in improving classroom practices.
However, when referring to a specific study conducted at a particular time, the
past tense should be used.
Example:
Khan (2019) found that teachers in rural schools lacked access to instructional
materials.
Many Pakistani students incorrectly use present tense throughout the
Literature Review, which weakens the academic tone. Distinguishing between
trends and specific studies significantly improves clarity.
Methodology
The Methodology chapter describes what was done in the research. Since
these actions are completed, the past tense is used almost exclusively in this
section.
Example:
The
study
was
conducted
in
government
primary
schools.
Data were collected through questionnaires and classroom observations.
Using present tense in Methodology is a common error and often leads
supervisors to question the student’s understanding of academic conventions.
Results / Findings
In the Results or Findings chapter, two different functions appear side by side,
which is why students often get confused.
When describing what the data revealed, the past tense is used because the
analysis has already been completed.
Example:
The results showed that Grade 3 students performed below the expected
reading level.
However, when referring to tables, figures, or charts, the present tense is used

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
because these visual elements exist in the thesis and can be seen by the reader.
Example:
Table 4.2 shows the percentage of students achieving reading fluency.
Understanding this distinction helps students avoid unnecessary tense
switching.
Discussion
The Discussion chapter is the most flexible section in terms of tense usage. It
often requires a combination of past tense, present tense, and modal verbs.
•
Past tense is used to refer back to the study’s findings.
•
Present tense is used to explain what the findings mean.
•
Modal verbs (may, might, can) are used to avoid overgeneralization.
Example:
The findings showed a significant improvement in reading scores. This
suggests that targeted teacher training may improve classroom instruction in
similar contexts.
Pakistani students often struggle here because they attempt to keep one tense
throughout the paragraph. In reality, careful mixing is both normal and
necessary.
Conclusion
The Conclusion performs two main tasks:
(1) summarizing the study, and
(2) presenting implications or recommendations.
When summarizing what the study did and found, the past tense is used.
Example:
This study examined the impact of teacher training on reading outcomes.
When discussing implications, significance, or recommendations, the present
tense is preferred because these points are relevant now and into the future.
Example:
The findings provide useful insights for education policymakers in Pakistan.
13.8 High-Risk Areas Where Pakistani Students Go Wrong
Despite understanding basic tense rules, Pakistani students often make
recurring errors in specific areas. Being aware of these “high-risk zones” can
significantly improve thesis quality.
1. Mixing Tenses in One Sentence
Students sometimes combine past and present tense incorrectly within a single
sentence, usually due to translating ideas directly from Urdu.
The
study
was
conducted
and
shows
improvement.
The study was conducted and showed improvement.
Both actions occurred in the past, so the tense must remain consistent.
2. Writing Methodology in Present Tense
Another common mistake is describing research procedures as if they are
happening now.
The
researcher
distributes
questionnaires
to
teachers.
The researcher distributed questionnaires to teachers.
Since the action is already completed, the past tense must be used.
3. Overusing Present Tense in Findings
Students often use present tense in the Findings section because they see it as
“neutral” or “safe,” but this weakens accuracy.
The results show that students improved their reading skills.
The results showed that students improved their reading skills.
The improvement has already occurred; therefore, past tense is required.
Students should remember that tense choice is not about sounding
sophisticated, but about clearly communicating time, action, and meaning.
When tense aligns with function, academic writing becomes more precise,
professional, and convincing.
13.9 Using Modal Verbs Correctly (May, Might, Can)
In academic writing, especially in thesis and research work, students are
expected to present findings carefully and responsibly. One of the most
effective ways to do this is through the correct use of modal verbs, particularly
may, might, and can. These verbs help writers avoid making absolute or
exaggerated claims and instead reflect the tentative and evidence-based nature
of research.
Academic Function of Modal Verbs
Modal verbs serve two critical academic purposes:
First, they help avoid over-claiming.
Research findings are usually based on limited samples, specific contexts, or
particular time periods. Claiming something as a universal truth can weaken
the credibility of the study. Modal verbs allow the writer to acknowledge these
limitations.
Second, they show academic caution and maturity.
Examiners and supervisors expect students to demonstrate awareness that
research results suggest possibilities rather than final truths. The use of modal
verbs signals that the writer understands this academic norm.
Contextual Pakistani Examples
Consider the following examples drawn from education research in Pakistan:
“The results may indicate a link between teacher training and classroom
performance.”
Here, the word may shows that the relationship is suggested by the data but
not claimed as absolute. This is particularly important in Pakistani studies,
where contextual factors such as school resources, class size, and regional
differences can influence outcomes.
Another example:
“These findings can help policymakers improve teacher training programs.”
In this sentence, can is used to indicate potential usefulness, not guaranteed
impact. The statement remains realistic and academically appropriate,
especially when addressing policy-related recommendations in Pakistan.
Common Pakistani Student Error
Many students mistakenly write conclusions such as:
“This study proves that teacher training improves learning outcomes.”
A more academically acceptable version would be:
“This study suggests that teacher training may improve learning
outcomes.”
The second version reflects caution, professionalism, and alignment with
academic writing standards.
13.10 Before–After Examples (Real Student Fixes)
One of the most effective ways to understand tense and modal usage is to
examine real examples taken from student writing and observe how small
changes significantly improve clarity and correctness.
Example 1: Mixing Present and Past Tense Incorrectly
This study investigates teacher motivation and found many problems.

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
This sentence is incorrect because it mixes present tense (investigates) with
past tense (found) without a clear functional reason.
This study investigates teacher motivation and has found several
challenges.
In the corrected version, has found (present perfect) is used to connect the
ongoing focus of the study with findings that remain relevant. This structure
is particularly suitable in the abstract or introduction of a thesis.
Example 2: Misuse of Past Tense for Ongoing Research Trends
Previous studies showed that education improves literacy.
This sentence suggests that the research is no longer relevant, which is not the
intended meaning.
Previous studies have shown that education improves literacy.
The use of present perfect tense correctly indicates that earlier research
continues to be relevant today. This form is especially important in literature
review chapters, where students summarize existing knowledge rather than
isolated past events.
When writing your thesis, always ask yourself:
•
Am I stating a possibility, not a fact? → Use may or might
•
Am I suggesting potential usefulness? → Use can
•
Am I referring to ongoing or still-relevant research? → Use present
perfect
Mastering modal verbs and tense consistency will immediately make your
academic writing more professional, credible, and examiner-friendly.

Exercise 2: Fix the Paragraph (Tense Consistency)
Student Task
Rewrite the paragraph by correcting tense errors.
Given Paragraph (Incorrect)
The study investigates the reading habits of Grade 5 students in public
schools. Data were collected through questionnaires and classroom
observation. The results show that most students struggled with
comprehension, and many students do not receive reading support at home.
These findings indicated that limited parental involvement affects learning
outcomes.
Corrected Version (Answer Key)
The study investigates the reading habits of Grade 5 students in public

These findings indicate that limited parental involvement affects learning

Teacher Notes – Exercise 2
•

•
Sentence 2: Past tense → correct (method completed)
•
Sentence 3: Past tense → required (findings)
•
Sentence 4: Present tense → appropriate (interpretation/implication)
Common student error addressed:
Mixing results (past) with implications (present) in the same tense.

Exercise 3: Chapter-Wise Tense Identification
Student Task

•

2. Methodology Statement
•
Correct tense: Past
•
Example: The study was conducted in ten government secondary
schools in Karachi.
3. Result / Finding
•
Correct tense: Past
•
Example: The findings revealed a significant improvement in reading

4. Discussion Sentence
•
Correct tense: Present + modal verbs
•
Example: These findings may suggest that teacher mentoring
improves classroom practices.
Teacher Notes – Exercise 3
•
Encourage students to associate tense with chapter purpose
•
Discussion sentences often blend tenses, which is normal and
acceptable
•
Emphasize that methods and results are almost never in present tense

Before submitting any thesis chapter, students should ask:

13.13 Chapter Summary: Think Function, Not Grammar
Correct tense usage in thesis writing is not about advanced grammar—it is
about clarity of purpose. Once students understand whether a sentence
describes a fact, reports a completed action, or interprets findings, the correct
tense becomes obvious.
Academic tense use is logical, consistent, and learnable. When rules are
simplified and linked to real research tasks, confidence replaces confusion.
Students who think in terms of function rather than form write more clearly,
revise more efficiently, and rely less on repeated supervisor corrections.
Chapter 14: Connectors & Flow (Thinking in English)
Chapter Overview
This chapter focuses on developing coherence and logical flow in academic
writing through the effective use of connectors. Many Pakistani students
possess strong ideas and relevant content; however, their academic writing
often lacks clarity because sentences and paragraphs are presented as isolated
statements rather than logically connected arguments. This chapter addresses
this challenge by helping students understand how ideas are linked in English
academic discourse.
The chapter introduces connectors as essential tools that guide the reader
through an argument by signaling relationships such as addition, cause and
effect, contrast, comparison, sequence, emphasis, and conclusion. Special
attention is given to the difference between Urdu-influenced sentence
construction and English academic logic, encouraging students to “think in
English” rather than translate directly from their first language.
Through locally relevant examples and step-by-step practice activities,
students learn how to select appropriate connectors based on meaning and
purpose rather than memorization. The chapter concludes with practical
exercises that enable students to revise weak paragraphs and transform them
into coherent, well-structured academic writing suitable for assignments,
research reports, and theses.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to:
1. Explain the role of connectors in creating coherence and logical flow
in academic writing.
2. Differentiate between common types of connectors, including those
used for addition, cause and effect, contrast, comparison, sequence,
emphasis, and conclusion.
3. Identify logical relationships between ideas and select appropriate
connectors to express those relationships clearly.
4. Recognize
and
avoid
common
connector-related
errors,
particularly those influenced by Urdu-to-English translation.
5. Improve paragraph-level coherence by linking sentences into a
unified and logical argument.
6. Revise weak or disconnected paragraphs by applying suitable
connectors and transitions.
7. Demonstrate clearer academic thinking in English, moving beyond
sentence-level accuracy to paragraph-level flow.
14.1 Introduction: Why Ideas Fail Without Flow
In academic writing, ideas are not evaluated in isolation; they are judged by
how clearly they are connected and how logically they move from one point
to the next. This movement of ideas is known as flow. Flow refers to the
smooth progression of thoughts within a paragraph and across paragraphs,
allowing the reader to follow an argument without confusion or interruption.
Many Pakistani students produce grammatically correct sentences but still
receive low marks for their written work. This happens because correctness
alone does not guarantee clarity. A sentence may be free from grammatical
errors, yet the overall paragraph may feel fragmented, repetitive, or difficult
to follow. In academic writing, clarity emerges not only from correct sentence
structure but also from how ideas are linked to form a unified argument.
A common issue observed in assignments and theses submitted at Pakistani
universities is the presence of strong ideas presented as disconnected
statements. For example, a student may write several relevant sentences about
teacher training, student learning, and classroom conditions; however, if these
sentences are placed side by side without logical connections, the reader is left
to guess how one idea relates to the next. This lack of connection weakens the
argument, regardless of how important or accurate the individual ideas may
be.
Examiners and research supervisors pay close attention to this aspect of
writing. When evaluating academic work, they do not only assess language
accuracy or content knowledge; they also examine whether the writing
demonstrates logical progression. Paragraphs that flow smoothly signal clear
thinking, while abrupt or disconnected sentences suggest weak organization
or limited understanding of academic discourse. As a result, poor flow often
leads to comments such as “ideas not clearly linked,” “argument unclear,” or
“lack of coherence,” even when the topic itself is well chosen.
The key message of this chapter is simple but crucial: academic writing is not
about using advanced vocabulary; it is about establishing logical connections
between ideas. A well-connected paragraph written in simple English is far

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
more effective than a complex paragraph filled with sophisticated words but
lacking coherence.
14.2 What Are Connectors and Why Do They Matter?
Connectors are words or phrases used to link ideas within and between
sentences. They help readers understand how one point relates to another by
clearly signaling relationships such as addition, cause and effect, contrast,
comparison, or sequence. In academic writing, connectors function as
signposts that guide the reader through the writer’s argument.
The primary role of connectors is to guide the reader. Academic readers,
including examiners and supervisors, expect the writer to make relationships
explicit rather than implied. Connectors tell the reader whether a new idea
supports the previous one, contrasts with it, explains a reason, or presents a
result. Without these signals, readers must work harder to interpret the writer’s
intention, which often leads to misunderstanding or confusion.
Connectors also play a critical role in showing logic. For example, cause-andeffect connectors explain why something happened, contrast connectors
highlight differences, and sequence connectors indicate order or progression.
When used correctly, they transform a list of sentences into a structured and
meaningful argument.
It is important to distinguish connectors from simple conjunctions such as and,
but, and so. While conjunctions are useful in everyday communication, they
are often too vague or informal for academic writing. Academic connectors,
such as however, therefore, in addition, and as a result, provide clearer and
more precise relationships between ideas, making the writing more formal and
easier to follow.
Mini Example
Paragraph without connectors:
Teacher training programs were introduced in government schools. Student
reading levels remained low. Schools lacked sufficient learning materials.
Teachers reported heavy workloads.
Although each sentence is grammatically correct, the paragraph lacks flow.
The reader cannot clearly see how these ideas are related.
Paragraph with connectors:
Teacher training programs were introduced in government schools. However,
student reading levels remained low. This may be due to the lack of sufficient
learning materials. In addition, teachers reported heavy workloads, which
limited effective classroom implementation.
In the revised version, connectors clearly show contrast, cause, and addition.
As a result, the paragraph reads smoothly, and the logic of the argument
becomes clear.
14.3 Thinking in English: Moving Away from Urdu Sentence
Logic
One of the most common challenges faced by Pakistani students in academic
writing is not a lack of ideas, but the way those ideas are expressed. Many
students mentally construct their arguments in Urdu and then translate them
directly into English. While this approach may produce grammatically correct
sentences, it often results in weak flow and unclear logic.
Literal Urdu-to-English translation breaks academic flow because the two
languages organize meaning differently. In Urdu, connections between ideas
are often implied rather than stated, and readers are expected to infer
relationships from context. English academic writing, however, requires
writers to make these relationships explicit.
Urdu Writing Habits and Their Impact
In Urdu-influenced writing, students often:
•
Use long sentences connected by commas or conjunctions such as aur
or lekin
•
Assume the reader will automatically understand cause, contrast, or
sequence
•
Present ideas side by side without clearly signaling how they relate
These habits, when transferred into English, create paragraphs that feel
disjointed, confusing, or repetitive.
English Academic Requirement
English academic writing expects:
•
Shorter, more controlled sentences
•
Clear logical signals that guide the reader
•
Explicit connectors that show why one idea follows another
In academic English, the reader should never have to guess the relationship
between sentences.
Comparison Example
Urdu-style paragraph (translated):
Teacher training programs were introduced in government schools and
teachers attended sessions and student performance did not improve and
classrooms were overcrowded and materials were limited.
Although the ideas are relevant, the relationships between them are unclear.
The reader does not know whether the later points explain, contrast, or add to
the earlier ones.
English academic-style paragraph:
Teacher training programs were introduced in government schools. However,
student performance did not show significant improvement. This may be due
to overcrowded classrooms and limited availability of learning materials.
In the revised version, connectors make the logic clear. The reader understands
contrast (however) and cause (this may be due to), which improves coherence
and academic clarity.
14.4 Major Types of Logical Connectors in Academic Writing
Logical connectors help readers follow the writer’s line of thinking. Each type
serves a specific purpose, and effective academic writing depends on choosing
connectors based on meaning rather than habit.
14.4.1 Addition (Adding Information)
Purpose
Addition connectors are used to extend an idea or provide supporting
information. They help the writer build an argument step by step.
Common connectors
•
In addition
•
Furthermore
•
Moreover
•
Besides
•
As well as
Pakistani Contextual Example
Teacher training improved lesson planning.
Moreover, classroom
observations showed better student engagement.
Here, moreover signals that the second sentence strengthens the first point.

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
Common Mistake
Many students overuse “also” at the beginning of every sentence. While
grammatically acceptable, this weakens academic style and limits variation.
14.4.2 Cause and Effect
Purpose
These connectors explain reasons and results, which is essential in research
writing, especially in findings and discussion sections.
Common connectors
•
Because
•
Due to
•
As a result
•
Therefore
•
Consequently
•
Thus
Pakistani Contextual Example
Due to large class sizes, individual student feedback remained limited. As a
result, learning outcomes varied significantly.
The connectors clearly show why the problem occurred and what it led to.
14.4.3 Contrast and Opposition
Purpose
Contrast connectors highlight differences, contradictions, or unexpected
results.
Common connectors
•
However
•
On the other hand
•
In contrast
•
Nevertheless
•
Although
Pakistani Contextual Example
Urban schools showed better infrastructure. However, rural schools
demonstrated stronger community involvement.
This contrast adds depth to the analysis rather than presenting one-sided
conclusions.
Common Mistake
Students often begin every sentence with “However”, which makes writing
repetitive and signals poor control over transitions.
14.4.4 Comparison and Similarity
Purpose
These connectors show similarity between studies, results, or contexts,
especially useful in literature reviews.
Common connectors
•
Similarly
•
Likewise
•
In the same way
•
Correspondingly
Academic Example
Similarly, previous studies conducted in Punjab reported comparable
findings.
This indicates alignment between the current study and earlier research.
14.4.5 Giving Examples and Illustration
Purpose
Examples help clarify abstract or general statements by making them concrete.
Common connectors
•
For example
•
For instance
•
Such as
•
To illustrate
Pakistani Contextual Example
Many factors affect attendance, for example, seasonal migration and domestic
responsibilities.
The connector prepares the reader for specific illustrations.
14.4.6 Sequence and Process
Purpose
Sequence connectors are used to describe steps, stages, or procedures clearly
and logically.
Common connectors
•
First
•
Next
•
Then
•
After that
•
Finally
Use Cases
•
Methodology sections
•
Procedure descriptions
•
Intervention or training phases
These connectors help readers follow processes without confusion.
14.4.7 Emphasis and Importance
Purpose
Emphasis connectors draw attention to key points that the writer wants the
reader to remember.
Common connectors
•
Most importantly
•
Above all
•
In particular
•
Primarily
Example
Most importantly, teacher motivation played a central role in implementation
success.
This signals that the point is central to the argument.
14.4.8 Conclusion and Summary
Purpose
These connectors help close arguments, summarize ideas, or signal the end of
a section.
Common connectors
•
In conclusion
•
To summarize
•
In brief
•
Overall
Used effectively, they provide closure and reinforce the main message of the
paragraph or section.
14.5 Where Connectors Are Commonly Used in a Thesis
Connectors play a critical role in maintaining coherence across all sections of
a thesis. While their function remains consistent—guiding the reader through
the writer’s line of reasoning—their purpose and frequency vary by section.
Understanding where and how to use connectors appropriately helps students
construct arguments that are logical, persuasive, and easy to follow.
Connectors in the Introduction: From Background to Gap to Purpose
In the introduction, connectors help the writer move smoothly from general
background information to the specific research gap and finally to the purpose
of the study. This progression is essential in academic writing, as readers
expect a clear justification for why the study is being conducted.
Contextual example (Pakistan-focused):
In Pakistan, early grade reading outcomes have remained below national
benchmarks despite increased school enrollment. However, recent studies
have focused primarily on access rather than instructional quality. Therefore,
this study aims to examine the impact of teacher training on Grade 3 reading
fluency in government schools.
Here, however signals a research gap, while therefore clearly introduces the
purpose. Without these connectors, the paragraph would appear as a list of
unrelated statements rather than a logical argument.
Connectors in the Literature Review: Comparing and Contrasting
Studies
The literature review relies heavily on connectors because its primary function
is to compare, contrast, and synthesize previous research. Students often
summarize studies one by one; connectors help transform summaries into a
coherent scholarly discussion.
Contextual example:
Several international studies have reported a positive relationship between
teacher coaching and student achievement. Similarly, a study conducted in
Punjab found improvements in classroom practices following structured
mentoring. In contrast, research from rural Sindh reported limited impact due
to resource constraints.
In this paragraph, similarly highlights agreement, while in contrast signals
divergence due to context. Such connectors help the reader understand how
studies relate to one another rather than reading them as isolated findings.
Connectors in the Findings Section: Linking Data to Meaning
In the findings section, connectors are used to guide readers through tables,
charts, and patterns in the data. They help explain relationships such as trends,
comparisons, and outcomes without introducing interpretation that belongs in
the discussion.
Contextual example:

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
Table 4.2 shows that 68% of teachers reported improved lesson planning after
the training. In addition, classroom observations indicated increased student
participation. As shown in Figure 4.3, these improvements were more
pronounced in urban schools than in rural schools.
Here, connectors such as in addition and as shown link multiple data points
and help the reader follow the progression of evidence.
Connectors in the Discussion: Explaining Causes and Implications
The discussion section requires more analytical connectors, as the writer
explains why results occurred and what they mean. Connectors are essential
for linking findings to explanations, theories, and implications.
Contextual example:
The improvement in lesson planning may be attributed to continuous
mentoring support. However, the limited change in student reading outcomes
suggests that instructional time alone is insufficient. Therefore, additional
classroom resources may be required to achieve sustained improvement.
In this section, connectors such as however and therefore help balance
explanation and implication, allowing the writer to build a reasoned argument
rather than a descriptive summary.
Connectors in the Conclusion: Summarizing Key Arguments
In the conclusion, connectors signal closure and synthesis. They help restate
key findings and reinforce the overall contribution of the study.
Contextual example:
In conclusion, the study demonstrates that teacher training positively
influences classroom practices. Overall, the findings suggest that professional
development initiatives must be accompanied by material support to improve
student learning outcomes.
Such connectors guide the reader toward a clear and unified ending.
14.6 Common Connector Errors by Pakistani Students
Despite understanding the importance of connectors, many Pakistani students
struggle with their effective use. These challenges often arise from examoriented learning, spoken English influence, and direct translation from Urdu.
Overusing One Connector (Especially “Also” and “However”)
A frequent error is the repeated use of a single connector throughout a
paragraph, particularly also and however. This creates a mechanical and
monotonous writing style.
Weak example:
Teachers received training. Also, new materials were distributed. Also,
monitoring visits were conducted.
Improved approach: Vary connectors based on function (e.g., in addition,
furthermore, moreover).
Using Spoken Connectors in Academic Writing
Students often transfer spoken English into academic writing by using
informal connectors such as so, anyway, or and then.
Weak example:
The data was incomplete, so the results were affected.
Academic alternative:
The data was incomplete; therefore, the results were affected.
Academic writing requires formal connectors that reflect precision and
professionalism.
Using Connectors Without Logical Relationship
Another common issue is inserting connectors where no logical relationship
exists, simply to “sound academic.”
Weak example:
The questionnaire was distributed to 50 teachers. However, the study was
conducted in Sindh.
Here, however signals contrast, but no contrast is present. Misused connectors
confuse the reader and weaken clarity.
Starting Every Sentence with a Connector
While connectors are useful, beginning every sentence with one can make
writing feel forced and repetitive.
Example of poor flow:
However, the training was effective. Moreover, teachers showed interest.
Therefore, results improved.
Students should learn to integrate connectors naturally within sentences and
paragraphs rather than relying on them as sentence starters.
Key Reminder
Connectors do not improve writing by themselves; they improve writing only
when they reflect clear thinking.
14.7 Practical Strategy: How to Build Flow Step by Step
Many students believe that flow in academic writing happens automatically
once grammar and vocabulary are correct. In practice, however, coherence is
achieved through deliberate thinking. A well-structured paragraph reflects a
clear sequence of ideas, where each sentence is logically connected to the one
before it. The following step-by-step strategy can help students systematically
build flow in their academic writing.
The first step is to identify the main idea of each sentence. Every sentence in
an academic paragraph should serve a clear purpose. Some sentences
introduce an idea, others explain it, provide evidence, or show a result. When
students write without identifying the role of each sentence, paragraphs often
become a list of unrelated statements. For example, in a paragraph describing
teacher training in public schools, one sentence may present the intervention,
another may describe student outcomes, and a third may highlight
implementation challenges. Recognizing these roles is essential before
attempting to link them.
Once the main ideas are clear, the next step is to decide the relationship
between each sentence and the previous one. Academic writing relies on
logical relationships such as cause and effect, contrast, comparison, or
addition. For instance, if a sentence presents an intervention and the next
sentence shows an unexpected outcome, the relationship is likely contrast. If
a sentence explains why an outcome occurred, the relationship is cause and
effect. Identifying this relationship allows the writer to guide the reader’s
understanding rather than leaving the connection implicit.
After identifying the relationship, the writer should choose a connector that
accurately reflects that relationship. Connectors such as however, therefore, in

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
addition, and as a result act as signposts that signal how ideas are linked.
Pakistani students often rely on a limited number of connectors, such as also
or so, which weakens academic tone. Selecting a connector based on meaning
rather than habit significantly improves clarity and professionalism.
The final step is to read the paragraph aloud to check for smoothness and
clarity. Reading aloud helps writers notice abrupt shifts, repetition, or missing
links between ideas. If a sentence feels sudden or confusing when spoken, it
often indicates that the logical relationship has not been clearly signaled.
Revising at this stage allows students to refine both flow and readability before
final submission.
14.8 Practice Section: Rebuilding a Weak Paragraph
This section demonstrates how the step-by-step strategy can be applied in
practice. The example below reflects a common pattern found in Pakistani
students’ assignments and research writing.
14.8.1 Weak Paragraph (Without Flow)
Teacher training programs were introduced in government schools. The
reading level of students remained low. Schools lacked learning materials.
Teachers reported workload issues
Although each sentence is grammatically correct, the paragraph lacks
coherence. The reader is left to guess how these ideas are connected, which
weakens the overall argument.
14.8.2 Step-by-Step Improvement
To improve the paragraph, the first task is to identify the relationships between
the sentences.
•
The second sentence contrasts with the first (training was introduced,
yet outcomes did not improve).
•
The third sentence explains a possible cause of the low reading levels.
•
The fourth sentence adds another contributing
14.9 Chapter Checklist
Before finalizing any academic paragraph, students should review their
writing using the following checklist. This step ensures that ideas are not only
grammatically correct but also logically connected and easy to follow.
First, confirm that the logical relationship between sentences is clear. Each
sentence should relate meaningfully to the one before it. For example, if a
sentence explains a reason, the following sentence should clearly show its
result or implication. In a paragraph discussing low reading outcomes in public
schools, the reader should easily understand whether the writer is adding
information, explaining a cause, or presenting a contrast.
Second, check that connectors are varied. Relying on the same connector
repeatedly—such as also or however—weakens the flow of writing. Effective
academic writing uses a range of connectors, such as in addition, therefore, in
contrast, and as a result, to reflect different relationships between ideas.
Third, ensure that there is no overuse of connectors. While connectors are
essential, inserting them at the beginning of every sentence can make writing
sound mechanical. Some ideas flow naturally without explicit connectors, and
students should learn to balance clarity with simplicity.
Fourth, maintain an academic tone throughout the paragraph. Informal
expressions commonly used in spoken English, such as so, anyway, or a lot,
should be avoided. For instance, instead of writing so the results were very
bad, a more academic form would be therefore, the results remained
unsatisfactory.
Finally, read the paragraph as a whole to check whether it reads smoothly. A
well-connected paragraph should sound logical and natural when read aloud,
with ideas unfolding clearly and progressively.
14.10 Chapter Summary
Connectors play a crucial role in academic writing because they guide the
reader’s thinking. They signal how one idea relates to another, helping the
reader follow the writer’s argument without confusion.
Clear flow in writing reflects clarity of thought. When students organize their
ideas logically and use connectors purposefully, their writing becomes easier
to understand and more persuasive. Weak flow often indicates unclear
thinking, while strong flow demonstrates academic maturity.
In academic writing, strength does not come from complex vocabulary or long
sentences. Instead, strong academic writing is the result of clear ideas
combined with correct and appropriate connectors. When students master this
skill, they are better prepared to produce coherent assignments, research
reports, and theses that meet university expectations.
PART VIII — Practical Tools for Students
Part VIII translates academic writing principles into hands-on tools that help
Pakistani students apply what they have learned with confidence. This section
provides ready-to-use templates, checklists, and common error guides tailored
to local academic contexts, enabling students to plan, draft, review, and refine
their assignments, research proposals, and theses independently. By
addressing frequent challenges such as unclear structure, weak paraphrasing,
incorrect tense usage, and overreliance on foreign sources, this part supports
students in producing clear, original, and contextually relevant academic
writing that meets university and HEC expectations.
Chapter 15: Common Pakistani Student Errors (And
Fixes)
Chapter Overview
Pakistani students often possess strong ideas and subject knowledge; however,
their academic writing frequently loses clarity and impact due to recurring
language patterns shaped by school-level learning, exam-oriented writing, and
direct translation from Urdu into English. These patterns result in writing that
appears vague, repetitive, or difficult to follow, even when the underlying

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
argument is sound.
This chapter identifies the most common academic writing errors made by
Pakistani students and explains why these errors occur. Rather than treating
mistakes as weaknesses, the chapter presents them as habits that can be
corrected through awareness and practice. Each error is illustrated using
authentic, Pakistan-based academic examples, followed by clear revisions that
demonstrate improved academic tone, precision, and flow.
The chapter focuses on three critical problem areas: the overuse of intensifiers
such as “very,” the tendency to write long and unclear sentences, and the habit
of translating ideas directly from Urdu into English. Through side-by-side
comparisons, practical rewriting strategies, and guided exercises, students
learn how to express ideas concisely, think in English, and adopt the
conventions expected in academic writing.
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to recognize these errors in
their own writing and apply practical fixes that significantly improve clarity,
coherence, and academic credibility.
Learning Outcomes
After completing this chapter, students will be able to:
1. Identify common language patterns in their academic writing that
reduce clarity and academic impact.
2. Replace the overuse of “very” and similar intensifiers with precise
academic vocabulary.
3. Break down long and unclear sentences into concise, logically
connected academic statements.
4. Recognize the effects of direct Urdu-to-English translation on
sentence structure and meaning.
5. Rewrite Urdu-influenced sentences into natural academic English
without changing the intended meaning.
6. Apply practical revision strategies to improve tone, precision, and
readability in assignments and thesis chapters.
7. Self-edit academic writing using targeted checklists and examples
provided in the chapter
15.1 Error One: Overuse of the Word “Very”
One of the most frequent and noticeable weaknesses in Pakistani students’
academic writing is the excessive use of the word “very.” While this word is
common in everyday speech and school-level writing, it significantly weakens
academic prose. Understanding why students rely on “very” and how to
replace it with precise academic language is essential for improving writing
quality.
15.1.1 Why Pakistani Students Overuse “Very”
Pakistani students often overuse “very” due to direct translation from Urdu
intensifiers such as bohat, intehai, and nihayat. In Urdu, these words are
commonly used to strengthen meaning and add emphasis, and their frequent
use is culturally and linguistically acceptable. However, when this habit is
transferred directly into English academic writing, it results in vague and
emotionally loaded sentences.
Another reason lies in school-level writing practices, where students are
encouraged to express feelings and opinions rather than construct precise
arguments. Phrases like “very important” or “very bad” are often rewarded
in exams at earlier stages, reinforcing the belief that strong writing requires
strong emotional language.
In addition, many students have limited exposure to academic alternatives.
Without familiarity with precise academic vocabulary, “very” becomes a
convenient shortcut to sound emphatic. Ironically, students also use “very”
out of fear of sounding “too simple.” They believe that removing it will
weaken their sentence, when in fact the opposite is true in academic writing.
15.1.2 Why “Very” Weakens Academic Writing
In academic writing, “very” adds emotion but not information. It intensifies
feeling rather than clarifying meaning. For example, saying something is
“very important” does not explain why it is important or to what extent.
The frequent use of “very” signals informal or school-level writing and
reduces the precision expected in academic texts. Examiners and supervisors
often interpret repeated use of “very” as immature language, indicating that
the writer lacks control over academic vocabulary and analytical expression.
Academic writing values accuracy, objectivity, and clarity. Words like “very”
weaken these qualities because they are subjective and imprecise.
15.1.3 Common Pakistani Examples (Before)
The following sentences are typical in assignments and theses submitted by
Pakistani students:
•
“This is a very important issue in Pakistan.”
•
“The results were very bad.”
•
“Teachers face very many challenges.”
•
“Students showed very low performance.”
While these sentences are grammatically correct, they lack academic strength
and clarity.
15.1.4 Academic Fix: Replace “Very” with Precision
Weak Expression Academic Alternative
very important
critical / significant
very bad
poor / inadequate
very many
numerous / multiple
very low
minimal / limited
very high
substantial / considerable
very few
limited / marginal
Replacing “very” with precise academic vocabulary improves clarity and tone
without increasing sentence length.
15.1.5 Improved Pakistani Academic Examples (After)
•
“This is a significant issue in the Pakistani education system.”
•
“The results indicated poor reading comprehension among Grade 3
students.”
•
“Teachers face multiple instructional challenges in rural schools.”
These revised sentences are clearer, more objective, and more suitable for
academic assessment.
15.1.6 Practice Task
1. Rewrite ten sentences from your own assignment or thesis by
removing “very” and replacing it with appropriate academic
alternatives.
2. Identify sentences where no intensifier is needed at all and revise them
accordingly.
15.1.7 Self-Check Rule

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
If removing “very” does not change the meaning of the sentence, it
should not be there.
15.2 Error Two: Long, Unclear Sentences
Another major weakness in Pakistani students’ academic writing is the
tendency to write long, unclear sentences that contain multiple ideas without
clear structure. While long sentences are not incorrect by themselves, they
become problematic when they obscure meaning and confuse the reader.
15.2.1 Why Pakistani Students Write Long Sentences
Urdu allows long, flowing sentence structures where ideas are linked through
rhythm and context rather than explicit grammatical markers. When students
transfer this structure directly into English, the result is often a sentence that
is grammatically overloaded and difficult to follow.
Many students also believe that short sentences sound “simple” or less
academic. As a result, they combine multiple ideas into one sentence to appear
sophisticated. Memorization-based writing culture further reinforces this
habit, as students reproduce long sentences without fully controlling their
structure.
Additionally, some students write exactly as thoughts come to mind, without
revising for clarity. This stream-of-consciousness approach leads to sentences
that reflect thinking rather than organized academic reasoning.
15.2.2 Why Long Sentences Confuse Examiners
Long sentences often contain multiple ideas without clear hierarchy, making
it difficult for the examiner to identify the main argument. Important points
become buried under excessive detail, and grammatical errors increase as
sentence length grows.
From the reader’s perspective, long and unclear sentences cause fatigue and
reduce comprehension. Examiners may need to reread the sentence several
times, which negatively affects their evaluation of the writing.
15.2.3 Typical Pakistani Student Sentence (Problem Example)
“The teachers who were trained under the program which was launched in
2021 and aimed at improving reading skills were not able to fully implement
the strategies because of time constraints and lack of materials which affected
student outcomes.”
This sentence contains multiple ideas but no clear structure.
15.2.4 Academic Fix: One Idea Per Sentence
Step-by-step correction:
1. Identify the main idea
2. Separate supporting information
3. Use connectors to show relationships clearly
Revised Version:
“Teachers trained under the 2021 reading program were unable to fully
implement the strategies. This was mainly due to time constraints and limited
availability of materials. As a result, student learning outcomes were
affected.”
The revised version is clearer, more readable, and academically stronger.
15.2.5 Sentence Length Guideline
•
Ideal academic sentence length: 15–25 words
•
More than 30 words → revise
•
One sentence = one main idea
15.2.6 Practice Task
1. Break five long sentences from your writing into shorter, clearer
sentences.
2. Identify the main idea in each paragraph and ensure it is clearly stated.
15.2.7 Editing Checklist
✔ Does each sentence express one clear message?
✔ Can the sentence be split without losing meaning?
✔ Is the subject of the sentence clear?
15.3 Error Three: Translating Directly from Urdu
One of the most persistent and deeply rooted challenges faced by Pakistani
students in academic writing is direct translation from Urdu into English. This
issue does not arise because students lack ideas or understanding of the topic.
In fact, many students think critically and insightfully—but their thoughts are
first formed in Urdu (or another local language) and then translated word-forword into English. The result is writing that may be grammatically acceptable
but does not sound natural, academic, or professional.
This section explains why literal translation weakens academic writing and
how students can move from Urdu-thinking to English-thinking in an
academic context.
15.3.1 The Problem of Literal Translation
Most Pakistani students think in Urdu and write in English. This mental
process is natural, especially for students who studied in Urdu or mixedmedium schools. However, problems arise when entire Urdu sentence
structures are transferred directly into English.
A key misunderstanding among students is the belief that grammatical
correctness automatically means good academic English. In reality, a sentence
can be grammatically correct yet still sound informal, awkward, or nonacademic. Academic English has its own conventions, tone, and structure that
differ significantly from everyday speech or translated language.
Another challenge lies in the difference between cultural expression and
academic expression. Urdu allows emotional emphasis, repetition, and
indirect phrasing, which are culturally appropriate and powerful. Academic
English, however, values clarity, precision, and neutrality. Emotional
intensifiers and conversational phrases—when translated directly—often
weaken the academic tone of writing.
As a result, examiners and supervisors frequently describe such writing as:
•
“Informal”
•
“School-level”
•
“Not academic”
•
“Translated English”
15.3.2 Common Urdu-Influenced English Sentences
The influence of Urdu can be seen in many expressions that Pakistani students
commonly use in assignments and theses. These phrases are understandable,
but they do not meet academic standards.
For example, students often write:
•
“According to me...” This phrase is a direct translation of “mere
khayal mein”. While common in spoken English, it is considered
informal and subjective in academic writing.
•

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
“On the other side...” This comes from “doosri taraf”. In academic
English, this connector is incorrect and signals weak command of
discourse markers.
•
“Do the needful” This phrase is widely used in South Asian official
correspondence but is outdated and not used in modern academic
writing.
•
“Very less students” This reflects Urdu sentence structure and
incorrect adjective–noun agreement in English.
Such phrases do not usually lead to grammatical penalties alone, but they
reduce the overall quality and credibility of the writing.
15.3.3 Academic English Alternatives
Academic writing requires neutral, objective, and discipline-appropriate
expressions. The following alternatives convey the same meaning but in an
academically acceptable way:
•
Replace “According to me” with → “From the researcher’s
perspective” or “This study argues that”
•
Replace “On the other side” with → “On the other hand”
•
Replace “Very less” with → “Very few” or “Limited”
•
Replace “Do the needful” with → “Take appropriate action” or
“Implement necessary measures”
These alternatives demonstrate control over academic tone and show the
examiner that the student understands disciplinary conventions.
15.3.4 Thinking in English: A Practical Strategy
Moving away from translation does not require abandoning Urdu thinking
altogether. Instead, students must change the stage at which English enters the
writing process.
A practical and effective strategy includes:
•
Writing key points in English bullet form first, even if they are
simple
•
Avoiding full-sentence translation from Urdu notebooks
•
Reading academic articles related to the topic before writing, to
internalize structure
•
Imitating sentence structure, not vocabulary, from journal articles
and theses
This shift gradually trains the mind to organize ideas in English, reducing
dependence on translation.
15.3.5 Example: Urdu Thought → Academic English
Consider the following example, which reflects a very common situation.
Urdu thought “اس وجہ سے تعلیمی نظام پر بہت برا اثر پڑتا ہے۔”
Weak literal translation “Due to this, very bad effect comes on education
system.”
Although the meaning is understandable, the sentence sounds unnatural and
informal.
Academic English version “This situation has a negative impact on the
education system.”
The academic version:
•
Removes emotional language
•
Uses a standard academic collocation (“negative impact”)
•
Follows natural English sentence structure
15.3.6 Practice Task
To develop awareness and control over this issue, students should:
1. Convert five Urdu-based sentences into natural academic English.
2. Identify phrases they frequently translate from Urdu and list their
academic equivalents.
3. Compare their revised sentences with examples from academic
articles.
This exercise helps students recognize patterns in their own writing habits.
15.4 Combined Editing Exercise
15.4.1 Diagnostic Paragraph (With All Three Errors)
Students are now given a short paragraph that intentionally includes:
•
Overuse of “very”
•
Long, unclear sentences
•
Urdu-based sentence structure
The paragraph resembles real assignments submitted by Pakistani students and
serves as a diagnostic tool.
15.4.2 Guided Revision Steps
Students revise the paragraph using three clear steps:
1. Remove unnecessary intensifiers such as “very”
2. Break long sentences into shorter, focused ones
3. Replace translated phrases with academic alternatives
By following these steps, students experience how clarity, tone, and credibility
improve through careful editing.
Academic writing is not about translating ideas into English. It is about
thinking academically in English.
This realization marks a major shift in a student’s academic journey—and
significantly improves writing quality across all disciplines.
15.5 Final Editing Checklist for Pakistani Students
Before submitting an assignment, research paper, or thesis chapter, Pakistani
students are strongly encouraged to pause and conduct a final language review.
This stage is often skipped due to time pressure, yet it plays a decisive role in
how examiners and supervisors evaluate the overall quality of academic work.
Many scripts are downgraded not because of weak ideas, but because of
avoidable language habits that signal poor academic control.
The first question students should ask themselves is whether they have
removed unnecessary uses of the word “very.” In Pakistani academic writing,
this word frequently appears as a direct transfer from Urdu intensifiers such
as bohat or intehai. While acceptable in spoken English, “very” weakens
academic tone and adds emotion rather than meaning. For example, a sentence
such as “This is a very important issue in Pakistan” can be significantly
improved by replacing it with “This is a significant issue in Pakistan.”
Removing such fillers immediately makes writing more precise and
professional.
The second question relates to sentence length and clarity. Students should
examine whether their sentences are short, focused, and easy to follow. Long
sentences often reflect Urdu sentence structure, where multiple ideas can
comfortably exist within a single statement. In English academic writing,
however, clarity depends on expressing one main idea per sentence. If a
sentence feels difficult to read aloud or requires rereading to understand, it is
likely too long. Breaking such sentences into two or three smaller units not

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
only improves readability but also demonstrates control over academic
expression.
Next, students should reflect on whether they are thinking in English or
translating directly from Urdu. Literal translation is one of the most common
reasons Pakistani academic writing sounds awkward or informal. Phrases such
as “according to me,” “on the other side,” or “very less students” are
grammatically influenced by Urdu but are inappropriate in academic English.
Instead of translating full sentences, students should develop the habit of
forming ideas directly in English, using structures commonly found in
research articles and theses. Reading academic texts before writing can help
internalize these patterns.
Finally, students must consider whether their writing sounds academic rather
than conversational. Academic writing avoids personal opinions, casual
expressions, and spoken language patterns. Sentences like “I think this is very
bad” may be acceptable in classroom discussion but are unsuitable for formal
academic work. Reframing such statements into evidence-based language—
“The findings indicate a negative trend”—reflects maturity and scholarly
awareness.
Conducting this final review may take only ten to fifteen minutes, but it can
substantially improve the clarity, credibility, and academic tone of a student’s
work.
15.6 Chapter Summary
This chapter has highlighted that many language-related weaknesses in
Pakistani students’ academic writing are not the result of limited intelligence
or lack of subject knowledge. Rather, they are deeply rooted habits developed
through schooling, examination practices, and mother-tongue influence.
Recognizing these patterns is the first step toward improvement.
Academic writing is a skill that develops through awareness, reflection, and
repeated practice. When students consciously replace weak expressions,
shorten unclear sentences, and shift from translation-based writing to direct
academic thinking in English, their writing quality improves significantly.
Importantly, clarity in language reflects clarity in thought. Well-structured
sentences signal well-structured ideas, allowing readers to engage with the
argument rather than struggle with the language.
By applying the strategies discussed in this chapter, Pakistani students can
move from survival-level English to confident academic expression—an
essential step for success in higher education and research writing.
Chapter 16: Step-by-Step Writing Templates
Chapter Overview
This chapter is designed to bridge the gap between knowing academic writing
rules and applying them confidently in real academic tasks. Many Pakistani
students understand the theory of academic writing—such as tense usage,
connectors, and citation practices—but struggle to transform this knowledge
into coherent paragraphs when writing assignments, research papers, or theses.
To address this challenge, the chapter presents step-by-step writing templates
for key sections of academic work, including the Introduction, Literature
Review, Findings, and Discussion. Each template translates abstract language
rules into practical writing blueprints, enabling students to see how ideas are
logically organized and expressed at the sentence and paragraph level.
Rather than promoting memorization of isolated phrases, this chapter
emphasizes pattern recognition, structure, and purposeful sentence
construction. By following these guided templates, students are supported in
moving from uncertainty and hesitation to clarity and confidence in academic
writing.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to:
1. Apply academic language rules in practice by using structured
templates to write complete and coherent paragraphs.
2. Construct well-organized Introduction, Literature Review,
Findings, and Discussion paragraphs using appropriate academic
sentence patterns.
3. Translate theoretical knowledge of academic English into effective
written output, moving beyond rote learning.
4. Use sentence structures purposefully to introduce context, report
findings, compare studies, and explain results.
5. Write academic paragraphs with increased confidence and
reduced anxiety, particularly in English-medium academic settings.
6. Adapt provided templates to different disciplines and research
topics within the Pakistani higher-education context.
16.1 Introduction Template
Writing the introduction is often the most difficult part of academic writing
for Pakistani students. Many students understand the topic they want to
research, yet struggle to explain it clearly in English. This difficulty usually
arises because students attempt to write an introduction without understanding
its purpose and structure. As a result, introductions become either too general,
irrelevant, or confusing for the reader.
This section provides a step-by-step introduction template that helps students
move from ideas in their mind to a clear, academic introduction on paper.
16.1.1 Purpose of the Introduction
The introduction serves as the entry point of a research study. It prepares the
reader by explaining what the study is about and why it is important. A wellwritten introduction performs three essential functions.
First, it introduces the research context. This means placing the study within a
broader educational, social, or disciplinary setting so that the reader
understands where the issue exists.
Second, it identifies a clear research problem. Instead of making general
complaints or broad statements, the introduction highlights a specific gap,
issue, or challenge that requires investigation.
Third, it states the purpose and significance of the study. The reader should
clearly understand what the study aims to examine and why the findings
matter, particularly within the Pakistani context.

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
An effective introduction answers one key question: Why should the reader
care about this study?
16.1.2 Logical Structure of an Introduction
A strong introduction follows a logical narrowing pattern, moving from
broad ideas to specific focus. Pakistani students often reverse this order, which
confuses the reader. The recommended structure is as follows:
1. General background – Start with the broader issue at a global or
general level, then narrow it down to the national and local context.
2. Contextual gap or problem – Identify what is missing, weak, or
unresolved despite existing efforts.
3. Purpose and objectives – Clearly state what the study intends to
investigate.
4. Significance of the study – Explain who may benefit from the
research and how.
This structure helps the reader follow the writer’s thinking smoothly and
logically.
16.1.3 Sentence-Level Introduction Template
To support students in writing confidently, the following sentence patterns can
be used as guiding frames, not as lines to memorize.
A. Background of the Study
The background introduces the context of the research.
Common sentence patterns include:
•
In recent years, there has been increasing concern about...
•
In Pakistan, this issue is particularly evident in...
•
Several initiatives have been introduced; however...
These sentences help situate the study within a real-world context.
B. Problem Statement
The problem statement highlights the gap or challenge that remains
unresolved.
Typical sentence patterns:
•
Despite these efforts, ... remains a significant challenge.
•
Previous studies have not adequately addressed...
This part should be specific and evidence-based, not emotional or opinionated.
C. Purpose of the Study
The purpose clearly states what the research will examine.
Useful sentence patterns:
•
The purpose of this study is to examine...
•
This study aims to investigate...
The purpose must align with the identified problem.
D. Significance of the Study
The significance explains why the research matters.
Common sentence patterns:
•
The findings of this study may contribute to...
•
This research is expected to support policymakers, educators, and
researchers by...
This section shows the practical or academic value of the study.
16.1.4 Annotated Pakistani Example
