Topic: Early Grade Reading in Public Schools
Sample Introduction Paragraph
In recent years, improving early grade reading outcomes has become a global
priority, as strong literacy skills form the foundation for later learning.
➡ Function: Global background
In Pakistan, however, national and provincial assessments continue to
indicate low reading proficiency among students in early primary grades,
particularly in public sector schools.
➡ Function: National context
Despite multiple initiatives such as teacher training programs, revised
curricula, and provision of reading materials, many Grade 2 and Grade 3
students are still unable to read age-appropriate texts fluently.
➡ Function: Problem identification
Previous studies have largely focused on enrollment and access, while limited
attention has been given to classroom-level teaching practices that influence
reading development.
➡ Function: Research gap
The purpose of this study is to examine the relationship between classroom
teaching practices and early grade reading outcomes in public primary
schools.
➡ Function: Purpose
The findings of this study may contribute to improving instructional strategies
and informing policy decisions aimed at strengthening foundational literacy
in Pakistan.
➡ Function: Significance
16.1.5 Common Pakistani Student Mistakes
Pakistani students frequently make the following errors when writing
introductions:
•
Writing dictionary definitions, such as defining “education” or
“learning,” instead of contextualizing the issue.
•
Providing long historical backgrounds that are not directly relevant
to the research problem.
•
Mixing objectives with results, such as stating findings in the
introduction before the study is conducted.
Avoiding these mistakes improves clarity and academic credibility.
16.1.6 Practice Task
Using the introduction template provided in this section, write a 150–200
word introduction on one of the following topics (or a topic from your own
discipline):
•
Teacher professional development in public schools
•
Use of digital learning tools in higher education
•
Student motivation in secondary schools
Follow the logical structure discussed above.
16.1.7 Self-Check Checklist
Before finalizing your introduction, ask yourself:
• Have I moved logically from general context to specific problem?
• Is the research problem clearly stated?
• Is the purpose of the study explicit and focused?
• Have I avoided mentioning results or conclusions?
If all boxes are checked, your introduction is academically sound and ready
for submission.
16.2 Literature Review Template
16.2.1 Purpose of the Literature Review
The literature review is one of the most challenging sections for Pakistani
students, not because of a lack of reading, but because of difficulty in
organizing and synthesizing existing research in English. Many students
mistakenly assume that the purpose of the literature review is to summarize
everything they have read. In reality, its purpose is far more focused and
strategic.
The literature review serves three key functions. First, it demonstrates that the

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
researcher is aware of existing studies related to the topic. This reassures the
reader and the examiner that the study is grounded in established academic
work rather than personal opinion. Second, it helps to position the current
study within previous research, showing how it relates to, builds upon, or
differs from earlier findings. Finally, and most importantly, the literature
review justifies the research gap by explaining what has not yet been
adequately studied, particularly within a specific context such as Pakistan.
A well-written literature review therefore does not merely list studies; it tells
a logical story that leads the reader naturally toward the need for the current
research.
16.2.2 Logical Structure of a Literature Review Paragraph
To avoid confusion and repetition, a literature review paragraph should follow
a clear and predictable structure. This structure helps students maintain focus
and coherence.
The paragraph should begin by introducing the theme or focus area. This
signals to the reader what aspect of the topic is being discussed. Next, the
paragraph should present relevant previous studies, highlighting key findings
rather than excessive details. After that, the writer should compare or contrast
these studies, showing similarities, differences, or trends across the research.
Finally, the paragraph should identify a gap by explaining what remains
unexplored, under-researched, or insufficiently addressed.
Following this sequence ensures that the paragraph moves logically from
existing knowledge to unanswered questions, which is the ultimate purpose of
academic research.
16.2.3 Sentence-Level Literature Review Template
To support students who struggle to begin writing, the following sentence
patterns can be used as flexible guides rather than rigid formulas.
When introducing the theme, students may use expressions such as:
•
Several studies have examined teacher professional development in
public school systems.
•
Research on teacher training has focused on instructional
improvement and student outcomes.
When citing previous studies, the focus should be on findings, not lengthy
descriptions:
•
According to Khan (2019), continuous professional development
improved teachers’ instructional practices.
•
A study conducted by Ali et al. (2021) found that regular mentoring
had a positive impact on classroom engagement.
To compare or contrast findings, linking words become essential:
•
Similarly, Ahmed (2020) reported improvements in lesson planning
skills.
•
However, these findings differ from those of Hussain (2018), who
found limited impact due to weak follow-up mechanisms.
Finally, to identify the research gap, students should clearly state what is
missing:
•
Despite these studies, little attention has been given to sustained
school-based coaching models.
•
There is limited research focusing on teacher professional
development within the Sindh context.
These sentence patterns help students express academic ideas confidently
while maintaining clarity and coherence.
6.2.4 Annotated Pakistani Example
(Topic: Teacher Professional Development in Sindh)
Several studies have examined the role of teacher professional development
in improving instructional quality in public schools. According to Khan
(2019), short-term training programs enhanced teachers’ subject knowledge
but had limited influence on classroom practices. Similarly, Ali et al. (2021)
found that mentoring-based professional development led to improved student
engagement and lesson delivery. However, Hussain (2018) reported that the
impact of training diminished over time due to the absence of continuous
support and monitoring. Despite these findings, little attention has been given
to the effectiveness of structured, district-level professional development
models in Sindh. As a result, there remains a need for research that examines
sustained and system-level approaches to teacher professional development in
this context.
Annotation:
•
First sentence introduces the theme
•
Middle sentences synthesize and compare studies
•
Final sentence clearly identifies the research gap in Sindh
16.2.5 Common Pakistani Student Mistakes
Pakistani students often struggle with the literature review due to predictable
but avoidable mistakes. One common issue is copy-paste without synthesis,
where paragraphs are lifted directly from sources with minor word changes.
Another frequent mistake is writing one study per paragraph, which results in
a descriptive list rather than a critical discussion. Additionally, many students
fail to include any comparison or evaluation, leaving the reader unsure how
the studies relate to one another or to the current research.
Recognizing these mistakes is the first step toward improving academic
writing quality.
16.2.6 Practice Task
Using at least three academic sources, write one synthesized literature review
paragraph (150–200 words) on a topic related to your field of study. Ensure
that your paragraph introduces the theme, integrates findings from multiple
studies, compares or contrasts the results, and clearly identifies a research gap
relevant to Pakistan.
16.2.7 Self-Check Checklist
Before moving to the next paragraph, ask yourself:
• Have I integrated multiple sources rather than summarizing them
separately?
• Have I used author names and years correctly?
• Have I clearly identified what is missing in existing research?
If all three boxes are checked, your literature review paragraph is academically
sound and ready for further development.
16.3 Findings Paragraph Template

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
The findings section is a critical component of any academic study, as it is the
point where evidence gathered through research is formally presented to the
reader. Unlike the discussion section, the purpose of the findings section is not
to explain, justify, or evaluate results, but to report them accurately and
objectively. For many Pakistani students, this distinction is difficult to
maintain, as there is a strong tendency to mix opinions, explanations, or
recommendations while presenting data. This section therefore focuses on
helping students develop the discipline of neutral reporting.
16.3.1 Purpose of the Findings Section
The primary purpose of the findings section is to present research results in a
clear, factual, and systematic manner. It guides the reader through tables,
charts, and figures by highlighting the most important numerical results
without adding personal interpretation. In the Pakistani academic context,
where exam-oriented writing is common, students often attempt to “explain”
results immediately. However, effective academic writing requires that
patterns be highlighted without attaching meaning or judgment at this stage.
In simple terms, the findings section answers the question: “What does the
data show?”—not “Why does this happen?”
16.3.2 Logical Structure of a Findings Paragraph
A well-written findings paragraph follows a predictable and logical structure
that helps the reader understand the data without confusion. The paragraph
typically begins by directing the reader to a specific table or figure, ensuring
transparency and traceability. This is followed by the key numerical result,
which draws attention to the most important data point. Next, the writer
identifies a pattern or trend evident in the data, such as increases, decreases,
or differences between groups. Finally, the paragraph ends with a neutral
explanatory sentence that summarizes what is visible in the data, without
offering reasons or conclusions.
This structure ensures clarity and prevents students from drifting into
interpretation or discussion prematurely.
16.3.3 Sentence-Level Findings Template
To support students in writing objectively, certain sentence patterns are
commonly used in academic findings sections.
When introducing a table or figure, writers typically use neutral, present-tense
constructions such as:
“Table 4.1 shows the percentage of...” or
“Figure 3 illustrates...”
These sentences serve as signposts, helping readers locate the evidence being
discussed.
To highlight key findings, writers then focus on the most important numerical
results using sentences such as:
“The results indicate that...” or’ “A majority of respondents (65%)
reported...” At this stage, only observable facts should be stated.
When describing trends or patterns, careful and cautious language is used, for
example: “An increasing trend can be observed...” or “A noticeable
difference exists between...”
These phrases allow students to comment on patterns without assigning causes
or value judgments.
16.3.4 Annotated Pakistani Example
Topic: Teacher Survey Results from Public Schools
Table 4.2 shows the percentage of public school teachers who reported
receiving subject-specific training during the past academic year.
→ (Reference to table)
The results indicate that 68% of teachers reported attending at least one
professional development session.
→ (Key numerical result)
In contrast, only 32% reported participating in more than three training
sessions during the same period.
→ (Comparison within data)
Overall, the data suggests a higher concentration of teachers receiving limited
training exposure rather than sustained professional development.
→ (Neutral summary of pattern, not interpretation)
This paragraph does not explain why training participation is low or whether
it is effective. Such explanations are reserved for the discussion section.
16.3.5 Common Pakistani Student Mistakes
One of the most frequent mistakes Pakistani students make in the findings
section is interpreting results instead of reporting them. Statements such as
“This shows that the government has failed” or “Teachers are not serious
about training” introduce judgment and must be avoided.
Another common issue is repeating numbers without explanation, where
students list percentages without guiding the reader toward the key pattern.
Academic writing requires synthesis, not data dumping.
Students also often use emotional or judgmental language, such as “poor
results,” “alarming situation,” or “very bad performance.” These
expressions weaken academic credibility and should be replaced with neutral,
evidence-based wording.
16.3.6 Practice Task
Using a provided data table (for example, student attendance rates or teacher
survey results), students should write one complete findings paragraph that:
•
Refers clearly to the table or figure
•
Highlights one key numerical result
•
Identifies a visible pattern or contrast
•
Avoids interpretation or explanation
16.3.7 Self-Check Checklist
Before finalizing a findings paragraph, students should ask themselves:
• Have I clearly referenced the correct table or figure?
• Have I reported the data without interpreting or explaining it?
• Have I used the correct tense (mostly present tense for tables and
figures)?
If all three boxes are checked, the paragraph is likely appropriate for the
findings section.
16.4 Discussion Paragraph Template
The discussion section is often the most challenging part of academic writing

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
for Pakistani students. While many students can describe results accurately,
they struggle to explain what those results mean, why they occurred, and how
they relate to existing research, particularly within the Pakistani context. This
section provides a clear, step-by-step approach to writing an effective
discussion paragraph that moves beyond description to analysis and
interpretation.
16.4.1 Purpose of the Discussion
The primary purpose of the discussion section is to interpret the findings of
the study rather than repeat them. In this section, the writer explains why
certain results occurred, connects these findings with previous research, and
highlights their significance for policy, practice, or further research.
For Pakistani students, the discussion is especially important because it
provides space to contextualize findings within local realities, such as resource
constraints, classroom conditions, cultural factors, or institutional practices. A
well-written discussion demonstrates not only language proficiency but also
critical academic thinking.
16.4.2 Logical Structure of a Discussion Paragraph
An effective discussion paragraph follows a clear and logical sequence. First,
the key finding is briefly restated to remind the reader of the result being
discussed. Next, the writer explains possible reasons for this finding, drawing
on contextual knowledge or theoretical perspectives. The paragraph then
compares the result with findings from previous studies, either supporting or
contrasting them. Finally, the discussion concludes with implications,
particularly those relevant to Pakistan.
This structure ensures that the paragraph moves logically from evidence →
explanation → comparison → implication, which is the hallmark of strong
academic writing.
16.4.3 Sentence-Level Discussion Template (Explained in Context)
To help students translate this logic into writing, the following sentence
patterns can be used as guides.
A. Restating the FindingThe discussion paragraph typically begins by
restating the main finding in neutral academic language. For example:
The findings of this study indicate that teachers who participated in
Continuous Professional Development (CPD) demonstrated improved use of
student-centered instructional strategies.
This sentence does not introduce new data; instead, it signals which result is
being interpreted.
B. Explaining the Result
After restating the finding, the writer explains why this result may have
occurred. Common sentence starters include:
This result may be explained by...
One possible reason for this finding is...
For instance:
This result may be explained by the practical nature of the CPD sessions,
which focused on classroom-based strategies rather than theoretical
instruction.
At this stage, explanations should be logical and grounded in context, not
personal opinion.
C. Linking to Literature
The next step is to connect the finding with previous research. This shows that
the student understands how their study fits within existing knowledge.
Examples include:
This finding is consistent with previous studies by...
However, it contrasts with earlier research which found...
For example:
This finding is consistent with previous studies which reported that ongoing
teacher coaching leads to improved classroom practices.
Or
However, it contrasts with earlier research which found limited impact of
short-term training programs.
D. Implications
Finally, the paragraph should explain why the finding matters. Implications
may relate to policy, practice, or future research. Common sentence starters
include:
These findings suggest that...
This has important implications for...
For example:
These findings suggest that sustained CPD initiatives are more effective than
one-time training workshops.
This has important implications for teacher professional development
programs in Pakistan, particularly in public-sector schools.
16.4.4 Annotated Pakistani Example: CPD Impact on Classroom
Practices
Sample Discussion Paragraph
The findings of this study indicate that teachers who participated regularly in
CPD activities demonstrated improved classroom practices, particularly in
the use of interactive teaching strategies. This result may be explained by the
continuous support and follow-up provided through coaching visits, which
allowed teachers to reflect on and improve their instructional methods. This
finding is consistent with previous studies that emphasize the role of sustained
professional development in improving teaching quality. However, it contrasts
with earlier research that reported limited impact of short-duration training
programs. These findings suggest that long-term, school-based CPD models
are more effective in the Pakistani context. This has important implications
for education policymakers and teacher training institutions seeking to
improve classroom instruction in public schools.
(Annotation: The paragraph restates the finding, explains the reason, links to
literature, and ends with clear implications for Pakistan.)
16.4.5 Common Pakistani Student Mistakes
Pakistani students frequently face difficulties in writing discussion paragraphs
due to several common issues. One frequent mistake is repeating the findings
without adding interpretation or explanation. Another common problem is
making unsupported claims, such as attributing results to causes without
evidence or logical reasoning. Additionally, many students fail to link their
discussion to the local context, writing in a generic manner that could apply to
any country rather than addressing Pakistani realities.
Avoiding these mistakes requires conscious attention to explanation,
evidence, and context.
16.4.6 Practice Task
Using the template and examples provided above, write one discussion

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
paragraph (150–200 words) based on a given finding from your own study
or a sample dataset. Ensure that your paragraph includes all four elements:
restating the finding, explaining the result, linking to previous research, and
discussing implications for Pakistan.
16.4.7 Self-Check Checklist
Before finalizing your discussion paragraph, review it using the following
checklist:
• Have I explained why the result occurred?
• Have I linked the finding to previous research?
• Have I clearly stated implications, particularly for Pakistan?
Chapter Summary
This chapter emphasizes that writing templates are guides rather than fixed
formulas. They are designed to support students in organizing their ideas
clearly, not to restrict academic thinking or creativity. Students are encouraged
to adapt the templates according to their discipline, research focus, and
academic context. With consistent practice and a clear structural framework,
students can gradually build confidence and develop independence in
academic writing.
Chapter 17: Final Checklist Before Submission
Chapter Overview
This chapter serves as a comprehensive pre-submission quality assurance
guide for undergraduate and postgraduate students. It is designed to help
students systematically review their thesis, dissertation, or research report
before final submission, with a specific focus on common weaknesses
observed in Pakistani universities.
Despite having strong research topics and relevant data, many students lose
marks—or are asked to revise or resubmit—due to avoidable issues such as
language inaccuracies, weak logical flow, plagiarism concerns, and noncompliance with HEC formatting guidelines. This chapter addresses these
challenges by offering a clear, step-by-step self-review framework that
enables students to critically evaluate their work from an examiner’s
perspective.
The chapter is organized around four key areas of academic quality: language
accuracy, logical coherence, academic integrity, and formatting compliance.
Through structured checklists and reflective questions, students are guided to
identify errors, make necessary corrections, and strengthen the overall clarity,
credibility, and presentation of their academic writing. By using this chapter
as a final audit tool, students can significantly improve the quality of their
submission and approach the evaluation process with greater confidence.
Learning Outcomes
After completing this chapter, students will be able to:
1. Evaluate the language quality of their academic writing by
identifying and correcting common grammatical, stylistic, and tenserelated errors.
2. Assess logical coherence and flow within and across chapters,
ensuring that arguments are clearly structured and aligned with
research questions and objectives.
3. Identify and address plagiarism risks by improving paraphrasing
skills, ensuring accurate citation, and reviewing similarity reports in
line with institutional policies.
4. Apply academic integrity principles consistently throughout their
work, demonstrating ethical research and writing practices.
5. Verify compliance with HEC-aligned formatting requirements,
including structure, headings, tables, figures, references, and
preliminary pages.
6. Conduct a systematic self-review of their thesis or research report
using a practical checklist approach before submission.
7. Submit their work with confidence, having minimized the risk of
avoidable revisions, examiner criticism, or formal rejection.
17.1 Language Accuracy Checklist
Language accuracy is often the first element noticed by examiners and one of
the most common reasons why otherwise strong research work receives low
grades or revision comments. In the Pakistani academic context, students
frequently demonstrate sound understanding of their research topic but
struggle to communicate their ideas clearly and accurately in English. This
section guides students through a systematic review of language accuracy,
focusing on clarity, grammar, tense use, and academic tone.
17.1.1 Clarity and Simplicity
Clear and simple language is a hallmark of effective academic writing.
Examiners do not reward complex vocabulary or lengthy sentences; instead,
they value precision, clarity, and ease of understanding. Students should
carefully review whether their sentences communicate ideas directly and
efficiently.
A common issue observed in Pakistani student writing is the tendency to
construct unnecessarily long and complex sentences, often by joining multiple
ideas with “and,” “which,” or “that.” Such sentences may appear sophisticated
but frequently confuse the reader and weaken the argument. Breaking long
sentences into shorter, well-structured ones improves both readability and
impact.
Another frequent problem is the direct translation of ideas from Urdu into
English. This often results in awkward sentence structures that sound
unnatural in academic English. For example, phrases such as “According to
my point of view” or “It is worth mentioning here that” are widely memorized
but rarely necessary. Instead of relying on memorized expressions, students
should focus on expressing ideas in their own words using straightforward
academic language.
Pakistani students also tend to overuse vague intensifiers such as “very,”
“many,” and “a lot.” In academic writing, such words add little meaning and
reduce precision. For instance, instead of writing “very many students faced a
lot of problems,” a clearer and more academic alternative would be “a large
proportion of students encountered significant challenges.”
Self-check question:
Are my sentences clear, concise, and free from unnecessary words or
memorized phrases?
17.1.2 Grammar and Sentence Structure

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
Grammatical accuracy plays a crucial role in establishing the credibility of
academic work. Errors in grammar can distract the reader and create doubt
about the overall quality of the research. Students should therefore review their
writing carefully for common grammatical issues.
One of the most frequent errors among Pakistani students is subject–verb
disagreement, particularly in longer sentences where the subject and verb are
separated. For example, “The results of the study shows...” should be
corrected to “The results of the study show...”. Reading sentences aloud can
often help identify such errors.
The correct use of articles (a, an, the) is another challenge, especially for
students whose first language does not use articles in the same way as English.
While perfection is difficult, consistency and awareness are essential. Students
should review whether they are introducing something for the first time (a
study, an approach) or referring to something specific (the study, the
approach).
Students should also check for sentence fragments and run-on sentences. A
sentence fragment occurs when a sentence lacks a subject or a main verb,
while a run-on sentence joins multiple complete ideas without proper
punctuation. Both issues reduce clarity and must be corrected before
submission.
Quick self-test: Can each sentence stand alone and make complete sense
without relying on the sentence before or after it?
17.1.3 Tense Consistency
Correct and consistent use of tense is essential in academic writing, as it helps
readers understand what is established knowledge, what was done in the study,
and what the findings suggest. Inconsistency in tense usage is a common
weakness in theses submitted at Pakistani universities.
As a general guideline, students should use the present tense when discussing
general facts, theories, and the overall purpose of the study, particularly in the
introduction. The literature review typically uses the past tense or present
perfect tense when referring to previous studies. The methodology and results
sections should be written primarily in the past tense, as they describe actions
and findings that have already occurred. In contrast, the discussion and
implications often shift back to the present tense and make use of modal verbs
such as may, might, and can to interpret results and suggest implications.
Students should carefully review each chapter to ensure that tense usage is
internally consistent and appropriate for the function of the section.
Checklist question: Have I reviewed tense usage separately for the
introduction, literature review, methodology, results, and discussion sections?
17.1.4 Academic Tone and Objectivity
Maintaining an appropriate academic tone is essential for presenting research
in a professional and credible manner. Academic writing should be formal,
objective, and evidence-based, avoiding conversational language and personal
opinions that are not supported by data.
Students should eliminate informal words and expressions such as “kids,”
“stuff,” “lots of,” or “a big issue.” These may be acceptable in everyday
conversation but weaken academic writing. Similarly, emotional or
opinionated statements such as “This is a very bad system” should be replaced
with evidence-based analysis, for example, “The findings indicate significant
systemic challenges.”
Effective academic writing also requires the use of hedging language to avoid
overgeneralization. Words such as may, might, appears to, and suggests allow
students to present interpretations cautiously and respectfully, which is
especially important in research conducted within complex social contexts
such as education, governance, or development in Pakistan.
Final reflection: Does my writing sound professional, balanced, and
supported by evidence rather than personal opinion?
17.2 Logic and Coherence Checklist
One of the most common reasons examiners raise concerns during thesis
evaluation is not weak data, but weak logic. In many Pakistani universities,
students conduct relevant research yet struggle to present their ideas in a clear,
connected, and convincing manner. Logic and coherence refer to how well
ideas are organized within paragraphs, how smoothly sections flow into one
another, and how consistently arguments are developed throughout the thesis
or research report.
This section guides students in reviewing their work to ensure that every
paragraph, section, and chapter contributes meaningfully to the overall
argument of the study.
17.2.1 Paragraph Structure
A well-written academic paragraph is not a collection of sentences; it is a
complete unit of meaning. Each paragraph should perform a clear function and
guide the reader logically from one idea to the next.
Every paragraph should contain four essential components:
1. A topic sentence that clearly states the main idea of the paragraph.
2. Supporting evidence, such as data, citations, or examples.
3. Explanation or interpretation of the evidence, showing why it is
important.
4. A link to the research question or objective, explicitly or implicitly.
Contextual example (Education research in Pakistan):
Weak paragraph:
Teachers face many problems in classrooms. There are large class sizes. Many
schools lack materials. Training is also limited.
Improved academic paragraph:
Large class sizes significantly affect teaching effectiveness in public primary

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
schools in Pakistan. Classroom observation data from Sindh indicate that
teachers managing classes of over 50 students struggle to provide individual
feedback. This limitation reduces opportunities for student engagement and
differentiated instruction, particularly in early grades. These findings directly
relate to the study’s research question on barriers to effective classroom
practices in government schools.
Self-check for students:
After writing a paragraph, ask yourself:
Can the topic sentence alone summarize what this paragraph is about?
If the answer is no, the paragraph needs revision.
17.2.2 Flow Between Sections
Academic writing should guide the reader smoothly, not force them to jump
between disconnected ideas. Poor flow often occurs when paragraphs are
written independently without considering how they connect to preceding and
following sections.
To ensure smooth flow:
•
Use logical connectors such as however, therefore, moreover, in
contrast, and as a result.
•
Begin paragraphs by briefly referencing the previous idea.
•
Avoid sudden shifts in topic without explanation.
Contextual example:
Abrupt transition:
Student attendance was low in rural schools. Teacher motivation is also an
important factor.
Improved transition:
While low student attendance remains a challenge in rural schools, teacher
motivation also plays a critical role in shaping classroom outcomes. Therefore,
the following section examines factors influencing teacher motivation in
underserved areas.
This approach signals to the reader why the discussion is moving forward and
how the ideas are connected.
17.2.3 Alignment with Research Questions
A coherent thesis maintains a clear alignment between research questions,
objectives, findings, and discussion. Examiners frequently note that Pakistani
students include interesting information that does not directly address their
stated research questions.
During final review, students should verify that:
•
Each chapter contributes directly to answering at least one research
question.
•
Results are explicitly linked to the stated objectives.
•
The discussion explains why the findings matter, particularly within
Pakistan’s social, educational, or institutional context.
Contextual example:
If a research question asks:
What factors influence early grade reading outcomes in Sindh?
Then the discussion should not end with:
Teachers require better training.
Instead, it should explain:
The findings suggest that limited access to reading materials, rather than
teacher training alone, is a major constraint in Sindh’s public schools. This
indicates that policy interventions must combine professional development
with classroom-level resource provision.
This directly answers the implicit examiner question: “So what does this
mean for Pakistan?”
17.2.4 Consistency of Argument
Consistency refers to the internal harmony of the thesis. A coherent academic
work does not contradict itself across chapters, nor does it make claims that
are unsupported by the research design or data.
Students should carefully review their work to ensure that:
•
Claims made in the discussion are supported by the findings.
•
The methodology is capable of answering the research questions
posed.
•
Conclusions do not introduce new ideas or evidence.
Contextual example:
Inconsistency:
•
Methodology: Survey of 60 teachers
•
Conclusion: The study proves national trends in teacher performance.
Improved consistency:
Based on the responses of 60 teachers from selected districts, the study
provides insights into localized teaching challenges rather than national-level
generalizations.
This demonstrates academic honesty and strengthens credibility.
Key Reflection for Students
Before submission, students should read their thesis as an examiner, asking:
•
Do the ideas build logically?
•
Does each section have a clear purpose?
•
Are conclusions firmly grounded in data?
A logically coherent thesis not only communicates research effectively but
also reflects academic maturity and critical thinking, qualities highly valued
by supervisors and examiners.
17.3 Plagiarism and Academic Integrity Checklist
Academic integrity is a fundamental requirement of higher education and
research. In Pakistani universities, concerns related to plagiarism are among
the most common reasons for thesis revision, delayed approval, or outright
rejection. Many students unintentionally violate academic integrity standards
due to limited training in academic writing, fear of English, or
misunderstanding of citation practices. This section guides students in
identifying plagiarism risks and ensuring ethical use of sources before
submission.
17.3.1 Understanding Plagiarism (Contextualized for Pakistan)
Plagiarism is not limited to intentional cheating; it often occurs unintentionally
when students are unaware of acceptable academic practices. In the Pakistani
context, the following forms of plagiarism are particularly common:
Copy-paste without citation
This occurs when students copy text directly from books, journal articles,
websites, or reports without acknowledging the original author. For example,
a student may copy a paragraph from an HEC report or an international journal
and insert it into the literature review without citation. Even if the source is
academic or publicly available, this practice constitutes plagiarism.
Poor paraphrasing
Many students attempt to avoid plagiarism by changing a few words while
keeping the original sentence structure intact. For instance, replacing
synonyms but retaining the same sentence order and logic still counts as
plagiarism. Examiners and plagiarism detection software can easily identify
such patterns.
Over-quoting

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
Excessive use of direct quotations, even when properly cited, weakens
academic writing. Pakistani students often rely heavily on quotations due to
lack of confidence in their own English. While limited quoting is acceptable,
academic work should primarily reflect the student’s own analytical voice.
Self-plagiarism (reusing previous assignments)
Reusing content from one’s own previously submitted assignments, research
proposals, or published work without acknowledgment is also considered
unethical. For example, copying parts of a BS or MA research project into an
MPhil thesis without citation may lead to serious academic consequences.
17.3.2 Citation and Referencing Accuracy
Accurate citation is essential for demonstrating scholarly honesty and
engagement with existing research. Before submission, students must
carefully cross-check citations and references.
Students should confirm that:
•
Every in-text citation appears in the reference list, and
•
Every entry in the reference list is cited at least once in the text.
A common error in Pakistani theses is the inclusion of long reference lists
copied from sample theses or supervisors’ documents, without corresponding
in-text citations. This raises serious academic integrity concerns.
Additionally, students must ensure that the correct referencing style is used
consistently throughout the document. Most Pakistani universities require
APA style, as recommended by HEC, though some institutions specify
alternatives. Mixing styles (e.g., APA and Harvard) within the same thesis
should be avoided.
17.3.3 Paraphrasing Quality Check
Effective paraphrasing demonstrates both understanding and academic
maturity. Before submission, students should critically evaluate the quality of
their paraphrasing.
A strong paraphrase:
•
Rewrites ideas in the student’s own academic voice
•
Changes sentence structure, not just vocabulary
•
Preserves the original meaning accurately without distortion
For example, instead of rewriting an author’s sentence word by word, the
student should first understand the idea, then explain it as if teaching it to
another reader. Paraphrasing should reflect comprehension, not mechanical
rewriting.
A useful self-check question is:
“Could I explain this idea orally without looking at the original source?”
If the answer is no, the paraphrase likely needs revision.
17.3.4 Turnitin / Similarity Report Review
Most Pakistani universities require submission of a Turnitin similarity report
prior to final approval. Students should treat this report as a diagnostic tool,
not merely a formality.
Before submission, students should ensure that:
•
The similarity index falls within the acceptable range set by the
university or HEC
•
The following sections are excluded, where permitted:
o Reference list
o Direct quotations
o Standard methodology descriptions or templates (if allowed by
policy)
High similarity percentages often result from poorly paraphrased literature
review sections or copied definitions in the introduction. These sections
should be revised manually, rather than relying on software exclusions alone.
Students should carefully examine the similarity report to identify problematic
areas and rewrite them in original academic language. Simply reducing the
percentage without improving originality may still lead to examiner
objections.
By carefully reviewing plagiarism and academic integrity issues before
submission, students protect their academic credibility and reduce the risk of
penalties, delays, or rejection. Ethical writing is not only a requirement for
degree completion but also a foundation for responsible research and
professional scholarship.
17.4 Formatting Checklist (HEC-Aligned)
Formatting is often treated by students as a minor or purely technical
requirement; however, in academic evaluation, formatting plays a critical role
in shaping the examiner’s first impression. In Pakistani universities, a
significant number of theses and research reports are returned for revision—
not because of weak research—but due to non-compliance with HEC or
university formatting guidelines. This section guides students through the
essential formatting elements that must be reviewed carefully before final
submission.
17.4.1 General Document Formatting
The first step in formatting review is to ensure that the overall document layout
complies with HEC-aligned standards. Most Pakistani universities require the
thesis to be prepared on A4 page size, and students should confirm that this
setting has been applied consistently throughout the document, including
appendices.
Margins must be set according to HEC or departmental guidelines, typically
allowing sufficient space for binding and examiner comments. A common
mistake observed among students is applying margins correctly at the
beginning but unintentionally altering them in later chapters due to copied
tables, figures, or formatting changes.
Consistency in font type and font size is another critical requirement.
Academic writing demands uniformity; therefore, students should avoid
mixing fonts or sizes within the same document. For example, a thesis written
partly in Times New Roman and partly in Calibri creates a visually
unprofessional impression, even if the content is strong.
Line spacing should also be reviewed carefully. In most HEC-aligned formats,
1.5 line spacing is required for the main text, while single spacing may be
permitted in tables, figures, or footnotes. Students often overlook spacing
issues after inserting long quotations or tables, which can result in inconsistent
presentation.
17.4.2 Chapter and Heading Structure

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
A well-formatted thesis demonstrates a clear and logical structure, beginning
with properly numbered chapters. Each chapter title should be clearly labeled
(e.g., Chapter 1: Introduction, Chapter 2: Literature Review) and formatted
consistently throughout the document.
Headings and subheadings must follow a logical hierarchy. For example, a
Level 2 heading should never appear before a Level 1 heading, and formatting
styles (bold, font size, numbering) should remain consistent. A common
formatting error among Pakistani students is skipping heading levels or
manually changing font sizes instead of using built-in heading styles.
Such inconsistencies confuse examiners and suggest a lack of attention to
academic conventions. Students are strongly encouraged to use wordprocessing tools (such as automatic heading styles) to maintain structural
consistency and ensure smooth navigation through the document.
17.4.3 Tables, Figures, and Appendices
Tables and figures play an important role in presenting data clearly, especially
in quantitative and mixed-methods research. Each table and figure must be
numbered sequentially according to its chapter (e.g., Table 4.1, Figure 5.2),
and the numbering should remain consistent throughout the thesis.
Titles must be placed correctly: table titles are usually placed above the table,
while figure titles appear below the figure. This distinction is frequently
overlooked by students, leading to formatting remarks from examiners.
Where data has been adapted or sourced from previous studies, proper source
acknowledgment is mandatory. Even when data is self-generated, clarity in
labeling and presentation is essential. Additionally, every table and figure
included in the document must be explicitly referred to in the text, such as “As
shown in Table 3.2...” Failure to reference tables or figures suggests poor
integration of data into the analysis.
Appendices should also be clearly labeled (e.g., Appendix A, Appendix B)
and referred to at relevant points in the main text.
17.4.4 Front Matter (Preliminary Pages)
The preliminary section of the thesis, often referred to as the front matter, must
strictly follow HEC-approved formats. The title page should include all
required information, such as the thesis title, student name, registration
number, degree program, department, university name, and year of
submission.
Most Pakistani universities also require additional pages, such as a declaration
of originality, supervisor’s certificate, and plagiarism undertaking. Missing or
incorrectly formatted preliminary pages can delay thesis acceptance, even
when the main chapters are complete.
The abstract must remain within the prescribed word limit and should
accurately summarize the study’s purpose, methodology, key findings, and
implications. Students frequently exceed word limits or include unnecessary
details, which should be avoided.
The table of contents should be auto-generated rather than typed manually. An
auto-generated table ensures accurate page numbering and reflects changes
made during final revisions, reducing the risk of mismatches.
17.4.5 References and Appendices
The reference list must be formatted consistently and accurately, following the
required referencing style (commonly APA in Pakistani universities). All
entries should be arranged in alphabetical order, and formatting elements such
as italics, punctuation, and capitalization must be applied uniformly.
A frequent issue observed among students is inconsistency between in-text
citations and the reference list. Students should verify that every source cited
in the text appears in the reference list and vice versa.
Appendices should be properly labeled and clearly linked to the main text. For
example, a questionnaire discussed in the methodology chapter should be
included as an appendix and referred to explicitly. Appendices should support
the research without overwhelming the main document.
By carefully reviewing formatting elements outlined in this section, students
can ensure that their work meets HEC-aligned presentation standards,
enhances readability, and reflects academic professionalism. Proper
formatting not only improves the visual quality of the thesis but also signals
the student’s seriousness, discipline, and respect for academic conventions—
qualities that are highly valued by examiners.
17.5 Final Pre-Submission Self-Audit
The final stage before submitting a thesis or research report is not about adding
new content; rather, it is about ensuring clarity, completeness, and confidence.
At this point, students must shift their mindset from writer to evaluator and
conduct a deliberate self-audit of their work. This section introduces three
critical self-checks that help students avoid last-minute errors and strengthen
their readiness for submission and viva voce examination.
17.5.1 The One-Day Rule
One of the most effective yet often ignored academic writing strategies is
allowing the thesis to “rest” before the final review. Students are strongly
advised to leave their document untouched for at least 24 hours after
completing revisions. This short break creates cognitive distance, enabling the
writer to approach the text with fresh eyes.
For example, a student who has been repeatedly revising a chapter on teacher
professional development in Sindh may overlook unclear sentences or logical
gaps simply because of over-familiarity with the text. After a day’s break, the
same student is more likely to notice awkward phrasing, missing transitions,
or repetitive arguments during the final read.

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
During this final review, students should read the thesis as a reader, not as the
writer. This means asking questions such as: Is this idea clear without prior
explanation? Does this paragraph logically follow the previous one? Would
an external examiner understand this argument without additional
clarification? Reading aloud, or reading selected sections in printed form, can
further help identify errors that are often missed on screen.
17.5.2 Supervisor’s Feedback Integration
A common reason for delayed submission or negative examiner comments is
incomplete or selective incorporation of supervisor feedback. Before
submission, students must ensure that every comment, suggestion, or query
provided by the supervisor has been addressed.
For instance, if a supervisor has asked a student to clarify the sampling strategy
in a study conducted in government schools, simply editing the language
without strengthening the explanation may be insufficient. The student should
revisit the methodology section and ensure that the sampling process is clearly
explained, justified, and aligned with the research objectives.
Where required by the institution, changes should be clearly highlighted or
tracked using tools such as “Track Changes” or color coding. This allows
supervisors and reviewers to quickly verify that feedback has been acted upon.
Most importantly, there should be no unresolved comments or questions
remaining in the document. A thesis that contains unanswered supervisor
queries signals poor academic discipline and may raise concerns during
evaluation.
17.5.3 Final Confidence Check
The final self-audit is a test of academic ownership and confidence. Before
submission, students should honestly assess whether they are prepared to
defend their work in an oral examination.
First, students should ask themselves whether they can explain each chapter
orally without relying on the written text. For example, can they clearly
describe why a particular research method was chosen, or how the findings
contribute to existing knowledge in Pakistan’s context?
Second, students must ensure that they fully understand every citation used in
the thesis. Examiners often ask questions such as, “Why did you use this
study?” or “How does this reference support your argument?” Inability to
answer such questions suggests superficial engagement with the literature.
Finally, students should reflect on their readiness for a viva voce examination.
This includes the ability to justify research decisions, explain limitations, and
respond thoughtfully to critical questions. If a student feels confident
discussing their work without hesitation, it is a strong indicator that the thesis
is ready for submission.
The Final Pre-Submission Self-Audit is not a formality; it is a critical
academic practice that distinguishes a rushed submission from a well-prepared
scholarly work. By applying the One-Day Rule, systematically integrating
supervisor feedback, and conducting an honest confidence check, students
significantly increase their chances of successful evaluation and smooth
progression toward degree completion.
End-of-Chapter Tools
This chapter concludes with two practical tools designed to support students
during the most critical stage of their academic journey—the final submission
of a thesis or research report. These tools are intended not merely as checklists,
but as reflective quality-control mechanisms that help students view their work
through the lens of an examiner or supervisor.
Final Submission Checklist
Before submitting their work, students are strongly encouraged to conduct a
final, systematic review using a one-page submission checklist. This checklist
is structured around four essential dimensions of academic quality: language,
logic, plagiarism, and formatting. Addressing each of these areas carefully can
significantly reduce the likelihood of revisions or rejection.
From a language perspective, students should ensure that their writing is clear,
grammatically accurate, and appropriate for an academic audience. In the
Pakistani context, many students select strong and relevant research topics—
such as education reform, youth employment, or public health—but lose
marks due to unclear sentence structure, inconsistent tense usage, or
overreliance on memorized phrases. A final language check allows students to
simplify complex sentences, correct grammatical errors, and ensure
consistency across chapters.
The logic checklist focuses on the coherence and flow of ideas throughout the
document. Examiners frequently note that while individual sections may be
well written, the overall argument lacks continuity. For example, research
questions may be clearly stated in Chapter One, but the findings or discussion
chapters fail to respond directly to them. By reviewing logic and coherence,
students can confirm that each chapter contributes meaningfully to the central
argument and that conclusions are firmly grounded in the presented data.
The plagiarism review is particularly important in Pakistani universities,
where similarity reports are strictly monitored. Students should not rely solely
on software-generated similarity percentages; instead, they should manually
review highlighted sections to ensure proper paraphrasing and accurate
citation. Even when sources are cited, poor paraphrasing can raise academic
integrity concerns. A careful plagiarism check ensures that the work reflects
the student’s own academic voice while appropriately acknowledging existing
research.
Finally, the formatting checklist ensures compliance with HEC-aligned

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
guidelines and institutional requirements. Issues such as incorrect margins,
inconsistent headings, improperly labeled tables, or incorrectly formatted
references can negatively influence examiners’ first impressions. Since
formatting errors are easy to avoid, a final review of layout and structure is an
essential step toward a professional submission.
When used together, these four checklist areas function as a final academic
audit, allowing students to submit their work with confidence and credibility.
Common Rejection Reasons (Pakistan-Specific)
Understanding why theses and research reports are commonly rejected or
returned for major revisions can help students avoid repeating the same
mistakes. In the Pakistani higher education context, examiners consistently
report a small number of recurring issues.
One of the most frequent reasons for rejection is poor language despite a strong
research topic. Many students invest significant effort in selecting relevant and
socially important topics, yet weak English expression obscures their ideas. In
such cases, examiners struggle to understand the argument, regardless of the
quality of the data or analysis.
Another common issue is a weak discussion section. Students often
summarize findings without interpreting them or linking them back to research
questions, objectives, or existing literature. A discussion that merely repeats
results, without explaining their significance in the Pakistani context, is
viewed as academically insufficient.
A high similarity index is also a major cause of rejection or delayed
submission. This problem often arises not from intentional misconduct, but
from limited paraphrasing skills or excessive dependence on published texts.
Universities increasingly enforce strict similarity thresholds, making it
essential for students to address this issue proactively.
Finally, formatting non-compliance remains a surprisingly common reason for
resubmission. Even when the research content is sound, failure to follow HEC
or university-specific formatting guidelines can result in unnecessary delays.
Examiners and administrative offices expect theses to meet formal
requirements as a basic academic standard.
Students who use the final submission checklist and reflect on common
rejection reasons place themselves in a much stronger position to succeed.
These tools transform submission from a stressful, last-minute task into a
deliberate, informed, and professional process, reinforcing the habits of
quality, responsibility, and academic integrity expected at the university level.
Annexure A: Sample Annotated Thesis Pages
Sample Page 1: Annotated Introduction (Background of the Study)
Student Text (Model Paragraph)
Reading proficiency at the early grade level is a foundational skill that
significantly influences students’ later academic achievement. In Pakistan,
despite increased enrollment rates in primary education, learning outcomes—
particularly in reading—remain below expected benchmarks. Provincial
assessments conducted in recent years indicate that a large proportion of Grade
3 students are unable to read age-appropriate texts with fluency. These
findings highlight a persistent gap between access to schooling and quality of
learning, suggesting the need for focused instructional and policy-level
interventions.
Annotations (For Students)
Why this paragraph works
✔ Starts broad, then narrows
→ Begins with a general concept (reading proficiency) before
moving to Pakistan.
✔ Uses present tense correctly
→ General facts: “is,” “influences,” “remain”
✔ Avoids emotional language
No words like very poor, extremely bad, disastrous
✔ Uses local context
→ Mentions Pakistan and provincial assessments
✔ Does NOT cite yet
→ Background paragraph can introduce context before heavy citation
Common Student Mistake (Contrast Example)
Reading is very important for students. Many students in Pakistan are very
weak in reading. This is a big problem and the government should take steps.
Why this is weak
•
Opinion-based
•
No academic tone
•
No evidence
•
Too general
Sample Page 2: Annotated Literature Review Paragraph
Student Text (Model Paragraph)
Several studies have examined factors influencing early grade reading
outcomes in developing contexts. International research suggests that
structured phonics instruction plays a critical role in improving reading
fluency among young learners. However, studies conducted in Pakistani
public schools indicate that instructional quality and teacher preparedness
remain significant challenges. For instance, provincial-level assessments have
reported limited classroom-level support for reading instruction, particularly
in rural schools. These findings suggest that while instructional approaches
are important, their effectiveness is strongly shaped by local implementation
capacity.
Annotations
Source use
•
✔ Combines international research + local studies
•
✔ Does NOT list studies one by one
•
✔ Synthesizes ideas around a theme
Language features
•
“suggests,” “indicate,” “remain” → cautious academic tone
•
No long quotations
•
Student’s voice is dominant
What examiners like
•
Analytical thinking
•
Context awareness
•
Balanced literature use
Common Pakistani Student Error
According to Smith (2018), phonics is very effective. According to John
(2019), phonics is very useful. According to Ali (2020), phonics helps
students.
Why this fails
•
Source dumping
•
No analysis
•
No local context
Sample Page 3: Annotated Methodology Section
Student Text (Model Paragraph)
This study employed a descriptive survey design to examine reading practices
in government primary schools. Data were collected from 120 Grade 3

title: Academic-Writing-Made-Simple
text:
students and 15 teachers across five public schools in a rural district of Sindh.
Reading fluency was assessed using a standardized reading tool, while teacher
practices were documented through structured classroom observations. The
collected data were analyzed using descriptive statistics to identify prevailing
patterns in instructional practices.
Annotations
Tense usage
•
✔ Past tense used correctly (employed, were collected, were analyzed)
Clarity
•
Who? → students & teachers
•
Where? → rural Sindh
•
How? → survey, assessment, observation
No unnecessary theory
•
Method is explained simply
•
No decorative language
Sample Page 4: Annotated Findings Paragraph
Student Text (Model Paragraph)
The results revealed that only 38 percent of the assessed students were able to
read the Grade 3 level text with acceptable fluency. As shown in Table 4.2,
the majority of students struggled with word recognition and reading speed.
Teachers reported limited time for focused reading instruction due to large
class sizes and curriculum demands. These findings indicate a mismatch
between curricular expectations and classroom realities.
Annotations
Good practice
•
Refers to table without repeating numbers excessively
•
Interprets results instead of only reporting
Academic tone
•
“revealed,” “indicate”
•
No emotional judgment
Sample Page 5: Annotated Discussion Paragraph
Student Text (Model Paragraph)
The findings of this study are consistent with earlier research conducted in
Pakistani public schools, which highlights the role of instructional constraints
in shaping learning outcomes. While international studies emphasize
structured reading programs, the present findings suggest that such
interventions may have limited impact without parallel investments in teacher
support. This discrepancy underscores the importance of contextual adaptation
when applying international models within local education systems.
Annotations
High-level academic writing
•
Compares findings with literature
•
Explains why differences exist
•
Shows independent thinking
✔ This is the level expected in MPhil / MSc / strong BS theses
Sample Page 6: Final Checklist Annotation (For Students)
Before submitting, ask yourself:
✔ Is my voice stronger than my sources?
✔ Have I explained every citation?
✔ Have I used local research where relevant?
✔ Can I explain each paragraph without reading it?
If the answer is yes, your thesis is on the right track.
